# Generated TypeScript

ktor-svelte reads your Ktor routes and DTOs and writes a typed TypeScript client for them: types, one function per route, validation helpers and a few small utilities, with no npm dependencies. Change a field in Kotlin, and the frontend code that uses it stops compiling.

<Badge type="tip" text="Ktor plugin" /> <Badge type="info" text="Gradle" /> <Badge type="warning" text="Generated client" />

## Quick start

Turn it on in `install(Svelte)`:

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    generateTs = true
}
```

Start the app in development mode, and call your routes from the frontend:

```ts
import { api } from '#api';

const notes = await api.notes.list({ search: 'milk' });
const note = await api.notes.get(notes[0].id);
```

To see the output for your own API before installing anything, paste its OpenAPI document into the [generator playground](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/playground).

## What you get

| You write in Kotlin | You get in TypeScript | Section |
|---|---|---|
| A route | A typed function, such as `api.notes.list()` | [Service names](#service-names) |
| A `@Serializable` class | An interface, `empty()`, and `bounds` and `validate()` where it has rules | [Types and forms](#types-and-forms) |
| An enum | A `const` object and a type of the same name | [Enums](#enums) |
| `LocalDate`, `Instant`, ... | `IsoDate`, `IsoDateTime`, ... with helpers | [Dates](#dates) |
| `describe { summary }`, `@JsonSchema.Description` | JSDoc in the editor | [Documentation in the editor](#documentation-in-the-editor) |
| An object passed to `constants()` | The same values in `constants.ts` | [Shared constants](#shared-constants) |
| A value class | A branded type that cannot be mixed up | [IDs that cannot be mixed up](#ids-that-cannot-be-mixed-up) |
| `Decimal`, `Duration` | `Decimal`, `IsoDuration` with exact helpers | [Money and durations](#money-and-durations) |
| A sealed class | A union with an exhaustive `match` | [Sealed classes](#sealed-classes) |
| `resource<Note, Int>(...)` | `list`, `get`, `create`, `update`, `delete` | [Resource routes](#resource-routes) |

How to call the functions, handle errors, retry, stream and upload is on [Calling the API](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/calling-the-api).

## The generated files

Each time the app starts in development mode, ktor-svelte reads your routing tree, builds an OpenAPI document and writes this to `frontend/src/lib/api`:

| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| `types.ts` | An interface or union for every schema, an `empty()` factory for every object, `bounds` and `validate()` where the schema has constraints, a `const` object for every enum, and date types |
| `services.ts` | One object per resource, such as `api.notes.list()` |
| `client.ts` | The small `fetch` wrapper, `ApiError` and `apiConfig` |
| `index.ts` | Re-exports all of the above |
| `openapi.json` | The OpenAPI document itself |
| `.gitattributes` | Marks these files as generated and keeps their line endings the same on every machine, so Git on Windows does not warn about them and GitHub folds them in diffs |

Depending on what you use, a few more files appear next to them, such as `constants.ts` for [shared constants](#shared-constants) and `form-state.svelte.ts` for the [form helper](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/validation#form-state).

| Setting in `install(Svelte)` | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `generateTs` | `false` | Writes the client each time the app starts in development mode |
| `generateTsOutput` | `null` | Output directory. `null` means `src/lib/api` in your frontend |

### Commit the files

Commit these files. That way a frontend build never needs your app to run first.

- Unchanged files are not rewritten, so Vite does not reload for nothing.
- Nothing is generated in production.
- To refresh the files without your dev server, for example in CI, run the task below and check for a diff. It starts your app once, so the app's port must be free.

```bash
./gradlew svelteGenerateTs
```

### Keeping it in sync

With the `application` plugin, `check` runs `svelteVerifyTs`. It starts your app once, generates the TypeScript in memory and fails if the committed files differ, so a changed DTO or route can't drift away from the frontend unnoticed.

- Line endings are ignored.
- It passes when `generateTs` is off.
- To fix a failure, run `svelteGenerateTs`, or start the app in development mode, and commit the result.
- To leave it out of `check`, set `svelte.verifyTs=false` in `gradle.properties` or pass `-Psvelte.verifyTs=false`.

### The #api import

`svelteInit` also sets up the short `#api` import. For a frontend you already have, add it to `frontend/package.json`:

```json
{
  "imports": {
    "#api": "./src/lib/api/index.ts"
  }
}
```

## Service names

Every route becomes a function on `api`, grouped by resource. The names follow your routes:

| Route | Function |
|---|---|
| `GET /api/notes` | `api.notes.list()` |
| `GET /api/notes/{id}` | `api.notes.get(id)` |
| `POST /api/notes` | `api.notes.create(body)` |
| `PUT /api/notes/{id}` | `api.notes.update(id, body)` |
| `DELETE /api/notes/{id}` | `api.notes.delete(id)` |
| `POST /api/notes/{id}/archive` | `api.notes.archive(id)` |

Set `operationId` in `describe` to choose your own name.

A function takes its arguments in this order: the path parameters, the body, the query, and last the [request options](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/calling-the-api#request-options). Every function is also exported on its own, named after its group and service, such as `notesList` or `notesGet`, so a page can [import only what it uses](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/calling-the-api#import-single-functions).

## Typed path parameters

A path parameter is typed from the route's description. A [resource](#resource-routes) describes its id for you, so `api.notes.get` takes a `number` there. A parameter without a described type accepts `string | number`.

On the server, `call.pathParameter<T>(name)` reads a path parameter in the type you ask for:

```kotlin
get("/api/notes/{id}/summary") {
    val id = call.pathParameter<Int>("id")
    call.respondText("Note $id")
}
```

| Type | Accepts |
|---|---|
| `String` | Any text |
| `Int`, `Long` | A whole number that fits the type |
| `java.util.UUID` | A UUID in its usual 36 character form |
| An enum | One of its names, in any letter case |

- A value that does not fit, such as `/api/notes/abc`, is answered with 404 before the route does any work, because nothing is at that address.
- Asking for a name the path does not have, or for another type such as `Double`, is a mistake in the route and fails with a 500.

To give the generated function the exact type, describe the parameter:

```kotlin
get("/api/notes/{id}/summary") {
    call.respondText("Note ${call.pathParameter<Int>("id")}")
}.describe {
    parameters { path("id") { schema = jsonSchema<Int>() } }
}
```

## Typed request headers

A route that reads a header can say so, and the generated function then takes it as a typed argument instead of a loose `headers` object you have to remember:

```kotlin
get("/api/reports") {
    val tenant = call.request.headers["X-Tenant"] ?: return@get call.respond(HttpStatusCode.BadRequest)
    call.respond(listOf("Report for $tenant"))
}.describe {
    parameters {
        header("X-Tenant") { required = true }
        header("X-Report-Rows") { schema = jsonSchema<Int>() }
    }
}
```

```ts
import { api } from '#api';

const reports = await api.reports.list({ 'X-Tenant': 'acme', 'X-Report-Rows': 50 });
```

| In `describe` | In the generated function |
| --- | --- |
| `header("X-Tenant") { required = true }` | `headers: { 'X-Tenant': string }`, required |
| `header("X-Report-Rows") { schema = jsonSchema<Int>() }` | `'X-Report-Rows'?: number`, optional |
| Only optional headers | The whole `headers` argument is optional |

- The argument comes after the path parameters, the body and `query`, and before `options`.
- Values are sent as text; a header you leave `undefined` is not sent.
- Headers in `options.headers` win over the typed ones, so one call can still override a value.
- Headers the client sets by itself are left out of the argument even if a route lists them: `Accept`, `Content-Type`, `Content-Length`, `Cookie`, `X-Request-Id`, `Idempotency-Key` and `X-Time-Zone`.
- Headers that every call needs, such as `Authorization`, still belong in `apiConfig.headers`.

## Types and forms

### Empty objects

Every object type gets an `empty()` factory, handy as the initial state of a form:

```ts
import { NoteInput } from '#api';

let draft = $state(NoteInput.empty());
```

Every property is filled in, optional ones included:

| Property | Starts as |
|---|---|
| Text | `''` |
| Number | `0` |
| Boolean | `false` |
| List | `[]` |
| Map | `{}` |
| Nullable | `null` |
| Enum | Its first value |
| Nested object | Its own `empty()` |

Each call returns a fresh object.

### Bounds for inputs

Properties with [validation annotations](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/validation) also appear under `bounds`, named like the HTML attributes, so you can spread them onto an input:

```svelte
<input bind:value={draft.title} {...NoteInput.bounds.title} />
```

- Strings get `minlength`, `maxlength` and `pattern`, numbers get `min` and `max`.
- A strict bound on an integer moves by one, and on a decimal it is left out, because HTML has no strict bounds.
- The browser matches `pattern` against the whole value, while the server only looks for a match inside it, so write patterns with `^` and `$` to get the same result in both.

`required: true` is added only where the server would reject an empty field too, so the browser is never stricter than the server: strings with a minimum length of at least 1, and numbers that are required and not nullable, because an empty number input gives `null`. Nullable properties, booleans, lists, objects and enums never get it. A property with only `required` still gets a `bounds` entry.

#### Autocomplete and input types from names

Text properties whose names say what they hold also get `autocomplete`, and where it helps a `type`, so browsers and password managers fill them in and phones show the right keyboard. You write nothing:

| Property names (any case, `_` and `-` ignored) | `autocomplete` | `type` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `email`, `emailAddress`, `mail` | `email` | `email` |
| `password`, `currentPassword` | `current-password` | `password` |
| `newPassword`, `repeatPassword`, `confirmPassword`, `passwordRepeat`, `passwordConfirmation` | `new-password` | `password` |
| `name`, `fullName`, `displayName` | `name` | |
| `givenName`, `firstName`, `forename` | `given-name` | |
| `familyName`, `lastName`, `surname` | `family-name` | |
| `username`, `login`, `loginName` | `username` | |
| `phone`, `phoneNumber`, `tel`, `telephone`, `mobile`, `mobilePhone` | `tel` | `tel` |
| `street`, `streetAddress`, `address`, `addressLine` | `street-address` | |
| `postalCode`, `postcode`, `zip`, `zipCode` | `postal-code` | |
| `city`, `town`, `locality` | `address-level2` | |
| `country`, `countryName` | `country-name` | |
| `organization`, `organisation`, `company` | `organization` | |
| `birthday`, `birthdate`, `dateOfBirth` | `bday` | |
| `url`, `website`, `homepage` | `url` | `url` |
| `oneTimeCode`, `otp`, `verificationCode` | `one-time-code` | |

[Rule presets](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/validation#ready-made-rules) add the same: `@Rule.Email` gives `email`, `@Rule.WebAddress` `url`, `@Rule.Phone` `tel`, and `@Rule.StrongPassword` `new-password` with `type: 'password'`, whatever the property is called. A preset wins over the name, so a `password` with `@Rule.StrongPassword` is a new password.

- `use:field` and the generated components only add `autocomplete` and `type` when the input does not set its own, so `<Field autocomplete="username" ...>` keeps yours.
- `type` is only set on `<input>`, never on a `<textarea>` or `<select>`.
- Only text properties get hints; a `homepageVisits: Int` gets none.

### Checking in the browser

Every object type that the server checks against annotations, directly or through a nested object or list, also gets `validate()`. It runs the same checks in the browser and returns errors in the same shape as `fields` of a 422:

- the same messages, and paths such as `lines[1].sku`
- `Required.` for an empty required number
- an empty object when the value is valid

Types without annotations get no `validate()`, just as the server skips them. One error display then covers both instant feedback and the server answer:

```svelte
<script lang="ts">
    import { api, isValidationError, NoteInput } from '#api';

    let draft = $state(NoteInput.empty());
    let errors = $state<Record<string, string[]>>({});

    async function save(event: SubmitEvent) {
        event.preventDefault();
        errors = NoteInput.validate(draft);
        if (Object.keys(errors).length > 0) return;
        try {
            await api.notes.create(draft);
        } catch (error) {
            if (!isValidationError(error)) throw error;
            errors = error.body.fields;
        }
    }
</script>

<form onsubmit={save}>
    <input bind:value={draft.title} oninput={() => (errors = NoteInput.validate(draft))} {...NoteInput.bounds.title} />
    {#if errors.title}<p role="alert">{errors.title.join(' ')}</p>{/if}
</form>
```

Rules in `Validated.rules()` and in `validate { }` inside a route only run on the server, so their errors arrive with the 422. See [Validation](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/validation) for the rules themselves, and for `formState`, which does this bookkeeping for you.

### Read-only fields

Fields the server fills in, such as an ID or a creation time, are marked with Ktor's `@JsonSchema.ReadOnly`. They become `readonly` in TypeScript, and the generated functions that send the class leave them out:

```kotlin
import io.ktor.openapi.JsonSchema

@Serializable
data class Ticket(
    @JsonSchema.ReadOnly val id: Long = 0,
    val title: String,
    @JsonSchema.ReadOnly val createdAt: String = "",
)
```

```ts
export interface Ticket {
    readonly id: number;
    title: string;
    readonly createdAt?: string;
}

export const ticketsCreate = (body: Omit<Ticket, 'id' | 'createdAt'>, options?: RequestOptions) => ...
```

- A call that sends a `Ticket` takes `Omit<Ticket, 'id' | 'createdAt'>`, so you cannot pass an ID by mistake, and a whole record you edited can still be passed: the client takes the read-only fields out of the body before it is sent. Your object is not changed.
- Give read-only fields a default in Kotlin, as above, so `call.receive<Ticket>()` works on a body without them, and set the real values on the server.
- Only the fields of the class that is the body itself are left out, not those of nested classes, lists or upload forms.

### Created and updated stamps

Most records want to know when they were made and changed, and by whom. `Stamps` is a small ready type for that, filled on the server and typed on the client:

```kotlin
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.Stamps
import io.ktor.openapi.JsonSchema

@Serializable
data class Article(
    val title: String,
    @JsonSchema.ReadOnly val stamps: Stamps? = null,
)

fun newArticle(title: String, author: String): Article {
    return Article(title, Stamps.created(by = author))
}

fun renamed(article: Article, title: String, editor: String): Article {
    return article.copy(title = title, stamps = article.stamps?.touched(by = editor))
}
```

| Field | Set by | Type in TypeScript |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `createdAt` | `Stamps.created()` | `IsoDateTime` |
| `updatedAt` | `Stamps.created()`, then every `touched()` | `IsoDateTime` |
| `createdBy` | `Stamps.created(by = ...)`, optional | `string` |
| `updatedBy` | the last `touched(by = ...)`, optional | `string` |

- `Stamps.created()` and `touched()` use the current time; pass `at = ...` to choose it, for example in tests.
- `by` is whatever names a person in your app, such as `call.requireUser<User>().email`.
- Mark the property `@JsonSchema.ReadOnly`, as above, so the browser never sends it back and the server stays the one that sets it. Show it with `IsoDateTime.parse(article.stamps.updatedAt)` or the [relative time](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/i18n) helpers.

### Enums

Every Kotlin enum with two or more values becomes a `const` object plus a type of the same name, so you can use the values in code and not only in types:

```ts
import { Status } from '#api';

const archived = notes.filter((note) => note.status === Status.ARCHIVED);
```

Enums that appear in several classes with the same values share one generated name. The name comes from the property, such as `status` becoming `Status`. When two different enums would get the same name, the owning class is added in front, such as `NoteStatus`.

### Dates

Dates arrive as strings, but not as plain `string`, so a date can't be mixed up with ordinary text:

| Kotlin | TypeScript |
|---|---|
| `LocalDate` | `IsoDate` |
| `LocalTime` | `IsoTime` |
| `Instant`, `LocalDateTime` | `IsoDateTime` |

Helpers convert them safely:

```ts
import { IsoDate, IsoDateTime } from '#api';

const due = IsoDate.parse(task.due);
const created = IsoDateTime.parse(note.createdAt).toLocaleString();
const input = { due: IsoDate.today(), remindAt: IsoDateTime.now() };
```

- `IsoDate.parse` returns local midnight. `new Date('2026-11-10')` would give UTC midnight instead, which shows the previous day west of Greenwich.
- For an `Instant` use `IsoDateTime.from(date)`, which writes UTC. For a `LocalDateTime` use `IsoDateTime.fromLocal(date)`, which writes no offset. Both share one OpenAPI format, so the type can't tell them apart.
- The values of `<input type="date">`, `type="time"` and `type="datetime-local"` already have the right shape for `LocalDate`, `LocalTime` and `LocalDateTime`.
- The helpers are only generated when your API uses a date.

## Documentation in the editor

A `summary` and `description` set in `describe { }` end up as JSDoc on the generated function, so the editor shows them when you hover over a call:

```kotlin
post("/api/notes/{id}/attachments") { /* ... */ }.describe {
    summary = "Uploads files to a note."
    description = "Send the files as multipart form data."
}
```

```ts
/**
 * Uploads files to a note.
 *
 * Send the files as multipart form data.
 */
export const notesAttachments = (id: string | number, body: FormData, options?: RequestOptions) => ...
```

Types and their fields are documented the same way:

| On the Kotlin side | In TypeScript |
|---|---|
| `@JsonSchema.Description` on a class or property | JSDoc on the interface or the field |
| `@JsonSchema.DeprecatedSchema` on a property | `@deprecated`, which editors show struck through at every use |
| `deprecated = true` in `describe { }` on a route | `@deprecated` on the function |

```kotlin
@Serializable
@JsonSchema.Description("A note with its tags and its icon.")
data class Note(
    val id: Int,
    @JsonSchema.Description("Lowercase words the list can be filtered by.")
    val tags: List<String>,
    @JsonSchema.DeprecatedSchema
    val color: String? = null,
)
```

```ts
/** A note with its tags and its icon. */
export interface Note {
    id: number;
    /** Lowercase words the list can be filtered by. */
    tags: string[];
    /** @deprecated */
    color?: string | null;
}
```

Kotlin's own documentation comments and `@Deprecated` do not exist at runtime, where the schema is read, so they cannot be picked up. The annotations are the way to say it once for both sides.

### Where a route is declared

Every generated function also names the Kotlin file its route is declared in, as an `@see` line, whether you describe the route or not:

```ts
/** @see notes/Routes.kt */
export const notesCreate = (body: NoteInput, options?: RequestOptions) => ...
```

The path is the file's package folder and name, so it is the same on every machine. The line number is left out on purpose: it would change the generated file every time you edit above a route. To jump to the exact line, use the route list at `/_ktor-svelte/routes` while the app runs in development, or [`routes.json`](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/calling-the-api#find-the-kotlin-route-of-a-call).

## Routes nothing calls

A call to a route that no longer exists does not compile. The other direction needs a task: `svelteVerifyApiRoutes` lists the API routes that nothing in the frontend calls, so you can see what is safe to remove:

```bash
./gradlew svelteVerifyApiRoutes
```

```text
GET /api/notes/export  ->  nothing in the frontend calls api.notes.export
```

- A route counts as called when `api.notes.export`, a client from `apiWith`, the `notes` object or the `notesExport` function is used anywhere outside the generated folders, even when it is only passed along.
- The task only lists what it finds, because a route can also be called from outside the frontend, such as a webhook or another service.
- Add `--strict` to fail the build instead.

## What changed for callers

The frontend in the same repository is checked by the compiler. A mobile app, another service or a webhook sender is not, and for them a renamed field is an outage. `svelteApiChanges` compares the committed `openapi.json` with the one on another git revision and lists what a caller would notice:

```bash
./gradlew svelteApiChanges
```

```text
API changes against origin/main: 2 that can break callers, 3 other.

Can break callers
  GET /api/tasks  query  limit            was string, is integer
  POST /api/tasks  request  folder        is new and required

Other changes
  GET /api/tasks  response  items[].version  added
  POST /api/tasks  request  version          added
  PATCH /api/tasks/{id}                      added
```

It compares with `origin/main` unless you name another revision, such as the last release:

```bash
./gradlew svelteApiChanges --against=v1.1.0
```

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| `--against=<revision>` | The git revision to compare with. Defaults to `origin/main` |
| `--strict` | Fails the build on a change that can break callers, which is what you want in a pipeline for an API with callers you do not control |

What counts as able to break a caller:

- A route that is gone.
- In a response: a field that is gone, has another type, or can now be missing.
- In a request or the query: a field that is new and required, has become required, or has another type.

A new route, a new response field, a new optional request field and a request field that is no longer read are listed under the other changes.

**Limits**
- The task reads the committed file and never starts your app, so run it after `svelteGenerateTs`. Without `--strict` it only reports.
- It compares the type as the OpenAPI document states it, so a query parameter that was a plain string and is now an enum is listed as changed, even when every old call still works.
- It looks at the first successful response of a route, not at the error responses.

## Shared constants

A page size, a maximum number of labels, a list of plans: values like these are needed on both sides, and when they are typed in twice, one side changes and the other does not. Keep them in a Kotlin object and name it in `install(Svelte)`:

```kotlin
object Limits {
    const val PAGE_SIZE = 20
    const val MAX_LABELS = 5
    val PLANS = listOf("free", "team")
    val LABEL = Regex("[a-z0-9-]{1,20}")
}

install(Svelte) {
    generateTs = true
    constants(Limits)
}
```

`svelteGenerateTs` writes them to `constants.ts` next to the client, and `#api` exports the object under its Kotlin name:

```ts
import { Limits } from '#api';

const next = await api.notes.list({ limit: Limits.PAGE_SIZE });
```

```ts
export const Limits = {
    LABEL: '[a-z0-9-]{1,20}',
    MAX_LABELS: 5,
    PAGE_SIZE: 20,
    PLANS: ['free', 'team']
} as const;
```

- Every public `const val` and `val` of the object is shared, under the name it has in Kotlin. Private and internal ones stay out, so the object can hold more than it shares.
- `constants()` takes several objects at once.
- The values can be text, numbers, booleans, enums (by name), `Regex` (as its pattern text), and lists, sets and maps of those.
- Because the object is `as const`, TypeScript knows the exact values: `Limits.PLANS[number]` is `'free' | 'team'`.
- A value of another type stops generation with a message that names the property. That includes a `Duration` property, whose type is not visible from outside the object: share `timeout.inWholeMilliseconds` instead.

Like the rest of the client, `constants.ts` is checked by `svelteVerifyTs`, so a changed constant with a stale client fails `check`.

## IDs that cannot be mixed up

A note ID and a user ID are both numbers, so nothing stops code from passing one where the other belongs. In Kotlin a value class prevents that:

```kotlin
@JvmInline
@Serializable
value class NoteId(val value: Long)

@Serializable
data class Note(val id: NoteId, val authorId: UserId, val title: String)
```

The generated client keeps the distinction. In JSON the ID is still a plain number, but in TypeScript it is its own type:

```ts
export type NoteId = number & { readonly [brand]: 'NoteId' };

export interface Note {
    id: NoteId;
    authorId: UserId;
    title: string;
}
```

```ts
import { api, NoteId } from '#api';

const note = await api.notes.get(5);
await api.notes.delete(note.id);
await api.users.get(note.id); // fine today: path parameters take any number or text
const copy: Note = { ...note, authorId: note.id }; // does not compile: NoteId is not UserId

const fromUrl = NoteId(Number(page.params.id));
```

- Values that come from the server already have the type. To make one from a plain value, such as a route parameter, call the function of the same name: `NoteId(5)`.
- A branded ID is still a number or text to everything that only reads it: it can be printed, compared and passed to a path parameter.
- This applies to a value class over `Int`, `Long`, `Double` or `String`, wherever it appears in a DTO: alone, optional, in a list or as the values of a map. Value classes over anything else, or with validation annotations on the property, are generated as their underlying type, as before.

**Upgrading**
When you turn an existing `Long` field into a value class, or update to this version with value classes already in your DTOs, the frontend stops compiling where it builds such a value from a plain number. Wrap those places in the function, as above.

## Money and durations

Two kinds of value do not survive the trip to JavaScript as plain numbers or text: exact decimals, such as prices, and lengths of time.

```kotlin
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.Decimal
import kotlin.time.Duration

@Serializable
data class Invoice(val total: Decimal, val payWithin: Duration)
```

- `Decimal` is `java.math.BigDecimal` with a serializer that writes it as text, `"1234.50"`, so no digit is lost on the way.
- A `kotlin.time.Duration` is written as ISO text, `"PT1H30M"`, as kotlinx.serialization does by default.

In the generated client both have their own type and a few helpers:

```ts
import { Decimal, IsoDuration, type Invoice } from '#api';

declare const invoice: Invoice;

Decimal.add(invoice.total, Decimal.from('0.10')); // exact: 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.3
Decimal.times(invoice.total, 3);
Decimal.compare(invoice.total, Decimal.from(100)) > 0;
Decimal.format(invoice.total, 'de-DE', { style: 'currency', currency: 'EUR' });

IsoDuration.toMillis(invoice.payWithin);
IsoDuration.fromMillis(90 * 60 * 1000); // 'PT1H30M'
IsoDuration.format(invoice.payWithin); // '1:30:00'
```

| Helper | What it does |
|---|---|
| `Decimal.from(text or number)` | Makes a `Decimal`, and throws for anything that is not a plain decimal number. |
| `Decimal.add`, `subtract` | Exact, at the larger number of decimal places of the two. |
| `Decimal.times(value, count)` | Exact, for a whole `count`, such as a quantity. |
| `Decimal.compare` | -1, 0 or 1. `1.50` and `1.5` are equal. |
| `Decimal.format(value, locale?, options?)` | Text for people, through `Intl.NumberFormat`, keeping the decimal places. |
| `Decimal.toNumber` | A JavaScript number, when exactness no longer matters, such as for a chart. |
| `IsoDuration.toMillis`, `fromMillis` | To and from milliseconds. |
| `IsoDuration.add` | The sum of two. |
| `IsoDuration.format` | A clock text such as `1:30:00`. |

- The helpers are only in `types.ts` when the API uses one of the two types.
- A `BigDecimal` with your own serializer is recognised too, when the serializer writes text and its descriptor is named `BigDecimal` or `java.math.BigDecimal`.

**Upgrading**
A `Duration` field used to be generated as `string`. It is `IsoDuration` now, so code that assigns plain text to one needs `as IsoDuration`, or better `IsoDuration.fromMillis(...)`.

## Sealed classes

A sealed class or interface becomes a union of its subtypes, each with a literal `type` field, so TypeScript narrows it in a `switch`. The generated companion also lists the type names and has an exhaustive `match`: leave out a case and the code does not compile.

```kotlin
@Serializable
sealed interface Activity

@Serializable
@SerialName("created")
data class Created(val at: Instant) : Activity

@Serializable
@SerialName("archived")
data class Archived(val at: Instant, val title: String) : Activity
```

```ts
import { Activity, api } from '#api';

const lines = (await api.notes.getActivity(id)).map((item) =>
    Activity.match(item, {
        created: (created) => `Created at ${created.at}`,
        archived: (archived) => `Archived "${archived.title}"`
    })
);
```

| Generated | What it is |
|---|---|
| `Activity` (type) | The union of `Archived` and `Created`, narrowed by `item.type` |
| `Activity.types` | The type names, such as `['archived', 'created']` |
| `Activity.match(value, cases)` | Calls the case for the value's type. Every type needs a case |

Use `@SerialName` for short type names. Without it, the type name is the fully qualified class name.

## Resource routes

Most APIs have a few things that can be listed, read, created, changed and deleted, and for each of them the same five routes. `resource` registers them with the paths, statuses and names that the generated client expects:

```kotlin
routing {
    resource<Note, Int>("/api/notes") {
        missing<Problem> { Problem("That note does not exist.") }
        list<NoteQuery> { query -> store.list(query.search, query.tag) }
        get { id -> store.find(id) }
        create<NoteInput> { input -> store.create(input) }
        update<NoteInput> { id, input -> store.update(id, input) }
        delete { id -> store.delete(id) }
    }
}
```

| Block | Route | Returns | Client |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `list { }` | `GET /api/notes` | The list | `api.notes.list()` |
| `get { id -> }` | `GET /api/notes/{id}` | The item, or `null` for a 404 | `api.notes.get(id)` |
| `create<Input> { input -> }` | `POST /api/notes` | The new item, sent with a 201 | `api.notes.create(input)` |
| `update<Input> { id, input -> }` | `PUT /api/notes/{id}` | The changed item, or `null` for a 404 | `api.notes.update(id, input)` |
| `delete { id -> }` | `DELETE /api/notes/{id}` | `true`, or `false` for a 404. A 204 is sent | `api.notes.delete(id)` |

Each block returns its answer and does not call `respond`. That is what lets the types line up without anything being inferred:

- `Note` is the type of every answer.
- The type you name on `create` and `update` is the body.
- The second type of `resource` is the type of the id, so `api.notes.get` takes a `number` here. Leave the second type out and the id is a string. The id is read like [`pathParameter`](#typed-path-parameters), and an id that is not of that type is a 404.

These are ordinary Ktor routes. Every block is optional, a block that is left out is no route, and `call` is there in each block for anything else you need. Nothing is stored or generated for you: the blocks are your code.

- `list<NoteQuery> { query -> }` reads the query string into a `@Serializable` class, and the client gets the same fields as a typed query. See [Query parameters as a class](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/calling-the-api#query-parameters-as-a-class).
- `missing<Problem> { ... }` says what a 404 looks like. It comes first in the block, and the client then knows the type of that error for `get`, `update` and `delete`. Without it a 404 has no body of yours.
- Each block can be declared once. Declaring one twice, or `missing` after `get`, `update` or `delete`, fails with a message when the routes are set up.
- Other routes of the same thing, such as `POST /api/notes/{id}/archive`, go next to the resource in a normal `route("/api/notes") { }`.

`svelteAdd --crud` writes the first version of the pages for a resource. See [Pages for a class](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/routes#pages-for-a-class).

## Getting exact types

Ktor's compiler plugin reads `call.receive<T>()`, `call.respond()` and `call.queryParameters` for you, so plain routes get full types. Add the Ktor Gradle plugin:

```kotlin
plugins {
    id("io.ktor.plugin") version "3.6.1"
}

ktor {
    openApi {
        enabled = true
        codeInferenceEnabled = true
        onlyCommented = false
    }
}
```

Without it, describe routes by hand. A route with no description still gets a service, but it returns `unknown`:

```kotlin
get("/api/todos") { call.respond(todos) }.describe {
    responses {
        HttpStatusCode.OK { schema = jsonSchema<List<Todo>>() }
    }
}
```

## Full example

A notes app end to end: a resource with a typed query and a shared constant on the server, and a component that uses the generated types, enums, dates and the sealed `Activity` union.

::: code-group

```kotlin no-check [Model.kt]
object NoteLimits {
    const val PAGE_SIZE = 20
    const val MAX_TAGS = 5
}

enum class NoteStatus { ACTIVE, ARCHIVED }

@Serializable
@JsonSchema.Description("A note with its tags and its icon.")
data class Note(
    val id: Int,
    val title: String,
    val body: String,
    val tags: List<String>,
    val status: NoteStatus,
    val createdAt: Instant,
)

@Serializable
data class NoteInput(
    @Trim
    @JsonSchema.MinLength(1)
    @JsonSchema.MaxLength(80)
    val title: String,
    val body: String = "",
    val tags: List<String> = emptyList(),
)

@Serializable
data class NoteQuery(val search: String? = null, val tag: String? = null)

@Serializable
sealed interface Activity

@Serializable
@SerialName("created")
data class Created(val at: Instant) : Activity

@Serializable
@SerialName("archived")
data class Archived(val at: Instant, val title: String) : Activity
```

```kotlin no-check [Routes.kt]
fun Application.module(store: NoteStore) {
    install(Svelte) {
        generateTs = true
        constants(NoteLimits)
    }
    routing {
        resource<Note, Int>("/api/notes") {
            missing<Problem> { Problem("That note does not exist.") }
            list<NoteQuery> { query -> store.list(query.search, query.tag) }
            get { id -> store.find(id) }
            create<NoteInput> { input -> store.create(input) }
            update<NoteInput> { id, input -> store.update(id, input) }
            delete { id -> store.delete(id) }
        }
        get("/api/notes/{id}/activity") {
            val note = store.find(call.pathParameter<Int>("id")) ?: throw NotFoundException()
            val activity: List<Activity> = store.activity(note)
            call.respond(activity)
        }
    }
}
```

```svelte [NoteCard.svelte]
<script lang="ts">
    import { Activity, api, IsoDateTime, Status, type Note } from '#api';

    let { note }: { note: Note } = $props();

    let lines = $state<string[]>([]);

    async function showActivity() {
        const activity = await api.notes.getActivity(note.id);
        lines = activity.map((item) =>
            Activity.match(item, {
                created: (created) => `Created ${IsoDateTime.parse(created.at).toLocaleString()}`,
                archived: (archived) => `Archived as "${archived.title}"`
            })
        );
    }
</script>

<article class:opacity-60={note.status === Status.ARCHIVED}>
    <h2>{note.title}</h2>
    <time datetime={note.createdAt}>{IsoDateTime.parse(note.createdAt).toLocaleDateString()}</time>
    <p>{note.body}</p>
    <button onclick={showActivity}>Show activity</button>
    <ul>
        {#each lines as line, index (index)}
            <li>{line}</li>
        {/each}
    </ul>
</article>
```

Rename `title` in `Note`, restart the app, and `NoteCard.svelte` no longer compiles. Add a third `Activity` subtype, and every `Activity.match` that does not handle it fails too.

## Use cases

- A frontend and a backend in one repository that should never drift: commit the client and let `check` run [`svelteVerifyTs`](#keeping-it-in-sync).
- Forms that show the server's rules before sending: [bounds and `validate()`](#types-and-forms), or the [form helper](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/validation#form-state).
- Values both sides need, such as page sizes: [shared constants](#shared-constants).
- Prices and durations: [money and durations](#money-and-durations).
- Feeds of different kinds of events: [sealed classes](#sealed-classes).
- A public API with outside callers: run [`svelteApiChanges --strict`](#what-changed-for-callers) in CI.
- Cleaning up an old API: [`svelteVerifyApiRoutes`](#routes-nothing-calls).

## Good to know

- Only paths under the API prefix are generated. See `apiPrefixes` in the [Ktor reference](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/reference/ktor).
- The client is written in development mode only, never in production. When it seems stale, see [troubleshooting](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/reference/troubleshooting).
- With `lucide()` on, an icon property becomes the `LucideIcon` type, and with `publicConfig` set, the client gets [`readPublicConfig()`](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/runtime-config).
- How to call the functions is on [Calling the API](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/calling-the-api).

Source: https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/calling-the-api

# Calling the API

Call your Ktor routes from Svelte components and SvelteKit load functions through the [generated client](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/typescript), with typed results, typed errors, retries, streams, paged lists and uploads. Most features are one setting or one option on a call.

<Badge type="warning" text="Generated client" /> <Badge type="tip" text="Ktor plugin" />

| [Errors](#errors) | [Typed errors](#typed-errors), [Error codes](#error-codes), [Errors from StatusPages](#errors-from-statuspages), [Show errors automatically](#show-errors-automatically), [Ask before a call](#ask-before-a-call), [Request IDs](#request-ids) |
| [Reading data](#reading-data) | [Query parameters as a class](#query-parameters-as-a-class), [Share identical requests](#share-identical-requests), [Prefetch on hover](#prefetch-on-hover), [Search as you type](#search-as-you-type), [Paged lists](#paged-lists), [Event streams](#event-streams) |
| [Writing data](#writing-data) | [Refresh the page after a write](#refresh-the-page-after-a-write), [Changing some fields](#changing-some-fields), [Two people, one record](#two-people-one-record), [Writes that are safe to send twice](#writes-that-are-safe-to-send-twice), [Uploads](#uploads) |
| [The server talks back](#the-server-talks-back) | [Toasts from the server](#toasts-from-the-server), [Navigation from the server](#navigation-from-the-server), [Reload after a deploy](#reload-after-a-deploy), [The visitor's time zone](#the-visitor-s-time-zone) |

| [Full examples](#full-examples) | [A notes page](#a-notes-page), [A search box](#a-search-box), [A paged table](#a-paged-table) |

## Basics

### Quick start

```ts
import { api, apiConfig } from '#api';

const notes = await api.notes.list({ search: 'milk' });
const note = await api.notes.get(1);
await api.notes.update(1, { title: 'Oat milk' });

apiConfig.headers['Authorization'] = 'Bearer token';
```

Every function returns a promise of the route's response type and throws an [`ApiError`](#typed-errors) for any status that is not a success. How the functions are named is described in [Service names](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/typescript#service-names).

### In components

Call the client from a component's script, from an event handler or from an `{#await}` block:

```svelte
<script lang="ts">
    import { api, errorMessage } from '#api';

    const loading = api.notes.list();
</script>

{#await loading}
    <p>Loading...</p>
{:then found}
    <ul>
        {#each found as item (item.id)}
            <li>{item.title}</li>
        {/each}
    </ul>
{:catch error}
    <p role="alert">{errorMessage(error)}</p>
{/await}
```

For data a page needs before it shows, prefer a `load` function, below.

### In load functions

Inside a SvelteKit `load` function, every call has to go through the `fetch` SvelteKit gives you. `apiWith(event)` returns the same client, but every call goes through SvelteKit's `fetch`, which prerendering and client-side navigation need:

```ts
import { apiWith } from '#api';
import type { PageLoad } from './$types';

export const load: PageLoad = async (event) => {
    const api = apiWith(event);
    return { notes: await api.notes.list(), stats: await api.stats.list() };
};
```

For a single call, pass `fetch` as the last argument instead:

```ts
import { api } from '#api';
import type { PageLoad } from './$types';

export const load: PageLoad = async ({ fetch, params }) => {
    const note = await api.notes.get(params.id, { fetch });
    return { note };
};
```

A `fetch` passed in the options of a single call still wins over the one from `apiWith`.

With its own `fetch`, SvelteKit knows which requests a page depends on, reuses a response it already has during hydration, and can rerun the load when you invalidate it. Without it, the call still works, but the browser console warns with `window_fetch_in_load`.

`svelteVerifyLoads` finds the calls that forgot. It reads every `+page.ts`, `+page.js`, `+layout.ts` and `+layout.js`, and fails with the file, the line and the call:

```bash
./gradlew svelteVerifyLoads
```

```text
src/routes/notes/[id]/+page.ts:6  api.notes.get(params.id)  ->  use apiWith(event), or pass { fetch } as the last argument
```

It is not part of `check`. The [lint rule](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/frontend-libraries#lint-rules) `ktor-svelte/fetch-in-load` reports the same thing in the editor.

### Request options

Every generated function takes the request options as its last argument. They are the options of `fetch`, such as `signal` and `headers`, plus these:

| Option | What it does | Section |
|---|---|---|
| `fetch` | The `fetch` to use for this call | [In load functions](#in-load-functions) |
| `timeout` | Milliseconds before the call gives up | [Timeouts](#timeouts) |
| `retry` | `true`, `false` or `{ attempts, delay, maxDelay }` | [Retries](#retries) |
| `silent` | `true` keeps the error away from `apiConfig.onError`, and so from toasts | [Show errors automatically](#show-errors-automatically) |
| `refresh` | `false` skips `apiConfig.onWrite` after this write | [Refresh the page after a write](#refresh-the-page-after-a-write) |
| `onUploadProgress` | Called with `{ loaded, total }` while a body is sent | [Uploads](#uploads) |

```ts
import { api } from '#api';

const controller = new AbortController();
const found = await api.notes.list({ search: 'milk' }, { signal: controller.signal, timeout: 5000, silent: true });
```

### Client settings

`apiConfig` holds the settings for every call. Set them once, such as in your root layout or `src/hooks.client.ts`:

| Setting | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `baseUrl` | `''` | Put in front of every path |
| `headers` | `{}` | Sent with every call |
| `fetch` | the global `fetch` | The `fetch` every call uses, such as [`fixtureFetch`](#fixtures-for-frontend-tests) in a test |
| `timeout` | none | [Timeout](#timeouts) for every call, in milliseconds |
| `retry` | off | [Retries](#retries) for reads |
| `dedupeGets` | `false` | [Shares identical GET requests](#share-identical-requests) that are in flight |
| `idempotencyKeys` | on | `false` stops sending the [`Idempotency-Key`](#writes-that-are-safe-to-send-twice) header |
| `sendTimeZone` | on | `false` stops sending the [visitor's time zone](#the-visitor-s-time-zone) |
| `onError` | none | Called with every failed call. [Toasts](#show-errors-automatically) set it for you |
| `onWrite` | none | Called after successful writes, to [refresh the page](#refresh-the-page-after-a-write) |
| `onToast` | none | Shows [toasts from the server](#toasts-from-the-server) |
| `onNavigate` | none | Follows [navigation from the server](#navigation-from-the-server) |
| `onNewBuild` | none | Called when a [new build is deployed](#reload-after-a-deploy) |
| `onUnauthorized`, `loginPage`, `sessionWarning` | | For signed-in users. See [Auth](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/auth#the-login-page) |

### Import single functions

Every endpoint is also exported on its own, named after its group and service, such as `notesList` or `notesGet`. Import those in pages that use only a few endpoints, and the bundler leaves the rest of the client out of that page:

```ts
import { notesGet } from '#api';

const note = await notesGet(1);
```

### Find the Kotlin route of a call

In development, ktor-svelte also writes `build/ktor-svelte/routes.json`, which maps every generated service to the Kotlin route that serves it:

```json
"notes.get": { "method": "GET", "path": "/api/notes/{id}", "file": "notes/Routes.kt", "line": 43 }
```

- Search it for the operation name you see in the frontend, or let an editor plugin use it to jump from a call to its route.
- `file` is relative to your source root, and `line` is the line of the route's handler.
- It lives in `build/` because line numbers change with every edit.
- When ktor-svelte cannot read a handler's location, the entry has only `method` and `path`.

## Errors

### Typed errors

Every failed call throws an `ApiError` with the `status`, the parsed `body`, the `url`, the `operation` name and the [`requestId`](#request-ids). Errors are typed too. Ktor's compiler plugin finds error responses such as `call.respond(HttpStatusCode.NotFound, Problem(...))`, and `isApiError` narrows the body:

```ts
import { api, isApiError, isValidationError } from '#api';

try {
    await api.notes.create({ title: '' });
} catch (error) {
    if (isValidationError(error)) showErrors(error.body.fields);
    if (isApiError(error, 'notes.get')) console.log(error.body.message);
}
```

| Helper | True for |
|---|---|
| `isApiError(error, 'notes.get')` | An error the route declares, with its body typed |
| `isValidationError(error)` | A 422 with `fields`, from [validation](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/validation) |
| `isVersionConflict(error)` | A [version conflict](#two-people-one-record) |
| `isRateLimitError(error)` | A 429, with `retryAfter` in milliseconds. See [Rate limits](#rate-limits) |
| `isTimeoutError(error)` | A call that hit its [timeout](#timeouts) |
| `isAbortError(error)` | A call that was aborted, such as by [`latest`](#search-as-you-type) |
| `hasErrorCode(error, code)` | An answer with that one of your [error codes](#error-codes) |
| `isUploadError(error)` | A file that breaks the [upload rules](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/recipes/uploads#rules-for-both-sides) |

`errorCode(error)` returns the `code` of an error body, or `undefined` when there is none.

When you only need one line to show, `errorMessage` turns anything a call can throw into text: the `message` of the error body when the server sent one, and otherwise a sentence for a timeout, for a lost connection, or for everything else:

```ts
import { api, errorMessage } from '#api';

let problem = '';

try {
    await api.notes.create({ title: 'Buy milk' });
} catch (error) {
    problem = errorMessage(error);
}
```

To change or translate the three built-in sentences, assign to `errorMessages.network`, `errorMessages.timeout` and `errorMessages.failed` once at startup:

```ts
import { errorMessages } from '#api';

errorMessages.network = 'Keine Verbindung zum Server.';
```

### Error codes

A page that has to tell "this email is taken" from "the last admin cannot leave" should not compare status numbers or message text. Give the errors names, in one enum, and name it in `install(Svelte)`:

```kotlin
enum class AccountError { EmailTaken, LastAdmin }

install(Svelte) {
    generateTs = true
    errorCodes<AccountError>()
}
```

A route answers with a code, either directly or by throwing from anywhere below it:

```kotlin
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.ApiException
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.respondError

post("/api/register") {
    call.respondError(AccountError.EmailTaken, HttpStatusCode.Conflict)
}

put("/api/admin/users/{id}/role") {
    throw ApiException(AccountError.LastAdmin, HttpStatusCode.Conflict)
}
```

The answer is `{ "message": "Email taken.", "code": "EmailTaken" }` with the given status, 400 when none is given. `respondError` only takes an error status, 400 and above. The generated client knows the enum as the type `ErrorCode`, so a mistyped or removed code no longer compiles:

```ts
import { api, ErrorCode, hasErrorCode } from '#api';

try {
    await api.register.create(form);
} catch (error) {
    if (hasErrorCode(error, ErrorCode.EmailTaken)) emailProblem = error.body.message;
    else throw error;
}
```

The message is the code's name as a sentence unless you say otherwise. There are three places to say otherwise, and the first that applies wins:

| Where | How | Scope |
|---|---|---|
| One answer | `call.respondError(code, status, message = "...")`, or the `message` of `ApiException` | That answer |
| On the server | `errorCodes<AccountError> { call, code -> ... }` returns the text for a code, or null to leave it. It gets the call, so it can translate | Every answer |
| In the browser | `setCodeMessages({ EmailTaken: 'That email already has an account.' })` once at startup | `errorMessage`, and so the toasts of `toasts()`, use this text for the code and ignore what the server sent. A value can be a function, for a translation that depends on the current language |

An app has one enum of error codes. A class of your API named `ErrorCode` clashes with the generated type and stops generation.

### Errors from StatusPages

Errors that `StatusPages` sends are invisible to the compiler plugin, because its handlers are plain lambdas. Declare them once, and they join the typed errors of every API endpoint, unless a route already declares that status itself:

```kotlin
install(StatusPages) {
    exception<NotFoundException> { call, cause -> call.respond(HttpStatusCode.NotFound, Problem(cause.message.orEmpty())) }
}
install(Svelte) {
    errorResponse<Problem>(HttpStatusCode.NotFound, HttpStatusCode.Conflict)
}
```

### Show errors automatically

Turn on toasts in Gradle, and every failed API call shows a short message in the corner of the page, so you don't have to write error handling for the common case:

```kotlin
svelte {
    libraries {
        toasts()
    }
}
```

Run `svelteSync` once. It writes `src/lib/ktor-svelte/toasts.ts` and a `src/hooks.client.ts` that sets `apiConfig.onError`.

- The message comes from the error body's `message`, such as `Problem("That note does not exist.")`, or reads "Something went wrong (error 500)" with the request ID for server errors.
- Network failures and timeouts get their own message.
- With DaisyUI, toasts are DaisyUI alerts in your theme. Otherwise they bring their own small style.

Some errors are left to you, because a toast would be the wrong answer:

- 422 validation errors, which your form shows next to the fields.
- 401, which [the login page](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/auth#the-login-page) or `apiConfig.onUnauthorized` handles.
- Aborted requests, failed prefetches, and calls made with `silent: true`, such as `api.notes.get(id, { silent: true })`.

The promise still rejects, so you can add handling where you want more.

```ts
import { toast, toastMessages } from '#lib/ktor-svelte/toasts.ts';

toast('Saved.', { kind: 'success' });
toast('Note deleted.', { action: { label: 'Undo', run: restore } });
toastMessages.close = 'Schliessen';
```

| Function | What it does |
|---|---|
| `toast(message, { kind, duration, action })` | Shows your own message. `kind` is `info`, `success`, `warning` or `error`, `duration` is in milliseconds, and `action` adds a button: `{ label: 'Undo', run: restore }` |
| `toastMessages` | The built-in texts, to change or translate |

Without `toasts()`, `apiConfig.onError` is yours to set, for example to report errors to a monitoring service. See also [Toasts](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/frontend-libraries#toasts) among the frontend libraries.

### Ask before a call

A call that deletes something should ask first. `confirmed` asks, and only calls when the answer is yes:

```ts
import { api } from '#api';
import { confirmed } from '#lib/ktor-svelte/confirm.ts';

const deleted = await confirmed('Delete this note?', () => api.notes.delete(id), {
    details: 'It cannot be restored.',
    confirm: 'Delete',
    danger: true
});
```

It resolves to what the call returned, or to `undefined` when the answer was no.

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| `details` | A second line under the question |
| `confirm`, `cancel` | The button labels. Default to `confirmMessages.confirm` and `confirmMessages.cancel` |
| `danger` | `true` makes the confirm button red and puts the focus on Cancel |

- With DaisyUI on, the question is a modal in your theme. While the call runs, both buttons are disabled, so it cannot be sent twice. When it fails, the modal stays open and shows the error's `message`, and the user can try again or cancel. Escape cancels.
- Without DaisyUI it is the browser's own `confirm`, and a failed call rejects as usual.

`svelteSync` writes the helper to `src/lib/ktor-svelte/confirm.ts` for every project that has generated files. Set `confirmMessages.confirm` and `confirmMessages.cancel` once, such as to your translations.

### Request IDs

Every call from the generated client sends a fresh `X-Request-Id`. The server keeps it when it is well formed, letters, digits, dots, dashes and underscores up to 128 characters, or generates one, and sends it back in the response. Unhandled errors are logged with it, and `ApiError.requestId` carries it, so a user can quote one ID that support finds in the logs:

```ts
try {
    await api.notes.create(draft);
} catch (error) {
    if (error instanceof ApiError) showError(`Something went wrong. Reference: ${error.requestId}`);
}
```

- The ID is available in routes as `call.callId`, and with Ktor's `CallLogging` you can put it into every log line with `callIdMdc("requestId")`.
- The client only sends the header to its own origin, so it never causes CORS preflights.
- If you install Ktor's `CallId` yourself, your setup is used.
- `requestIds = false` in `install(Svelte)` turns it off.

## Reading data

### Query parameters as a class

A list route usually reads its query string one parameter at a time, converts each by hand and guesses what to do with a wrong one, and the generated client sees a handful of optional strings. Describe the query as a class instead:

```kotlin
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.query
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.queryOf

@Serializable
data class NoteQuery(
    val search: String? = null,
    val status: Status? = null,
    val mine: Boolean = false,
    @JsonSchema.Minimum(1.0) @JsonSchema.Maximum(100.0) val limit: Int = 20,
    val tags: List<String> = emptyList(),
)

get("/api/notes") {
    val query = call.query<NoteQuery>()
    call.respond(notes.find(query))
}.queryOf<NoteQuery>()
```

- `call.query<NoteQuery>()` reads the query string into the class. Numbers, booleans and enums are converted, a parameter that is given several times fills a list, and what is not there takes the property's default.
- A value that does not fit, such as `limit=many` or an unknown status, and a missing parameter without a default, are answered with the same 422 as a request body, with the field named. The `JsonSchema` annotations and `Validated` rules apply too.
- Parameters the class does not have are ignored, and an empty one counts as not given, as a form sends it for an empty field.
- `.queryOf<NoteQuery>()` tells the generated client about the parameters. Without it the function has no `query` argument.
- In a [resource](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/typescript#resource-routes), `list<NoteQuery> { query -> }` does both.

The generated function takes the same fields with their types:

```ts
await api.notes.list({ status: Status.OPEN, mine: true, limit: 50, tags: ['home', 'food'] });
```

The properties can be text, numbers, booleans, enums, value classes over those, types that are written as text such as dates, and lists of them. A nested class is refused when the route is declared.

### Share identical requests

When several components load the same data at the same time, set `apiConfig.dedupeGets = true`:

```ts
import { apiConfig } from '#api';

apiConfig.dedupeGets = true;
```

- Identical GET requests that are still in flight then share one network request and get the same parsed result, so do not mutate it.
- Calls with their own `headers`, `fetch` or `signal` are never shared.
- Nothing is cached after a response arrives.
- It is off by default.

### Prefetch on hover

Projects created by ktor-svelte set `data-sveltekit-preload-data="hover"` on `<body>`, so SvelteKit runs a page's `load` function when the pointer rests on a link to it. A `load` that calls the API through `apiWith(event)` therefore fetches its data before the click, and the page opens without waiting. Add the attribute to `src/app.html` in older projects.

For data a component fetches itself, prefetch the call. The next identical GET within 10 seconds gets that response instead of a new request, once:

```svelte
<script lang="ts">
    import { api, prefetchOnHover } from '#api';
</script>

{#each notes as note (note.id)}
    <a href="/notes/{note.id}" use:prefetchOnHover={() => api.notes.get(note.id)}>{note.title}</a>
{/each}
```

- `prefetchOnHover` starts after the pointer rests for 50 ms, or at once on focus or touch.
- Call `prefetch(() => api.notes.get(id))` yourself for other triggers, and pass a second argument to change how long the result is kept, in milliseconds.
- Only GET requests made synchronously inside the callback are prefetched, without their own `headers` or `signal`.
- A failed prefetch is simply forgotten.

```ts
import { api, prefetch } from '#api';

void prefetch(() => api.notes.get(id), 30_000);
```

### Search as you type

When every keystroke starts a request, an older, slower response can arrive after a newer one and overwrite it. Wrap the call in `latest`, and each call aborts the one before it:

```ts
import { api, isAbortError, latest } from '#api';

const search = latest(api.notes.list);

async function onInput(term: string) {
    try {
        notes = await search({ search: term });
    } catch (error) {
        if (!isAbortError(error)) throw error;
    }
}
```

A superseded call always rejects with an `AbortError`, even when it was cancelled while its body was being read. Your own `signal` still works alongside it. A complete component is in [A search box](#a-search-box).

### Paged lists

For paged lists, return `Page<T>` from `io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte` and read a `cursor` query parameter. `next` is the cursor of the following page, or `null` on the last one:

```kotlin
get("/api/notes/feed") {
    val cursor = call.queryParameters["cursor"]
    val page: Page<Note> = store.page(cursor, limit = 20)
    call.respond(page)
}
```

`getPage` writes those lines for you and reads `cursor`, `limit` and `total`. A page carries a total count only when the client asks with `total: true`, see [Show how many there are](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/recipes/pagination#show-how-many-there-are). See [Page through long lists](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/recipes/pagination) for its settings and for paging an Exposed query.

`pages` turns any such endpoint into an async iterator that fetches one page at a time, typed from the endpoint:

```ts
import { api, pages } from '#api';

for await (const notes of pages(api.notes.getFeed, { limit: '50' })) render(notes);
```

To fetch one page at a time on demand, such as behind a "Load more" button, call the endpoint with the `cursor` yourself, as in [A paged table](#a-paged-table).

### Event streams

Routes that declare a `text/event-stream` response, for example through `describe`, become async generators. Each event's `data` is parsed as JSON when possible, and the stream ends when the connection closes or you stop iterating:

```ts
for await (const tick of api.ticks.watch()) console.log(tick);
```

- Pass a `signal` and abort it when the component goes away, to close the connection.
- Event streams ignore `apiConfig.timeout`, because a live stream is supposed to stay open. Give one its own `timeout` if you want that.
- Streams are never retried.

The server side, with a complete component, is in [Stream live updates](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/recipes/live-updates).

## Writing data

### Refresh the page after a write

After you create, change or delete something, the lists and details on the page are out of date. Tell the client what to do after a successful write, once, in your root layout, and every page keeps itself current:

```ts
import { refreshAll } from '$app/navigation';
import { apiConfig } from '#api';

apiConfig.onWrite = () => void refreshAll();
```

- `onWrite` runs after every POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE that succeeds, and `refreshAll` reruns the `load` functions of the page you are on.
- Writes that finish together, such as three calls in a `Promise.all`, cause one refresh, not three.
- A failed write does not trigger it, and neither does a read.

A call that should not refresh the page, such as saving a draft while the user types, opts out:

```ts
await api.notes.update(id, draft, { refresh: false });
```

The client does not import SvelteKit itself, so nothing happens until you set `onWrite`. That also means you can do something else there, such as refreshing only one resource with `invalidate`.

### Changing some fields

A `PUT` replaces a record, so the browser has to send every field, also the ones the visitor never touched. A `PATCH` sends only what changed, but then the server has to tell a field that was left out from one that was set to null, and a nullable Kotlin property cannot: both arrive as null. `Patch<T>` can, without a second DTO:

```kotlin
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.Patch

patch("/api/notes/{id}") {
    val patch = call.receive<Patch<NoteInput>>()
    val stored = notes.find(id)
    val updated = patch.applyTo(stored.toInput())
    call.respond(notes.save(id, updated))
}
```

- `applyTo` returns the given object with the sent fields replaced. A field that was not sent keeps its value, and one sent as null becomes null.
- The result is checked like a received object: the bounds from annotations and the `Validated` rules, answered with the usual 422. `@Trim` and the other normalisers apply to the sent fields.
- A field the class does not have, null for a property that is not nullable, or a value of the wrong type is a 400.
- `NoteInput::title in patch`, `patch.has("title")` and `patch.fields` say what was sent, for a route that treats one field specially. `patch.isEmpty()` is true when nothing was sent.

In the generated client the body is the class with every field optional, and null allowed where the class allows it:

```ts
import { api, patchOf } from '#api';

await api.notes.patch(note.id, { dueOn: null });
await api.notes.patch(note.id, patchOf(original, draft));
```

| Helper | What it does |
|---|---|
| `patchOf(before, after)` | The fields that differ between two objects, with null for the ones that were cleared, so an edit form sends what the visitor changed and nothing else |
| `applyPatch(target, patch)` | Does on the client what `applyTo` does on the server, for showing the result before the answer is there |
| `Patch<T>` | The type of both |

### Two people, one record

Two people open the same record, both change it, both save. Without a check the second save silently replaces the first. With a version, the second one is told.

Give the record a number that changes on every save, a counter or the time of the last change, send it out with the record and take it back with an update:

```kotlin
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.respondIfStale

@Serializable
data class Note(val id: Int, val title: String, val version: Long)

@Serializable
data class NoteUpdate(val title: String, val version: Long? = null)

put("/api/notes/{id}") {
    val update = call.receive<NoteUpdate>()
    val stored = notes.find(id)
    if (call.respondIfStale(update.version, stored.version) { stored }) return@put
    call.respond(notes.save(id, update))
}
```

- When the version that came in is not the stored one, `respondIfStale` answers 409 with the code `version.conflict` and the record as it is now, and returns true. The block that gives the record only runs then.
- An update without a version is not checked, so make the field required if every client must send it.
- The third argument is the message, for your own wording or language. It defaults to "Someone else changed this in the meantime."

In the browser, `isVersionConflict` recognises the answer and gives you the other person's record:

```ts
import { api, isVersionConflict, type Note } from '#api';

try {
    note = await api.notes.update(note.id, draft, { silent: true });
} catch (error) {
    if (!isVersionConflict<Note>(error)) throw error;
    theirs = error.body.current;
}
```

From there the two usual ways out are one line each. To load their version, show `theirs` and start over. To save yours anyway, set `draft.version = theirs.version` and send again.

[`formState`](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/validation#form-state) does the bookkeeping: after a conflict, `form.conflict` holds their record, `form.takeTheirs()` resets the form to it, and `form.keepMine()` takes over their version so the next `form.submit` goes through. Pass `takeTheirs` a value when the form's type is not the record's type.

### Writes that are safe to send twice

A `GET` can be repeated without harm. A `POST` cannot: when the answer is lost on the way back, the browser does not know whether the order was placed, and sending it again may place it twice. That is why only `GET` requests are [retried](#retries) by default.

An idempotency key removes the doubt. The generated client adds a header, `Idempotency-Key`, with a fresh random value to every write, and uses the same value when it sends that call again. Turn on the server side, and a repeated key is answered with the stored first answer instead of doing the work again:

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    idempotency()
}
```

Now a write can be retried, when the call asks for it:

```ts
await api.orders.create(order, { retry: true });
```

- The repeat gets the same status, body and headers as the first answer, plus `Idempotency-Replayed: true`. [Toasts and navigation from the server](#toasts-from-the-server) are repeated with it, since the first ones never arrived.
- An answer with a status of 500 and above is not kept, so the retry does the work. A repeat that arrives while the first is still running is answered with 409 and the code `idempotency.inProgress`, which the client waits for and retries.
- A key counts for one caller (the same `Authorization` and `Cookie` headers), one method and one path. Somebody else sending the same key gets their own result.
- Streamed answers and answers above 1 MiB are not kept. Reads and routes outside the API prefixes are not looked at.

| Setting in `idempotency { }` | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `ttl` | `10.minutes` | How long an answer is kept |
| `maxEntries` | `10_000` | How many answers are kept, in memory |

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    idempotency {
        ttl = 30.minutes
        maxEntries = 50_000
    }
}
```

With several instances of the app behind a load balancer, a repeat only finds the answer on the instance that gave it.

`retry` in `apiConfig` still applies to reads only. A write is retried when its own call says `retry`, so the decision stays next to the routes where you know the server side is on. To stop sending the header, set `apiConfig.idempotencyKeys = false`, which also stops writes from being retried.

### Show that something is still saving

`pendingWrites` knows whether any write is still on its way: every call that is not a `GET`, `HEAD` or `OPTIONS`, from anywhere in the app. Use it for a "Saving..." badge, and `warnBeforeLeaving()` asks before the tab is closed while one is running:

```svelte
<script lang="ts">
    import { pendingWrites, warnBeforeLeaving } from '#lib/api/pending-writes.svelte.ts';

    $effect(() => warnBeforeLeaving());
</script>

{#if pendingWrites.active}
    <span role="status">Saving...</span>
{/if}
```

| Name | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `pendingWrites.active` | `true` while at least one write is in flight; reactive |
| `pendingWrites.count` | how many writes are in flight |
| `warnBeforeLeaving()` | adds a `beforeunload` guard that only asks while a write is running, and returns the function that removes it; returning it from `$effect`, as above, removes it with the component |
| `watchPendingWrites(listener)` | the same count without Svelte, from `#api`; returns a function that stops listening |

- A write counts from the call until its answer, retries included, and also when it fails.
- The browser shows its own "Leave site?" text; pages cannot change it.
- `warnBeforeLeaving()` covers closing and reloading the tab. Navigations inside the app keep running the write.
- Put both into your root layout once, as the showcase does.

### Uploads

Uploads work with `FormData`. Ktor cannot infer a multipart body from `receiveMultipart`, so describe it once, and the generated function takes `body: FormData`:

```kotlin
post("/api/notes/{id}/attachments") {
    call.receiveMultipart().forEachPart { part -> part.dispose() }
    call.respond(HttpStatusCode.NoContent)
}.describe {
    requestBody { ContentType.MultiPart.FormData() }
}
```

Pass `onUploadProgress` to follow the upload. `fetch` cannot report upload progress, so such a call uses `XMLHttpRequest` instead, with the same headers, errors and `signal` support:

```ts
const form = new FormData();
form.append('file', file);
await api.notes.attachments(id, form, {
    onUploadProgress: ({ loaded, total }) => (progress = total ? loaded / total : 0)
});
```

Uploads count towards `maxApiBodySize`, which is 1 MiB by default, so raise it for routes that accept files.

Rules for size and type that are checked in the browser and on the server, and forms with named fields, are in [Upload files](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/recipes/uploads).

## The server talks back

### Toasts from the server

Often the route knows best what to tell the user: that the note was saved, that it was the last free seat, that the export will arrive by mail. Say it there:

```kotlin
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.ToastKind
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.toast

post("/api/notes") {
    val note = store.create(call.receive<Note>())
    call.toast("Note saved", ToastKind.Success)
    call.respond(HttpStatusCode.Created, note)
}
```

With `toasts()` on, the browser shows it when the answer arrives, and no component has to know. The kinds are `Info` (the default), `Success`, `Warning` and `Error`. With [i18n](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/frontend-libraries#i18n), pass a message in the visitor's language, such as `call.toast(call.messages.noteSaved())`.

- The toast travels in a response header, so the body and its type stay what they are, and it works with any status, also with an error or an empty 204.
- Call `toast` before you respond.
- A response carries up to five toasts of up to 500 characters each.
- The generated client reads the header on answers from your own origin only, so another server cannot put words into your app.
- Without `toasts()`, set `apiConfig.onToast = (message, kind) => ...` to show them your way, and nothing is shown until you do.
- Calls made on the server during SSR do not show toasts.

### Navigation from the server

"Create it, then open it" is the same few lines in every form: wait for the answer, read the ID, call `goto`. The route already knows where to go, so let it say so:

```kotlin
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.navigateTo

post("/api/notes") {
    val note = store.create(call.receive<Note>())
    call.navigateTo("/notes/${note.id}")
    call.respond(HttpStatusCode.Created, note)
}
```

With [typed routes](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/routes) on, write `call.navigateTo(FrontendRoutes.notesId(note.id))`, and a renamed page cannot leave a stale path behind.

After the call succeeded, the browser opens that page with SvelteKit's `goto`, so it is a client-side navigation and not a reload. The code that awaited the call runs first, so it can still use the result. A failed call navigates nowhere.

With `toasts()` on, this is wired up for you. Without it, add one line to your root layout:

```ts
import { goto } from '$app/navigation';
import { apiConfig } from '#api';

apiConfig.onNavigate = (path) => void goto(path);
```

**Safe by design**
The path has to be one inside your app: `navigateTo` refuses anything that does not start with a single `/`, and the client ignores such a header as well, and reads it on answers from your own origin only. So the header cannot be used to send a visitor to another site.

### Reload after a deploy

Every API response carries the fingerprint of the frontend build the server runs, in the `X-Ktor-Svelte-Build` header. When a response reports a different build than the first one the page saw, the client calls `apiConfig.onNewBuild`, so you can offer a reload instead of running old code against a new API.

The toasts library has that prompt ready. Turn it on in Gradle and run `svelteSync`:

```kotlin
svelte {
    libraries {
        toasts { reloadPrompt() }
    }
}
```

After a deploy, the next API call shows "A new version is available." with a Reload button. The toast stays until the visitor reloads or closes it, and it shows once, not after every call. Change the texts through `toastMessages.newBuild` and `toastMessages.reload`.

To do something else, set the handler yourself. Your handler wins over the prompt:

```ts
import { apiConfig } from '#api';
import { toast } from '#lib/ktor-svelte/toasts';

apiConfig.onNewBuild = () => {
    toast('We just shipped an update.', { duration: 0, action: { label: 'Reload', run: () => location.reload() } });
};
```

Set `buildHeader = false` in `install(Svelte)` to leave the header out.

### The visitor's time zone

The server usually runs in UTC, and the visitor does not. The generated client sends the browser's time zone with every call to your app, and a route reads it as `call.timeZone`:

```kotlin
get("/api/report") {
    val today = java.time.LocalDate.now(call.timeZone)
    call.respondText("Report for $today")
}
```

- It is a `java.time.ZoneId`, such as `Europe/Zurich`, taken from the `X-Time-Zone` header.
- A request without the header, or with a name the JDK does not know, gets `defaultTimeZone` from `install(Svelte)`, which is `UTC` unless you change it. That covers requests the client does not make, such as a plain link to a download.
- The header only goes to your own origin, never to a `baseUrl` on another host.
- To stop sending it, set `apiConfig.sendTimeZone = false`.

## Slow and flaky networks

### Timeouts

A request that hangs blocks the UI until the browser gives up, which can take minutes. Set a timeout for every call, or for one:

```ts
import { api, apiConfig, isTimeoutError } from '#api';

apiConfig.timeout = 10_000;

try {
    const report = await api.reports.create(input, { timeout: 60_000 });
} catch (error) {
    if (isTimeoutError(error)) showError('The server took too long. Please try again.');
}
```

- A per-call `timeout` wins over `apiConfig.timeout`, and your own `signal` still works next to it.
- There is no timeout unless you set one.
- Event streams ignore `apiConfig.timeout`, because a live stream is supposed to stay open. Give one its own `timeout` if you want that.

#### A time limit per route

When a route knows how long it may take, say so on the route. The generated function then uses that as its timeout, and the server stops the handler when the time is up:

```kotlin
import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.seconds

get("/api/reports/summary") {
    call.respond(listOf("Summary"))
}.timeout(30.seconds)
```

```ts
const summary = await api.reports.summary();
const patient = await api.reports.summary({ timeout: 120_000 });
```

| Where | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| Generated function | Calls get `timeout: 30000` unless the call passes its own `timeout`. It wins over `apiConfig.timeout` like any per-call timeout. |
| Server | When the handler is still running after the limit, it is cancelled and the route answers `503` with `{"message": "This request took longer than its limit of 30s."}`. An answer that has already started is left alone. |

`timeout` takes a positive, finite `Duration`. Use it for slow reports, exports and calls to other services, so a stuck request fails in the same, known time on both sides.

### Retries

A GET that fails because the network dropped, the request timed out, or a proxy answered 502, 503 or 504 often works a moment later. Turn retries on once, and the client tries again by itself:

```ts
import { apiConfig } from '#api';

apiConfig.retry = true;
```

It then makes up to three attempts, waiting 300 ms before the second and 600 ms before the third. Only GET requests are retried, because repeating a write could do the work twice (see [Writes that are safe to send twice](#writes-that-are-safe-to-send-twice)). Every other answer, such as a 404 or a 500, fails at once as before, and `apiConfig.onError` only hears about the last failure.

To change the numbers, pass them instead of `true`. A single call can also set its own, or opt out:

```ts
apiConfig.retry = { attempts: 5, delay: 200, maxDelay: 2000 };

const notes = await api.notes.list({ retry: false });
const report = await api.reports.get(id, { retry: { attempts: 2 } });
```

| Setting | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `attempts` | `3` | Attempts in total, the first one included |
| `delay` | `300` | Milliseconds before the second attempt. It doubles after every attempt |
| `maxDelay` | `5000` | The longest wait between attempts, and the longest [rate limit](#rate-limits) wait the client sits out |

A call that is aborted through its `signal` stops waiting at once, and each attempt gets the full `timeout`.

### Rate limits
