- `img-src` and `font-src` allow `data:` because Tailwind, DaisyUI and Vite inline small images, icons and fonts as data URLs. `blob:` covers images made in the browser, such as upload previews.
- `frame-ancestors` follows `frameOptions`: `'none'` for `DENY`, `'self'` for `SAMEORIGIN`, and left out when `frameOptions` is `null`.

API responses, JavaScript, CSS and other files get no CSP, since it only matters for documents.

No CSP is sent while the dev proxy is active, because Vite injects its own scripts. The other headers are still sent.

### Allow other origins

To load something from another origin, such as an analytics script, add sources to a directive. A directive that is not in the policy yet is added with exactly the sources you list:

```kotlin
securityHeaders {
    allowCspSources("script-src", "https://plausible.io")
    allowCspSources("connect-src", "https://plausible.io")
    allowCspSources("img-src", "https://avatars.example.com")
}
```

### Your own policy

To use your own policy instead, set `contentSecurityPolicy`. It is then sent unchanged on every response, and `allowCspSources` is ignored. Inline scripts in your pages break unless your policy allows them, for example with SvelteKit's own `csp` option in `hash` mode.

### Opting out

```kotlin
securityHeaders { automaticContentSecurityPolicy = false }
securityHeaders { enabled = false }
```

The first turns off only the automatic CSP. The second turns off all security headers.

## API request guards

Two checks protect every path under your API prefixes: the origin check and the body size limit. Both are on by default. The [JSON shape check](#json-shape), [hidden error details](#error-details) and the [rate limit](#rate-limits) add to them.

| Setting | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `originCheck` | `true` | Refuses writes from other sites with 403 |
| `allowedOrigins(...)` | none | Origins whose writes are accepted anyway |
| `maxApiBodySize` | `1048576` (1 MiB) | Largest request body on API paths, in bytes. `null` removes the limit |
| `maxJsonDepth` | `64` | Deepest nesting of a JSON body. `null` turns the check off |
| `maxJsonStringLength` | `null` | Longest string in a JSON body |
| `hideErrorDetails` | `true` | Hides exception messages in production |

Paths outside your API prefixes, such as frontend files and the dev proxy, are not affected.

### Origin check

POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE and every other method except GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE from a browser on another site are refused with 403, so a cookie session cannot be used for cross-site request forgery. A request is refused when:

- its `Origin` header names a different host than the request, or is `null`, or
- it has no `Origin` but sends `Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site`.

Only the host is compared, ignoring case, scheme and port, so a TLS-terminating proxy or the Vite dev port does not cause false rejections. The request host comes from Ktor's `origin`, so it follows `XForwardedHeaders` or `ForwardedHeaders` when you install them. Requests with neither header, such as curl, server-to-server calls and tests, are allowed, because browsers always send one of them. GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE are never checked.

To accept writes from another frontend, such as a separate admin app, list its exact origin:

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    allowedOrigins("https://admin.example.com")
}
```

List every origin in one call: a second call replaces the list.

A refused cross-origin write gets `{"message":"Cross-origin API request refused."}`. In development mode the message also says how to allow the origin, which production leaves out so it does not tell attackers which setting to look for.

### Body size limit

Request bodies on API paths are limited to 1 MiB. Larger bodies get 413, whether they send `Content-Length` or are chunked, with a JSON body such as `{"message":"Request body is larger than the limit of 1048576 bytes."}`. It uses Ktor's `RequestBodyLimit` plugin, so do not install that plugin yourself unless you set `maxApiBodySize = null`.

A compressed request body is a way around a size limit, because a few kilobytes can unpack to gigabytes. Ktor only unpacks request bodies when its `Compression` plugin is installed for requests, which `transport { compression() }` does. ktor-svelte then applies the same limit to the unpacked size, so such a body gets 413 as well. The default API compression only compresses responses and never unpacks requests. If you install `Compression` yourself, set its `maxDecodedContentLength`.

To raise the limit, or turn the origin check off:

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    originCheck = false
    maxApiBodySize = 10L * 1024 * 1024
}
```

Set `maxApiBodySize = null` to remove the limit. An app that takes uploads raises it to the largest upload it accepts, as in [Upload files](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/recipes/uploads).

### JSON shape

A small body can still be expensive to parse when it nests thousands of arrays. JSON bodies on API paths are checked while they stream in, before any parsing: more than 64 levels of nesting answers 400 with `{"message":"Request JSON is nested deeper than 64 levels."}`. Set `maxJsonStringLength` to also refuse long strings, which is off by default because the body limit already caps them:

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    maxJsonDepth = 32
    maxJsonStringLength = 10_000
}
```

Set `maxJsonDepth = null` to turn the depth check off.

### Error details

In production, an exception that no route handles answers with its status and a generic message, such as `{"message":"Internal Server Error."}` on API paths, instead of the exception message, which Ktor sends by default and which can reveal internals. Malformed or unreadable bodies keep their 400 or 415 without naming your classes. The exception is still logged. In development mode, or when you install `StatusPages`, nothing changes. Set `hideErrorDetails = false` to send the messages again.

### Counting refusals

ktor-svelte counts every refused request, so attacks and misconfigurations show up as numbers, not only as log lines. Read the counters from `application.svelteMetrics`, or from the `refusals` object of the [status endpoint](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/endpoints#status-endpoint).

| Counter | Counts |
| --- | --- |
| `crossOriginRefusals` | Writes refused by the origin check |
| `bodyTooLargeRefusals` | Bodies refused by the size limit |
| `rateLimitRefusals` | Requests refused by a rate limit |

To export them, bind them to your metrics library, for example Micrometer:

```kotlin
val metrics = svelteMetrics
registry.gauge("svelte.refusals", listOf(Tag.of("reason", "cross_origin")), metrics) { it.crossOriginRefusals.toDouble() }
registry.gauge("svelte.refusals", listOf(Tag.of("reason", "body_too_large")), metrics) { it.bodyTooLargeRefusals.toDouble() }
registry.gauge("svelte.refusals", listOf(Tag.of("reason", "rate_limit")), metrics) { it.rateLimitRefusals.toDouble() }
```

## Rate limits

Each client may send 120 writes per minute to your API paths, meaning every method except GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE. More get 429 with a `Retry-After` header. Reads and frontend files are never limited. Clients are told apart by `call.request.origin.remoteAddress`, so behind a reverse proxy install `XForwardedHeaders` or `ForwardedHeaders`, or every user shares one limit.

| Setting | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `apiWrites` | `120` | Writes per client and period. `0` drops the default limit and keeps the named ones |
| `period` | `1.minutes` | The period of the default limit |
| `algorithm` | `RateLimitAlgorithm.FixedWindow` | How the default limit counts. See [Algorithms](#algorithms) |
| `key { call -> }` | The client address | What tells clients apart |
| `limit(name, requests, per, algorithm, key)` | none | A named limit for the routes you wrap in `rateLimit(RateLimitName(name))` |
| `enabled` | `true` | `false` turns off rate limiting |

```kotlin
rateLimit {
    apiWrites = 600
    period = 5.minutes
}
```

### A tighter limit for one route

Routes such as login need a much tighter limit. Name one, and wrap the routes in Ktor's own `rateLimit`:

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    rateLimit {
        apiWrites = 300
        limit("login", requests = 5, per = 1.minutes)
    }
}

routing {
    rateLimit(RateLimitName("login")) {
        post("/api/login") { /* ... */ }
    }
}
```

A named limit applies on top of the default one. The generated client knows about 429 answers: see [Rate limits in the client](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/calling-the-api#rate-limits).

### Algorithms

Limits use a fixed window by default: the budget refills completely at the end of each period, so a client can send a full budget just before the edge and another just after it. Pick another algorithm when that matters:

| Algorithm | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `RateLimitAlgorithm.FixedWindow` | The default. Cheapest, but allows a burst of twice the limit around the window edge |
| `RateLimitAlgorithm.SlidingWindow` | Never more than the limit in any period, wherever it starts |
| `RateLimitAlgorithm.TokenBucket` | Allows a burst up to the limit, then refills steadily over the period |

```kotlin
rateLimit {
    algorithm = RateLimitAlgorithm.SlidingWindow
    limit("login", requests = 5, per = 1.minutes, algorithm = RateLimitAlgorithm.TokenBucket)
}
```

### Who counts as one client

By default every client address gets its own budget. Choose another key when that is wrong, for example many users behind one office address. `key` applies to every limit, and a named limit can take its own:

```kotlin
rateLimit {
    key { call -> call.sessions.get<UserSession>()?.userId ?: call.request.origin.remoteAddress }
    limit("export", requests = 2, per = 1.hours) { call -> call.sessions.get<UserSession>()?.userId ?: "anonymous" }
}
```

The default limit runs before routing, so read the user from the session there, not from `call.principal()`, which only `authenticate` routes set. Do not read the request body in a key: it would be gone by the time your route receives it.

It uses Ktor's `RateLimit` plugin, so do not install that plugin yourself unless you set `rateLimit { enabled = false }`. `apiWrites = 0` keeps the named limits but drops the default one.

## Malformed requests

A path with a broken percent escape, such as `/%zz`, and a `Host` header that cannot be parsed answer 400. They are the client's mistake, so they do not show up as errors in your log.

## Internal endpoints

The [status endpoint](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/endpoints#status-endpoint) answers only requests from this machine, and the [API docs](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/endpoints#api-docs) exist only in development. To open them to a monitoring job, an office network or your admins, and to nobody else, use `internalAccess { }`: see [Who may see internal endpoints](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/endpoints#who-may-see-internal-endpoints). The health endpoint answers everyone, since it reveals nothing beyond up or down.

## Full example

A public app behind a reverse proxy, with a sign-in route, an analytics script and a separate admin frontend:

```kotlin
install(XForwardedHeaders) // so the origin check and the rate limit see the real client

install(Svelte) {
    siteUrl = "https://notes.example.com"
    allowedOrigins("https://admin.notes.example.com")
    maxApiBodySize = 5L * 1024 * 1024 // uploads up to 5 MiB
    maxJsonDepth = 32
    securityHeaders {
        allowCspSources("script-src", "https://plausible.io")
        allowCspSources("connect-src", "https://plausible.io")
    }
    rateLimit {
        algorithm = RateLimitAlgorithm.SlidingWindow
        key { call -> call.sessions.get<UserSession>()?.userId ?: call.request.origin.remoteAddress }
        limit("login", requests = 5, per = 1.minutes, algorithm = RateLimitAlgorithm.TokenBucket)
    }
    statusEndpoint = true
    internalAccess { token = env("INTERNAL_TOKEN") }
}

routing {
    rateLimit(RateLimitName("login")) {
        post("/api/session") { /* check the password, set the session */ }
    }
}
```

## Use cases

- **Cookie sessions:** the origin check is what keeps a cookie session safe from cross-site request forgery. See [Sign in with a session cookie](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/recipes/sessions).
- **Login and sign-up routes:** a named rate limit, as above.
- **Uploads:** raise `maxApiBodySize` to the largest file you accept. See [Upload files](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/recipes/uploads).
- **Analytics, maps, avatars from a CDN:** `allowCspSources`.
- **A second frontend on another domain:** `allowedOrigins`.
- **Monitoring:** the refusal counters in `svelteMetrics` and the status endpoint.

## Good to know

**Behind a reverse proxy**
Install Ktor's `XForwardedHeaders` or `ForwardedHeaders`. Without it, the origin check compares against the proxy's host, every user shares one rate limit, and `networks` in `internalAccess` lets nobody in.

- The guards only cover paths under your API prefixes. Routes outside them, such as a webhook at `/hooks/stripe`, need their own checks.
- Ktor's `RequestBodyLimit` and `RateLimit` plugins are installed by ktor-svelte. Install them yourself only after turning ktor-svelte's version off.
- Server-sent events count as a GET, so they are never rate limited or blocked by the origin check.

## What runs on your machine

ktor-svelte runs other people's code in three places, and it is worth knowing which.

**The setup script.** `setup.sh` and `setup.ps1` ask Maven Central for the latest version, download `scripts/Setup.java` for that version's tag from this repository over HTTPS, and run it with your `java`. Nothing is installed globally. The shell script does nothing until it has arrived completely, and both scripts refuse a version that is not made of letters, digits, dots and dashes. If you would rather read the code first, download it and run it yourself:

```bash
curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nijasc/ktor-svelte/v<version>/scripts/Setup.java
```

```bash
java Setup.java --version=<version>
```

**Your package manager.** `svelteInstall` runs `bun install --frozen-lockfile`, `npm ci`, `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` or `yarn install --frozen-lockfile`, so a build only installs what your lockfile names. Install scripts of dependencies run as your package manager allows: Bun and pnpm only run them for packages you trust explicitly, npm and Yarn run them for every package unless you set `ignore-scripts`. ktor-svelte does not change that setting for you. Only `svelteSync`, `svelteInit` and `svelteUpdateDependencies` change `package.json` or the lockfile, and never as part of a build.

**The pinned Bun.** With `bunVersion` set, the plugin downloads that exact Bun release from GitHub and checks it against the release's `SHASUMS256.txt` before unpacking it. See [Pin Bun](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/reference/gradle#pin-bun).

## Software bill of materials

Every [GitHub release](https://github.com/nijasc/ktor-svelte/releases) has a [CycloneDX](https://cyclonedx.org) SBOM for each artifact attached: `ktor-svelte-server-<version>.cdx.json` and `ktor-svelte-gradle-plugin-<version>.cdx.json`. They list the runtime dependencies with versions, licenses and hashes, so you can feed them to Dependency-Track or a license scanner before approving an upgrade. Test and compile-only dependencies are left out. The plugin's own list is short, because Gradle provides the rest.

## Verifying a release

Every JAR of a release, for the runtime and for the Gradle plugin, has signed [SLSA build provenance](https://slsa.dev/spec/v1.0/provenance). It records that the file was built by the release workflow of this repository from the tagged commit, and it is signed with [Sigstore](https://www.sigstore.dev) through GitHub artifact attestations. To check a JAR you downloaded, for example from Maven Central or your Gradle cache, use the GitHub CLI:

```bash
gh attestation verify ktor-svelte-server-<version>.jar --repo nijasc/ktor-svelte
```

It fails if the file was changed or built anywhere else. Maven Central also has the usual PGP signature next to every file.

## Reporting a vulnerability

See [SECURITY.md](https://github.com/nijasc/ktor-svelte/blob/main/SECURITY.md) for how to report a vulnerability privately, and for a table of every secure default.

Source: https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/endpoints

# Built-in endpoints

Small endpoints that every app ends up writing: a sitemap and `robots.txt`, a favicon, a status page for you, a health check for your load balancer and Swagger UI for your API. The status and health endpoints and Swagger UI are off by default; the sitemap, `robots.txt` and the favicon are on until your build brings its own.

<Badge type="tip" text="Ktor plugin" />

## Quick start

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    siteUrl = "https://example.com"
    healthEndpoint = true
    statusEndpoint = true
    apiDocs = true
}
```

| Endpoint | Path | Default | Who may call it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Sitemap](#sitemap-and-robots-txt) | `/sitemap.xml` | On, unless your build has one | Everyone |
| [robots.txt](#sitemap-and-robots-txt) | `/robots.txt` | On, unless your build has one | Everyone |
| [Favicon](#default-favicon) | `/favicon.ico`, `/favicon.svg`, `/favicon.png`, `/apple-touch-icon.png` | On, until your build has an icon | Everyone |
| [Status](#status-endpoint) | `/_ktor-svelte/status` | Off | This machine, or [whom you allow](#who-may-see-internal-endpoints) |
| [Health](#health-endpoint) | `/_ktor-svelte/health` | Off | Everyone |
| [API docs](#api-docs) | `/api/docs` | Off | Development only, or [whom you allow](#who-may-see-internal-endpoints) |

## Sitemap and robots.txt

Search engines find your pages through `/sitemap.xml` and read `/robots.txt` first. ktor-svelte serves both for you when your build has neither:

- `/sitemap.xml` lists every prerendered page in the build, so `about.html` becomes `/about` and `docs/index.html` becomes `/docs/`. The SPA fallback and the 404 page are left out.
- `/robots.txt` lets crawlers read all pages, keeps them out of your API prefixes and `/_ktor-svelte/`, and points to the sitemap.

Pages that only exist at runtime, such as `/notes/42`, can't be listed, because there is no file for them. URLs in both files must be absolute, so set the public address of your site. Otherwise it is taken from the request, which behind a proxy needs Ktor's `ForwardedHeaders` or `XForwardedHeaders` plugin:

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    siteUrl = "https://example.com"
}
```

| Setting | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `sitemap` | `true` | `false` turns off both `/sitemap.xml` and `/robots.txt` |
| `siteUrl` | `null`, taken from the request | The public address used in both files |

- To write your own, put `sitemap.xml` or `robots.txt` in `frontend/static/`. Files from the build always win.
- With `routing = SvelteRouting.Manual`, they are only served where you route `svelte()`. Put them in the `public` list if the rest is [behind a login](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/auth#put-the-frontend-behind-a-login).
- With [i18n URL prefixes](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/frontend-libraries#i18n), every language's pages are prerendered, so each one is listed.

## Default favicon

Browsers ask every site for `/favicon.ico`. Until your app has its own icon, ktor-svelte answers with a ktor-svelte one, so tabs and bookmarks show something and the log has no 404s for it. It serves `/favicon.ico`, `/favicon.svg`, `/favicon.png` and `/apple-touch-icon.png`, cached for a day.

As soon as your build has any of `favicon.ico`, `favicon.svg` or `favicon.png`, for example in `frontend/static/`, none of the defaults are served and yours are used. In development, ktor-svelte checks `frontend/static/` instead.

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    defaultFavicon = false
}
```

turns the default off.

## Status endpoint

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    statusEndpoint = true
}
```

`GET /_ktor-svelte/status` returns JSON about the running app:

| Field | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `present`, `formatVersion`, `files`, `fingerprint` | The bundled build |
| `proxy`, and when active `url` and `reachable` | The dev proxy |
| `refusals`: `crossOrigin`, `bodyTooLarge`, `rateLimit` | How many requests the [security guards](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/security#api-request-guards) refused |

It is off by default, never cached, hidden from the OpenAPI document, and answers only requests from this machine with a local `Host`. Everything else gets 403, unless you [open it to more callers](#who-may-see-internal-endpoints).

```bash
curl -s http://localhost:8080/_ktor-svelte/status
```

## Health endpoint

For load balancers, container orchestrators and uptime checks:

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    healthEndpoint = true
    healthCheck { database.isReachable() }
}
```

`GET /_ktor-svelte/health` answers `200` with `{"status":"up"}` when the frontend can be served and every `healthCheck` returns `true`, and `503` with `{"status":"down"}` otherwise.

- Add as many `healthCheck { }` blocks as you need. Each is a `suspend` function that returns `true` when its part is fine.
- A check that throws counts as down and is logged.
- Unlike the status endpoint, it answers every client, because it reveals nothing beyond up or down.
- It is off by default, never cached and hidden from the OpenAPI document.

A Docker health check, for example:

```text
HEALTHCHECK CMD curl -fs http://localhost:8080/_ktor-svelte/health || exit 1
```

## API docs

`apiDocs = true` serves Swagger UI at `/api/docs` in development mode only, using the same OpenAPI document as `generateTs`.

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    apiDocs = true
    apiDocsPath = "/api/reference"
}
```

| Setting | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `apiDocs` | `false` | Serves Swagger UI |
| `apiDocsPath` | `/api/docs` | Where it is served |

The page loads its scripts from a public CDN, so it needs internet access.

To have the docs on a deployed app as well, say [who may see them](#who-may-see-internal-endpoints). Without that they stay a development tool.

## Who may see internal endpoints

The status endpoint and the API docs are for you and your tools, not for visitors. By default the status endpoint answers this machine only, and the docs exist in development only. One block opens both to the callers you name, and to nobody else:

```kotlin
import io.ktor.server.sessions.get
import io.ktor.server.sessions.sessions

install(Svelte) {
    statusEndpoint = true
    apiDocs = true
    internalAccess {
        token = env("INTERNAL_TOKEN")
        networks("10.0.0.0/8", "fd00::/8")
        allow { call -> call.sessions.get<UserSession>()?.userId == "admin" }
    }
}
```

A request gets in when any one of them lets it in. Requests from this machine always do.

| Setting | Lets in | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| `token` | Requests with `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. At least 16 characters, compared in constant time | A monitoring job that reads the status endpoint |
| `networks(...)` | Clients whose address is in one of the ranges, IPv4 or IPv6 | An office network or a VPN |
| `allow { call -> ... }` | Whatever your own check accepts, such as a signed-in user with a role | Opening the API docs in a browser, which cannot send a token |

- With `internalAccess` set, `apiDocs = true` serves the docs outside development too, behind the same rules.
- Everyone else gets 403, or 401 with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer` when a token is configured and none was sent. The answer says `This endpoint is internal.` and is never cached.
- The app does not start with a token that is too short or a range it cannot read. A long random value, such as the output of `openssl rand -hex 32`, makes a good token.

A monitoring job then reads the status with its token:

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $INTERNAL_TOKEN" https://example.com/_ktor-svelte/status
```

With [permissions](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/auth#permissions), `allow` can ask for one, so your admins open the docs in their browser:

```kotlin
internalAccess {
    allow { call -> call.can(Permission.UsersManage) }
}
```

**Behind a reverse proxy**
Every request reaches the app from the proxy's address, which is usually a private one. A network range would then let the whole internet in, so ktor-svelte refuses it: when a request carries `X-Forwarded-For`, `Forwarded` or `X-Real-IP` and the app has not told Ktor to trust the proxy, `networks` lets nobody in. Install Ktor's `XForwardedHeaders` or `ForwardedHeaders` plugin, and the range is checked against the client's real address.

The health endpoint and the public build info stay open, since they are made for callers you do not know.

## Use cases

- **A public site:** set `siteUrl`, and search engines get a sitemap and `robots.txt` that match your build.
- **Kubernetes, Docker or a load balancer:** `healthEndpoint` with a `healthCheck` per dependency, such as the database.
- **Watching a deployed app:** `statusEndpoint` with a `token` for your monitoring, to see the build fingerprint and the refused requests.
- **Sharing the API with a frontend team or a partner:** `apiDocs` with `internalAccess`, opened to signed-in admins or an office network.

## Good to know

- The status, health and docs endpoints are hidden from the OpenAPI document, so they never show up in the generated client.
- The paths under `/_ktor-svelte/` are kept out of `robots.txt`.
- To check that the JAR you ship really starts and answers, see the [smoke test](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/deployment#smoke-test).

Source: https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/transport

# Transport and compression

JSON, XML and other formats, and compressed API responses. ktor-svelte can set up Ktor's `ContentNegotiation` and `Compression` for you, and compresses API responses by default.

<Badge type="tip" text="Ktor plugin" />

## Quick start

Choose how your API talks inside `install(Svelte)`. Without a `transport` block, nothing is installed and you stay in control.

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    transport {
        json { prettyPrint = true }
        xml()
        compression()
    }
}
```

## Formats

| Function | Effect |
|---|---|
| `json()` | Adds JSON to Ktor's `ContentNegotiation`. Takes a `kotlinx.serialization` `Json` builder |
| `xml()` | Adds XML. Needs `implementation("io.ktor:ktor-serialization-kotlinx-xml")` in your build |
| `negotiation { }` | Registers any other format, such as CBOR, on `ContentNegotiation` directly |
| `compression { }` | Installs Ktor's `Compression`. Takes its normal configuration, and defaults to gzip and deflate |

- The client picks a format with its `Accept` header, and the first format you list is the default.
- The generated TypeScript client always speaks JSON.

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    transport {
        json { ignoreUnknownKeys = true }
    }
}
```

**Already installing these plugins yourself?**
You will get a clear error at startup, so remove one of the two.

## API compression

API responses are compressed by default, without any `transport` block. Responses of 1 KiB or more on your API paths with a JSON, XML, CBOR or text content type are sent with gzip or deflate, whichever the client prefers.

- Browsers decompress them natively, so the generated client and DevTools see plain JSON.
- Clients that send no `Accept-Encoding`, such as curl, get plain JSON too.
- Server-sent events, small responses, other content types and frontend files are left alone.
- Request bodies are never decompressed.
- Files precompressed by your adapter are left alone.

| Setting in `install(Svelte)` | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `apiCompression` | `true` | Compresses API responses as described above |

### zstd

Add Ktor's zstd module, and current browsers get zstd instead, which compresses about as well as gzip at a fraction of the CPU time:

```kotlin
implementation("io.ktor:ktor-server-compression-zstd:<ktor version>")
```

It adds a native library of about 7 MB to your JAR, which is why it is not included by default.

### Your own configuration

If you install `Compression` yourself, before or after `install(Svelte)`, or use `transport { compression() }`, your configuration is used instead. To send API responses uncompressed:

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    apiCompression = false
}
```

### Compression and secrets

**BREACH**
A response that contains a secret, such as an API key, next to text an attacker can choose can leak that secret byte by byte through its compressed size (the BREACH attack). ktor-svelte's own CSRF protection uses no tokens, so it is not affected. If one of your endpoints returns such a mix, turn `apiCompression` off or install `Compression` yourself with a condition that skips that route.

### Why compression and not a binary format

For 5000 notes, measured from server to parsed data:

| | 50 Mbit connection | 4G |
|---|---|---|
| Plain JSON | 318 ms | 1537 ms |
| gzip | 152 ms | 381 ms |
| zstd | 84 ms | 345 ms |

CBOR was 7 percent smaller than JSON before compression and larger after it, and decoding it in JavaScript took about seven times as long as `JSON.parse`, so it never came out ahead.

## Full example

An API that serves JSON to the generated client, XML and CBOR to other callers that ask for them, and compresses with your own settings.

::: code-group

```kotlin no-check [build.gradle.kts]
dependencies {
    implementation("io.ktor:ktor-serialization-kotlinx-xml")
    implementation("io.ktor:ktor-serialization-kotlinx-cbor")
}
```

```kotlin no-check [Application.kt]
@OptIn(ExperimentalSerializationApi::class)
fun Application.module() {
    install(Svelte) {
        generateTs = true
        transport {
            json { ignoreUnknownKeys = true }
            xml()
            negotiation { cbor() }
            compression {
                gzip { priority = 1.0 }
                deflate { priority = 0.5 }
            }
        }
    }
    routing {
        get("/api/notes") { call.respond(store.all()) }
    }
}
```

```bash
curl http://localhost:8080/api/notes
curl -H "Accept: application/xml" http://localhost:8080/api/notes
curl -H "Accept-Encoding: gzip" --compressed http://localhost:8080/api/notes
```

JSON stays the default, because it is listed first. A caller that sends `Accept: application/xml` gets XML, and one that asks for `application/cbor` gets CBOR.

## Use cases

- Most apps: nothing to do. JSON through your own `ContentNegotiation`, and API compression on by default.
- One place for the setup: `transport { json() }` instead of installing `ContentNegotiation` yourself.
- Partners that need XML or CBOR: `xml()` or `negotiation { }`.
- Large lists on slow connections: keep `apiCompression` on, and add zstd.
- Responses that mix secrets with user input: turn `apiCompression` off for them, see [Compression and secrets](#compression-and-secrets).

## Good to know

- The generated TypeScript client always speaks JSON, whatever else you add.
- Installing `ContentNegotiation` or `Compression` yourself and through `transport` fails at startup with a clear error.
- See [Calling the API](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/calling-the-api) for the client, and the [Ktor reference](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/reference/ktor) for every setting.

Source: https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/dev-workflow

# Dev workflow

One command runs Vite, the Kotlin compiler and your app together. Save a Svelte file and the page hot reloads, save a Kotlin file and the app restarts, and a panel in the page shows every API call it made.

<Badge type="info" text="Gradle" /> <Badge type="tip" text="Ktor plugin" />

## Quick start

```bash
./gradlew svelteDevAll
```

Then open Ktor's port, not Vite's: `http://localhost:8080`. In IntelliJ, this is the `Dev` run configuration, and `./gradlew dev` is the [short name](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/reference/gradle#short-task-names).

| You change | What happens |
|---|---|
| A `.svelte` or `.ts` file | Vite hot reloads the page |
| A Kotlin file | The app restarts, open pages reload their data, and with `generateTs` on the TypeScript client updates a moment later, so type errors show up in the editor right away |
| A file in `src/main/resources` | The app restarts |
| A page folder (added, moved, deleted) | `routes.ts` updates at once, and `FrontendRoutes` follows with a restart |

A restart loses anything your app keeps in memory. Stopping the task stops all three processes.

## The ready banner

Once the app is listening, it prints the links you need, so they do not get lost in the output:

```text
ktor-svelte is ready. Open the app URL, not the Vite one:
  App:      http://localhost:8080
  API docs: http://localhost:8080/api/docs
  Vite:     http://localhost:5173
```

- It also opens the app in your default browser, the first time only, so restarts do not open new tabs. It never does so in CI or on a Linux machine without a display. Turn it off with `svelte { dev { openBrowser = false } }`.
- The API docs line appears when `apiDocs = true`.
- After a restart it prints one line with the app URL instead.
- The URL comes from Ktor's `Responding at` log line, so keep Ktor's INFO logging on for the application logger.
- With [HTTPS in development](#https-in-development) on, the banner and the browser use the HTTPS address.

## One console for everything

Vite, the compiler and the app write to one console in the same shape, so you can tell them apart at a glance:

```text
10:17:17  app      INFO   Application started in 0.959 seconds.
10:17:17  vite     INFO   (ssr) connected.
10:17:31  kotlin   ERROR  file:///home/me/shop/src/main/kotlin/shop/Routes.kt:24:16 Initializer type mismatch: expected 'Int', actual 'String'.
10:17:32  kotlin   ERROR  does not compile: 1 error
10:17:34  kotlin   INFO   compiled
```

- Each source has its own color, and warnings and errors stand out. Colors are off when `CI` or `NO_COLOR` is set, or the terminal is `dumb`.
- Compiler errors and browser stack traces point to your files as `file:///...:line:column` links, which IntelliJ opens at that line when you click them. Browser frames such as `http://localhost:8080/src/routes/+page.svelte:12:5` are turned into links to the file in `frontend/`.
- App lines keep the time and level your logging framework printed, and show the logger's class name when it isn't `Application`.
- Left out on purpose: Vite's start banner, its copies of browser console messages (ktor-svelte forwards those itself), and Gradle's build failure boilerplate. The ready banner already lists the URLs and the compiler errors say what failed.

### Shorter stack traces

Stack traces from your app are shortened so the lines that matter stay on screen. Runs of frames from Netty, coroutines and the Ktor engine become one `... framework frames hidden` line, and your own frames stay.

The frames that come from your own source files are named first, right under the exception, each with a link that opens the file at that line. In the stack trace itself they keep their normal color, and every frame from a library is dimmed:

```text
09:28:32  app      ERROR  Errors Request failed
09:28:32  app             java.lang.IllegalStateException: No such note
09:28:32  app                 your code: app.notes.NoteStore.find  file:///home/you/app/src/main/kotlin/app/notes/NoteStore.kt:42
09:28:32  app                 your code: app.notes.RoutesKt$noteRoutes$1.invokeSuspend  file:///home/you/app/src/main/kotlin/app/notes/Routes.kt:17
09:28:32  app             	at io.ktor.utils.io.ByteChannel.getClosedCause(ByteChannel.kt:350)
09:28:32  app             	at app.notes.NoteStore.find(NoteStore.kt:42)
09:28:32  app             	at app.notes.RoutesKt$noteRoutes$1.invokeSuspend(Routes.kt:17)
09:28:32  app             	... framework frames hidden
```

A frame is yours when its file name and package match a file in your main source folders. Up to three are named first, and each `Caused by` gets its own.

### Repeated errors

When the same error is logged again, only its first line is printed, with how often it has happened and since when:

```text
09:28:33  app      ERROR  Errors Request failed
09:28:33  app             java.lang.IllegalStateException: boom  (seen 3 times since 09:28:32, stack trace hidden)
```

An error counts as the same when its log message and its exception line are the same. A restart forgets what was seen, so the first error after a Kotlin change always shows its stack trace.

To see everything in full:

```bash
./gradlew svelteDevAll --full-stack-traces
```

## Hot reload and restart

### Open pages reload their data

After a Kotlin change the app restarts, and every page you have open loads its data again by itself. Only the `load` functions rerun, through SvelteKit's `refreshAll`, so what you typed into a form and the state of your components stay as they are.

If your sessions do not survive a restart, such as with a signing key that is generated at startup, the refreshed page finds you signed out, exactly as a manual reload would. Turn it off with:

```kotlin
dev { refreshAfterRestart = false }
```

### Compile errors in the browser

When Kotlin stops compiling, the app keeps running its last good version, and the compiler errors appear in the browser in Vite's error overlay, with the file and line of each. Click the file to open it in your editor, or press Esc to hide the overlay until the errors change. It disappears once the code compiles again.

### What each restart cost

After every restart, `svelteDevAll` sums it up in one line: which file caused it, how long compiling and starting took, and whether the generated API client is different now:

```text
ktor-svelte: restarted in 4.7 s after TaskRoutes.kt changed: 2.2 s to compile, 2.5 s to start. The API client changed: openapi.json, services.ts.
```

- "To compile" runs from the moment the file was saved until the classes were written, so it includes the time Gradle takes to notice the change.
- When several files changed, the one saved last is named with the number of others.
- "The API client did not change" tells you the frontend has nothing new to pick up, and the list of files tells you where to look when it has.

### Why the app runs from a copy

The app that `svelteDevAll` starts runs from a copy of your compiled classes and resources, taken at the moment it starts. So nothing changes underneath a running app: while the compiler rewrites class files, the app keeps answering from what it started with, and then it is restarted once, as a whole. A change in `src/main/resources` restarts it too.

Ktor's own auto-reload, which watches the class folders and reloads inside the running process, has nothing to react to and stays out of the way. Without that, a Kotlin change was applied twice, once by each, and requests in between failed.

## Startup timing

Every restart costs you the app's startup time, so in development the app also logs what that time was spent on:

```text
ktor-svelte: started in 2.3 s: 800 ms for the JVM and your code before install(Svelte), 120 ms in install(Svelte), 1.2 s in your code after it, 150 ms to open the port.
```

Most of it is usually your own module: opening the database, running migrations, loading seed data. Give those parts a name with `startupStep` and they are listed, largest first:

```kotlin
fun Application.module() {
    val connection = startupStep("Database") { openDatabase() }
    startupStep("Migrations") { runMigrations(connection) }
    install(Svelte)
}
```

```text
ktor-svelte: started in 2.3 s: ... Steps: Migrations 900 ms, Database 250 ms.
```

`startupStep` returns what its block returns and costs nothing in production, where the line is not logged. Turn the line off with `dev { startupTiming = false }`.

## Settings at startup

At startup in development, the app logs which protections and settings are active, so a 403, 413 or 429 does not come as a surprise:

```text
ktor-svelte settings:
  API prefixes: /api
  Dev proxy: http://localhost:5173
  Origin check: on (same host only)
  Body limit: 1 MiB, JSON depth: 64
  Rate limit: 120 writes per 1m per client, FixedWindow
  Content-Security-Policy: off while proxying to Vite
  Error details: hidden in production, shown now
  API compression: on, request IDs: on
```

Production logs only the version and the build fingerprint. See [Monitoring](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/monitoring#startup-log).

## Slow API calls

In development, API calls that take 500 ms or longer are logged with the route that served them, so you can jump straight to the code:

```text
ktor-svelte: slow API call GET /api/notes?search=milk took 812 ms (notes/Routes.kt:19)
```

Change the threshold, or set it to `null` to turn it off. Production never logs these.

```kotlin
dev { slowApiCall = 200.milliseconds }
```

## The dev panel

An **API** button in the bottom right corner of the page opens the dev panel. It only exists while ktor-svelte proxies to Vite, so production pages never contain it. Turn it off with `dev { panel = false }`.

| Part | What it gives you |
|---|---|
| [Request log](#request-log) | The last 100 API calls, with status, timing, size, validation errors, SQL cost and duplicates |
| [Replay and curl](#replay-and-copy-as-curl) | Send a call again, or copy it as a `curl` command |
| [Open route in your editor](#open-the-route-in-your-editor) | Click a path to open the Kotlin route that answered it |
| [Server errors](#server-errors-in-the-browser) | The Kotlin exception of a failed call, as an overlay |
| [Save fixtures](#save-fixtures) | The calls of this page as JSON for frontend tests |
| [Status](#status) | Versions, health, Vite, refusals and the settings in effect |
| [Environment](#environment) | Config, environment variables and system properties the app sees, secrets hidden |
| [Cookies](#cookie-inspector) | What this browser sends, as the server reads it, with Clear buttons |
| [Routes](#route-map) | Every page and API route with the file behind it |
| [Accessibility](#accessibility-check) | An axe check of the page you are looking at |
| [Public config](#public-config) | Try other `publicConfig` values in this browser |
| [Theme colors and Not translated](#theme-colors-and-not-translated) | Shown when DaisyUI or i18n are on |

### Request log

The panel lists the last 100 API calls the app answered: method, path, status, how long the server took, how big the answer was, and the `X-Request-Id` on hover. Calls that failed validation show the message for each field, and the button turns red while any call failed. **Clear** empties the list.

**Database cost.** When your app uses [Exposed](https://www.jetbrains.com/exposed/), each call also shows what it cost in the database, such as `7 SQL, 12 ms`: the number of statements it ran and the time they took together. When one statement ran five times or more in a single call, the line says so in yellow, with the statement on hover. That is the usual sign of a query inside a loop, the kind that is fast with ten rows and slow with ten thousand.

- No setup and no code: ktor-svelte registers itself with Exposed when both are in the app.
- Statements count for the call that started them, also when they run on another thread or in a child coroutine.
- It works with Exposed 1.0 and newer, and only measures while the dev panel is on.

**Payload size.** Each call shows how big its answer was, such as `48.2 KB`, measured before compression, so it is what the server had to build and the browser has to parse. Hover the size to see the three largest fields of a JSON answer:

- A field of the answer counts with the size of its JSON, such as `items 47.9 KB (120 items)`.
- For a list of objects the fields of all its items add up, such as `items[].description 31.0 KB`, so a field that is small once but repeated in every row stands out.
- From 100 KB on the size turns yellow and the largest fields are written under the call, since that is usually a list that should be paged or a field the page does not need.

Streamed answers, such as server-sent events, have no size.

**Asked for twice.** When a page asks for the same thing twice, the second call is marked: `asked for twice within 12 ms, from src/routes/+layout.svelte:33 and from src/routes/board/+page.svelte:18`. That happens easily when a layout and a page both load the same data, and it costs a second trip to the server and the database for nothing. The two files tell you where to remove one, or to share the result.

- Only `GET` calls made within two seconds of each other count.
- A replay from the panel does not count.
- The line numbers are those of the code the browser runs, which can be a few lines off your source.

### Replay and copy as curl

Each call has two buttons:

- **Replay** sends it again, with the same method, path, headers and body, so you can repeat a call after changing the Kotlin code without clicking through the page again.
- **curl** copies it as a `curl` command, with its body and its `X-Request-Id`, to paste into a terminal or a bug report.

**What curl carries**
The command carries no cookies, so add your session yourself for a call that needs one. It carries the body as it was sent, except for fields you marked [`@Sensitive`](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/validation#sensitive-fields), so look at it before you share it.

The buttons work for calls this page made, since that is where the body is known, and for every `GET`. For other calls, such as an upload or one from another tab, they are disabled.

### Open the route in your editor

Click the path of a call and the Kotlin route that answered it opens in your editor, at its line. Hovering a call shows the file and line.

The app hands this to Vite's "open in editor", the same one Vite's error overlay uses: it finds the editor that is running, or takes the one named in the `LAUNCH_EDITOR` environment variable, such as `idea` or `code`. Only this machine can ask for it, and only for files of routes that are in the list.

### Server errors in the browser

When an API call from the page fails with an exception on the server, the browser shows it the way Vite shows a frontend error: an overlay with the exception, its message and the stack trace without the framework frames, and a link to the first line of your own code in it. Click it or press Escape to close it. You do not have to switch to the terminal to see why a call answered 500.

- The overlay only appears for calls the open page made itself, and only for exceptions that reach Ktor.
- An exception your own `StatusPages` handler turns into an answer is yours, and shows up as its status in the list.
- Turn it off with `dev { errorOverlay = false }`. It needs the panel, so `panel = false` turns it off too.

### Save fixtures

**Save fixtures** in the panel's header downloads the calls this page made, with their answers, as a JSON file that [frontend tests can replay](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/calling-the-api#fixtures-for-frontend-tests) without a backend.

### Status

The **Status** section shows what the app is running with, in plain rows:

- the versions of ktor-svelte, Ktor, Kotlin and Java,
- the version and commit of your own build,
- whether your health checks pass, and whether Vite is reachable,
- how many requests the security guards refused,
- the settings in effect, such as the API prefixes, the body limit and the rate limits.

It is what the [status endpoint](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/endpoints#status-endpoint) and the startup log tell you, without `statusEndpoint = true` and without reading JSON. Open it again to refresh it.

### Environment

The **Environment** section shows what the running app sees, so you can answer "which database is it talking to" or "did my variable arrive" without a debugger:

- **Config**: every value of the Ktor config the app runs with (`application.yaml` or `application.conf`, after substitutions), as dotted names such as `ktor.deployment.port`.
- **Environment variables**: what the app process got, which is not always what your terminal has, for example when the IDE starts it.
- **System properties**: the `-D` values, without the JVM's own ones such as `java.version`.

Type into the filter to narrow it down by name or value.

Secrets are hidden as `***`:

- a value whose name has a word such as `password`, `secret`, `token`, `key`, `auth`, `session` or `salt` in it, such as `DATABASE_PASSWORD`, `apiKey` or `jwt.secret`,
- a value whose name is a field you marked [`@Sensitive`](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/validation#sensitive-fields),
- the password inside a URL, such as `postgres://app:***@db/app`, and `password=` or `token=` parameters in a connection string.

The hiding goes by names, so a secret in a variable with a plain name, such as `DB=...`, is shown. Like the rest of the panel, it only answers this machine unless `allowRemote` is on.

### Cookie inspector

The **Cookies** section shows what this browser sends, as the server reads it.

- Each cookie is listed with its text.
- A [typed cookie](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/recipes/sessions#typed-cookies) also shows its type, its options and the value the server reads from it. It is listed even when the browser has not set it, with the default it reads as. A value that does not fit its type is marked.
- A cookie that holds a Ktor session shows the session object the server gets from it, with [sensitive fields](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/validation#sensitive-fields) hidden.
- That includes `HttpOnly` cookies, which the browser's own tools show but scripts cannot read.

**Clear** next to a cookie ends that one, and **Clear all** ends every cookie the browser sent, which signs you out. It is the quick way to see the app as a first-time visitor. The server ends them, so `HttpOnly` cookies go too. A cookie that was set for a path other than `/` and is not a typed cookie cannot be ended this way, because the request does not say which path it belongs to.

### Route map

The **Routes** section is a map of the whole app: every page with the Svelte file behind it, and every API route with its method and the Kotlin file and line that answers it.

- Type into the filter to narrow it down by path, method or file name.
- A page without parameters is a link that takes you there.
- A file name opens that file in your editor.
- When `apiDocs` is on there is a link to the API docs.

It answers "where does this URL come from" without searching the project. A similar table is also a page of its own, see [Route table](#route-table).

### Accessibility check

The **Accessibility** section checks the page you are looking at with [axe](https://github.com/dequelabs/axe-core), the engine behind most accessibility tests, so you find a missing label or a low contrast while you build the page and not when CI or a user does.

- Open the section and it lists what axe found, worst first as axe ranks it, with how many elements each problem affects and a link to the rule's explanation.
- Click a problem and the elements get a red outline and scroll into view.
- **Check again** runs it once more after you changed something.

It needs `axe-core` in your frontend, and tells you so when it is missing:

```bash
cd frontend && bun add -d axe-core
```

axe only sees what is on the screen at that moment, so open the dialog or the menu you want checked first. A page without findings is not proof that it is accessible. It is the automatic part of the check. To check every page in CI, use [`svelteVerifyA11y`](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/browser-tests#accessibility).

### Public config

The **Public config** section lists the values of your [`publicConfig`](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/runtime-config) and lets you change them for this browser only: flip a feature flag, lower a limit, see the page with another name, without editing a config file and without a restart.

- Values are written as JSON, so text goes in double quotes.
- **Apply and reload** saves them in the browser's local storage and reloads the page. From then on `loadPublicConfig()` and `readPublicConfig()` return the changed values in this browser.
- A yellow "config changed" mark on the API button reminds you.
- **Reset all** goes back to what the server sends.

Only the browser is told something different. The server keeps its own values, so a limit the server enforces is still enforced, and nobody else sees the change. It exists in development only, like the rest of the panel.

### Theme colors and Not translated

Two more sections appear when the matching library is on:

- **Theme colors**, with [DaisyUI](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/frontend-libraries#daisyui): a color picker for each theme color that recolors the open page at once, and **Copy for Gradle** to take the result into `build.gradle.kts`.
- **Not translated**, with [i18n](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/frontend-libraries#i18n), when you look at the app in another language than the default one: the messages on the page whose text is the same as in the default language.

## Browser console in the server log

Browser console output lands in the same console as your app. Every `console.log`, `info`, `debug`, `warn` and `error`, uncaught errors and unhandled promise rejections are sent to the app and logged by the `ktor-svelte.browser` logger, with the page they came from:

```text
10:21:19 WARN  ktor-svelte.browser Probe warning {"id":7} [/notes]
10:21:19 ERROR ktor-svelte.browser Error: Probe crash
```

- Objects are written as JSON, and errors with their stack trace.
- `console.debug` uses the DEBUG level, so it only shows when you enable it in your logging configuration.
- Like the panel, this only exists while ktor-svelte proxies to Vite, and only for requests from this machine.
- Turn it off with `dev { browserLogs = false }`.

In production, [frontend error reporting](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/monitoring#errors-from-the-browser) does the part of this that matters there.

## Route table

Open `http://localhost:8080/_ktor-svelte/routes` to see every Ktor route next to every SvelteKit page, with the file and line of each route and a warning on routes that hide a page. Ask for `application/json` to get the same table as JSON:

```bash
curl -H 'Accept: application/json' http://localhost:8080/_ktor-svelte/routes
```

It exists only in development and answers only requests from this machine.

## Debugging

### Kotlin

Start `Dev` as usual and then start the `Debug app` run configuration in debug mode.

IntelliJ debugs Gradle tasks only when they run a JVM through Gradle, and `svelteDevAll` starts the app itself, so the app instead listens for a debugger on `127.0.0.1:5005` (see `dev.debugPort` in the [Gradle settings](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/reference/gradle)). `Debug app` has auto restart on, so it reconnects after each restart.

- Outside IntelliJ, attach any JDWP debugger to that port.
- Two apps running `svelteDevAll` at once need different debug ports.
- `debugPort = 0` turns the debugger port off.

```kotlin
svelte {
    dev {
        debugPort = 5006
    }
}
```

### Both in one click

Run `Dev and debug`. It starts `Dev` and attaches the Kotlin debugger, and stopping it stops both.

### The frontend

Run `Debug frontend` in debug mode while `Dev` runs. IntelliJ opens the app at `http://localhost:8080` in Chrome with its JavaScript debugger attached, and breakpoints in `.svelte` and `.ts` files under `frontend/` work through Vite's source maps. If your app runs on another port, change the URL in that run configuration.

## IDE run configurations

`svelteInit` writes IntelliJ run configurations to `.run/` for you. In an existing project, write them with:

```bash
./gradlew svelteGenerateRunConfigurations
```

It keeps any configuration that already exists.

| Configuration | What it runs |
|---|---|
| `Dev` | `svelteDevAll` |
| `Dev and debug` | `Dev`, with the Kotlin debugger attached |
| `Debug app` | Attaches the debugger to the app `svelteDevAll` started |
| `Debug frontend` | Chrome with the JavaScript debugger on the app |
| `Ktor` | The app on its own |
| `Vite` | Vite on its own |
| `Generate TypeScript` | `svelteGenerateTs` |
| `Build JAR` | The runnable JAR |
| `Type check frontend` | The frontend's type check |
| `Update frontend dependencies` | `svelteUpdateDependencies` |

## Live templates

For the edits you make most, install the live templates once and restart the IDE:

```bash
./gradlew svelteLiveTemplates --install
```

| Template | Language | Writes |
|---|---|---|
| `ksget` | Kotlin | A GET route |
| `kspost` | Kotlin | A POST route that receives a validated body |
| `kspage` | Kotlin | A paged GET route |
| `ksdto` | Kotlin | A serializable DTO |
| `ksinput` | Kotlin | A request body with bounds and rules |
| `ksapi` | TypeScript | A call through the generated client |
| `ksload` | TypeScript | A `load` function with `apiWith` |
| `kserror` | TypeScript | Typed error handling around your code |

Type the name and press Tab. Without `--install`, the task only writes the templates to `build/ktor-svelte/live-templates/`. `--install` copies them into every IntelliJ IDEA and WebStorm configuration it finds, and `--config-dir=...` picks another JetBrains folder.

## Separate terminals

Prefer separate terminals? Run these instead:

```bash
./gradlew svelteDev
```

```bash
./gradlew run -Psvelte.dev=true
```

`svelteDev` starts Vite on `dev.port`. `-Psvelte.dev=true` skips the frontend build and starts the app with `-Dio.ktor.development=true`. With two terminals there is no restart on Kotlin changes, no restart summary and no cleanup of [leftover processes](#when-a-port-is-still-in-use).

## The dev proxy

In development mode the runtime proxies page requests to Vite. In order:

1. If Vite is reachable, the page comes from Vite.
2. Otherwise it serves built files if they exist.
3. Otherwise it returns a 503 explaining how to start Vite.

API prefixes are never proxied, whatever the method.

**Only this machine.** The proxy only answers requests from this machine, so your frontend source is not open to everyone on your network, even though Ktor listens on all interfaces. Requests from elsewhere get your built files, or a 403 if there are none. It never forwards cookies or `Authorization` headers. It also refuses to start if `dev.url` points at another machine.

To test from your phone or use Vite in another container, allow it, and only on a network you trust:

```kotlin
dev { allowRemote = true }
```

**Methods.** The proxy forwards HTTP only. POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE requests are forwarded too, with their body, so Vite endpoints and SvelteKit form actions work in dev.

**Hot reload connection.** `server.hmr.clientPort` in `vite.config.ts` makes Vite's client connect straight to Vite, and `protocol: 'ws'` keeps that working on a page served over HTTPS. Without it HMR still works, but the browser logs one WebSocket error before Vite falls back. Either way, the browser must be able to reach Vite's port, so a remote machine or container needs that port exposed.

**Vite somewhere else.** `dev.url` sets the Vite address, and the `KTOR_SVELTE_DEV_SERVER` environment variable overrides it. `dev.mode` decides when the proxy is on: `Auto` follows Ktor's development mode, `Always` and `Never` force it.

## HTTPS in development

Some things only work on a page served over HTTPS: cookies marked `Secure`, service workers on any host but `localhost`, and sign-in providers that refuse plain HTTP callback URLs. To develop with them, turn HTTPS on:

```kotlin
svelte {
    dev {
        https = true
        httpsPort = 8443
    }
}
```

`svelteDevAll` then serves the app at `https://localhost:8443` as well as on its usual port, and the ready banner and the browser it opens use the HTTPS address. A small proxy in the Gradle task ends TLS and passes each request on to the app, WebSockets included. Your app keeps listening on plain HTTP, so `application.conf` and `embeddedServer` stay as they are.

### The certificate

The certificate is made on the first run with the JDK's `keytool`: a development certificate authority for your user, and a certificate for `localhost`, `127.0.0.1` and `::1` signed by it. Both live in `~/.ktor-svelte/dev-https`, and every project on your computer shares them. The certificate for `localhost` is renewed after about a year.

Your browser does not trust the authority until you tell it to. The first run prints the command for your system, such as `certutil -addstore -user Root` on Windows. ktor-svelte never runs it for you. Firefox keeps its own list, so import `ca.crt` there under Settings, Certificates, Authorities. Without that step the page still works after you accept the browser's warning, but service workers and some sign-in providers refuse an untrusted certificate.

**Keep the folder to yourself**
Anyone who has the files in `~/.ktor-svelte/dev-https` can sign certificates your browser then trusts, so do not copy that folder to other machines. When you stop using HTTPS in development, delete the folder and remove the authority from your system's trust store.

### What the app sees

In development mode the app treats requests from this proxy as HTTPS: `call.request.origin.scheme` is `https` and the port is the HTTPS port, so redirects, absolute URLs and `Secure` cookies come out right. It only does so for requests from this machine that carry the proxy's mark, and never outside development mode.

### Hot reload over HTTPS

Vite's hot reload still talks to Vite over plain `ws` on its own port, which browsers allow from a secure page on `localhost`. Projects from `svelteInit` and the generated `vite.config.ts` set `protocol: 'ws'` for that. A hand-written `vite.config.ts` needs it too:

```ts
import { sveltekit } from '@sveltejs/kit/vite';
import { defineConfig } from 'vite';

export default defineConfig({
    plugins: [sveltekit()],
    server: { hmr: { clientPort: 5173, protocol: 'ws' } }
});
```

## When a port is still in use

`svelteDevAll` stops Vite, the compiler and the app when it ends, even when its terminal is closed. If it gets killed hard, such as when the Gradle daemon or the IDE crashes, they can keep running and hold their ports.

The next `svelteDevAll` cleans that up by itself: it remembers the processes it started in `build/ktor-svelte/dev-processes`, and stops the ones that are still alive before it starts new ones. It tells you which:

```text
ktor-svelte: stopping what an earlier svelteDevAll of this project left running: node (PID 4242), java (PID 4310).
```

It only ever stops processes it started itself. When some other program holds Vite's port or the debug port, the task stops before starting anything and names it:

```text
Port 5173, which Vite needs, is in use by node.exe (PID 9120). svelteDevAll did not start it, so it was left alone.
Stop it, or use another port with svelte { dev { port = 5174 } }.
```

- The app's own port is set in your Ktor configuration, which Gradle does not read, so a foreign program on that port shows up as the app's own "Address already in use" error in the log.
- With two terminals instead of `svelteDevAll`, nothing is remembered: run `./gradlew --stop`, or stop the process listening on that port yourself.

## Dev settings

Everything on this page that you can turn on or off, in one place. Gradle settings go in `svelte { dev { } }`, Ktor settings in `install(Svelte) { dev { } }`.

| Setting | Where | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `port` | Gradle | `5173` | Port Vite runs on |
| `script` | Gradle | `"dev"` | `package.json` script that starts Vite |
| `debugPort` | Gradle | `5005` | Debugger port of the app, on `127.0.0.1`. `0` turns it off |
| `openBrowser` | Gradle | `true` | Opens the app once it is ready, the first time only |
| `https` | Gradle | `false` | Serves the app over HTTPS too |
| `httpsPort` | Gradle | `8443` | Port of the HTTPS address, on `127.0.0.1` |
| `url` | Ktor | `"http://localhost:5173"` | Vite address. `KTOR_SVELTE_DEV_SERVER` overrides it |
| `mode` | Ktor | `DevMode.Auto` | When the proxy is on: `Auto`, `Always`, `Never` |
| `allowRemote` | Ktor | `false` | Lets other machines use the dev proxy |
| `panel` | Ktor | `true` | The dev panel |
| `errorOverlay` | Ktor | `true` | Server exceptions as a browser overlay. Needs `panel` |
| `browserLogs` | Ktor | `true` | Browser console in the server log |
| `refreshAfterRestart` | Ktor | `true` | Open pages rerun their `load` after a restart |
| `slowApiCall` | Ktor | `500.milliseconds` | Logs slower API calls. `null` turns it off |
| `startupTiming` | Ktor | `true` | Logs what the startup time was spent on |

## Full example

A project that runs Vite on another port, debugs on another port and develops over HTTPS:

::: code-group

```kotlin [build.gradle.kts]
svelte {
    dev {
        port = 5174
        debugPort = 5006
        openBrowser = false
        https = true
    }
}
```

```kotlin [Application.kt]
install(Svelte) {
    generateTs = true
    apiDocs = true
    dev {
        url = "http://localhost:5174"
        slowApiCall = 200.milliseconds
        refreshAfterRestart = false
    }
}
```

## Good to know

- Everything on this page exists in development only. Production pages carry no panel, no browser logging and no proxy.
- The proxy, the panel, the route table and "open in editor" only answer requests from this machine.
- For checks and helper tasks you run while developing, see [Checks and tooling](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/checks-and-tooling).
- For problems while developing, see [Troubleshooting](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/reference/troubleshooting#development).

Source: https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/checks-and-tooling

# Checks and tooling

Every check and helper task ktor-svelte adds to your build, in one place: what it catches, how to run it, how to make it fail the build, and what its output looks like.

<Badge type="info" text="Gradle" />

## Quick start

Run the everyday checks before you push:

```bash
./gradlew check svelteVerifyRoutes svelteVerifyLoads svelteVerifyLinks --strict
```

And let a git hook keep formatting and generated files right on every commit:

```bash
./gradlew svelteGitHooks
```

## Overview

| Task | Catches | Runs by itself | Fails the build |
|---|---|---|---|
| [`svelteVerifySync`](#svelteverifysync) | Frontend libraries out of sync with `build.gradle.kts` | Before every frontend build | Always |
| [`svelteVerifyTs`](#svelteverifyts) | Generated TypeScript out of date | Part of `check` | Always |
| [`svelteVerifyLeaks`](#svelteverifyleaks) | Secret values in the frontend build | Before the build goes into the JAR | Always |
| [`svelteVerifyRoutes`](#svelteverifyroutes) | Links to pages written as strings | No | Always. `--fix` rewrites them |
| [`svelteVerifyLoads`](#svelteverifyloads) | API calls in `load` without SvelteKit's `fetch` | No | Always |
| [`svelteVerifyLinks`](#svelteverifylinks) | Internal links that lead nowhere | No | With `--strict` |
| [`svelteVerifyMessages`](#svelteverifymessages) | i18n messages nothing uses | No | With `--strict` |
| [`svelteVerifyApiRoutes`](#svelteverifyapiroutes) | API routes nothing in the frontend calls | No | With `--strict` |
| [`svelteApiChanges`](#svelteapichanges) | API changes that can break callers | No | With `--strict` |
| [`svelteVerifyA11y`](#svelteverifya11y) | Accessibility problems on prerendered pages | No | Always |
| [`svelteSmokeTest`](#sveltesmoketest) | A production JAR that does not serve its pages | No | Always |
| [`svelteDoctor`](#sveltedoctor) | A broken frontend setup | No | On errors. `--fix` repairs some |
| [`formatCheck`](#format-and-formatcheck) | Unformatted Kotlin or frontend code | No | Always |

Helpers that change or describe your project: [`svelteConfig`](#svelteconfig), [`format`](#format-and-formatcheck), [`svelteGitHooks`](#the-git-pre-commit-hook), [`svelteAdd`](#svelteadd), [`svelteRename`](#svelterename), [`svelteLiveTemplates`](#sveltelivetemplates), and the [lint rules](#lint-rules) in your editor. Every task is listed in the [Gradle reference](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/reference/gradle#gradle-tasks).

## Checks that run by themselves

### svelteVerifySync

**Catches:** `build.gradle.kts` changed the [frontend libraries](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/frontend-libraries), but `package.json`, the lockfile or the generated files were not updated.

**Runs:** before every frontend build, so a JAR is never built from a stale setup. Run it by hand with `./gradlew svelteVerifySync`.

```text
Frontend libraries are out of sync: src/lib/ktor-svelte/routes.ts, package.json. Run svelteSync and commit the result. See https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/features/frontend-libraries
```

**Fix:** `./gradlew svelteSync`, then commit. The [pre-commit hook](#the-git-pre-commit-hook) runs this check too.

### svelteVerifyTs

**Catches:** a route or DTO changed, but the committed TypeScript client in `frontend/src/lib/api` did not.

**Runs:** as part of `check`. It starts your app once, like `svelteGenerateTs`.

```text
Generated TypeScript is out of date: frontend/src/lib/api/services.ts. Run svelteGenerateTs, or start the app in development mode, and commit the result.
```

**Fix:** `./gradlew svelteGenerateTs` and commit. Leave it out of `check` with `-Psvelte.verifyTs=false`. With `generateTs` off, it has nothing to verify and says so.

### svelteVerifyLeaks

**Catches:** a secret value from the environment or a `.env` file that ended up in the frontend build, which is sent to every browser.

**Runs:** after `svelteBuild`, before the build is packed into the JAR.

```text
ktor-svelte found secret values in the frontend build. Everything in that folder is sent to browsers.

  SESSION_SIGN_KEY (declared as a secret)  _app/immutable/chunks/B3kq9.js
  STRIPE_KEY (.env)                        _app/immutable/nodes/2.Dx1.js
```

It names the variable and the file, never the value. What it looks for and what it leaves out is in [Secrets in the frontend build](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/runtime-config#secrets-in-the-frontend-build). Turn it off with `svelte { verifyLeaks = false }`.

## Checks you run

### svelteVerifyRoutes

**Catches:** links to your pages written as strings, in `href`, `goto` and `redirect` in the frontend and in `respondRedirect` in Kotlin, when a [typed route](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/routes) exists.

```bash
./gradlew svelteVerifyRoutes
```

```text
src/routes/+page.svelte:12  href="/notes/{note.id}"  ->  routes.notesId({ id: note.id })
src/lib/NoteForm.svelte:31  goto("/notes/" + created.id)  ->  routes.notesId({ id: created.id })
src/main/kotlin/notes/Routes.kt:48  respondRedirect("/notes/${note.id}")  ->  FrontendRoutes.notesId(note.id)
```

**Fix it for you:** `--fix` rewrites what it can without losing anything and adds the `#routes` import. Links with a query string or a fragment, paths too dynamic to read and Kotlin redirects with parameters stay listed for you.

```bash
./gradlew svelteVerifyRoutes --fix
```

**Strict:** it always fails when it finds a link. It needs typed routes on (`routes()` in `libraries`), otherwise it says there is nothing to verify. Details: [Finding links that are still strings](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/routes#finding-links-that-are-still-strings).

### svelteVerifyLoads

**Catches:** an API call inside a `load` function that uses neither `apiWith(event)` nor `{ fetch }`, so SvelteKit cannot track or reuse it.

```bash
./gradlew svelteVerifyLoads
```

```text
src/routes/notes/[id]/+page.ts:6  api.notes.get(params.id)  ->  use apiWith(event), or pass { fetch } as the last argument
```

**Strict:** it always fails when it finds one. It reads every `+page.ts`, `+page.js`, `+layout.ts` and `+layout.js`. Details: [In load functions](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/calling-the-api#in-load-functions).

### svelteVerifyLinks

**Catches:** internal links whose path is not one of your pages, not under your API and not a file in `static`, such as a typo in an `href`.

```bash
./gradlew svelteVerifyLinks
```

```text
src/routes/+page.svelte:14  href="/abuot"  ->  nothing is served at /abuot
src/main/kotlin/notes/Routes.kt:52  respondRedirect("/notes/${id}/edit")  ->  nothing is served at /notes/{}/edit
ktor-svelte: 2 internal link(s) lead to no page, no API route and no static file. Add --strict to fail the build on them.
```

**Strict:** `--strict` fails the build. It works with or without typed routes. Details: [Finding links that lead nowhere](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/routes#finding-links-that-lead-nowhere).

### svelteVerifyMessages

**Catches:** [i18n](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/frontend-libraries#i18n) messages that are in every locale file but used nowhere.

```bash
./gradlew svelteVerifyMessages
```

```text
old-banner  ->  nothing calls oldBanner() and no source names 'old-banner'
ktor-svelte: 1 message(s) are in every locale file but used nowhere. Add --strict to fail the build on them.
```

**Strict:** `--strict` fails the build. Details: [Messages nothing uses](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/frontend-libraries#messages-nothing-uses).

### svelteVerifyApiRoutes

**Catches:** API routes that nothing in the frontend calls, so you can see what is safe to remove.

```bash
./gradlew svelteVerifyApiRoutes
```

```text
GET /api/notes/export  ->  nothing in the frontend calls api.notes.export
ktor-svelte: 1 API route(s) are not called by the frontend. Add --strict to fail the build on them.
```

**Strict:** `--strict` fails the build. Leave it off when other callers, such as a webhook or another service, use routes the frontend does not. Details: [Routes nothing calls](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/typescript#routes-nothing-calls).

### svelteApiChanges

**Catches:** changes to the API that a caller outside this repository would notice, compared with `origin/main` or the revision you name.

```bash
./gradlew svelteApiChanges --against=v1.1.0
```

```text
API changes against v1.1.0: 2 that can break callers, 3 other.

Can break callers
  GET /api/tasks  query  limit            was string, is integer
  POST /api/tasks  request  folder        is new and required

Other changes
  GET /api/tasks  response  items[].version  added
  POST /api/tasks  request  version          added
  PATCH /api/tasks/{id}                      added
```

**Strict:** `--strict` fails on a change that can break callers. It reads the committed `openapi.json`, so run it after `svelteGenerateTs`. Details: [What changed for callers](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/typescript#what-changed-for-callers).

### svelteVerifyA11y

**Catches:** accessibility problems that axe finds on every prerendered page, in light and in dark.

```bash
./gradlew svelteVerifyA11y --path=/pricing
```

```text
axe found 2 accessibility problems on 4 pages:
  /about in the light theme shadcn-light: image-alt: Images must have alternative text ([img])
  /about in the dark theme dracula: color-contrast: Elements must meet minimum color contrast ratio thresholds ([#content > p])
```

**Strict:** it always fails on a problem. It needs a browser and the environment the app needs, so it is not part of `check`. Details: [Accessibility](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/browser-tests#accessibility).

### svelteSmokeTest

**Catches:** a production JAR that does not start, or does not serve its prerendered pages, its frontend files or its `GET` API routes.

```bash
./gradlew svelteSmokeTest
```

```text
ktor-svelte: build/libs/my-app-all.jar runs in production mode on port 55269.
  200  /
  200  /about
  200  /_app/immutable/assets/0.CtcRfiw7.css
  200  GET /api/greeting
  401  GET /api/me
ktor-svelte: the production build answered 2 pages, 1 asset, 2 API routes correctly.
```

**Strict:** it always fails on a wrong answer. Options: `--path`, `--skip` and `--start-seconds`. Details: [Smoke test](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/deployment#smoke-test).

### svelteDoctor

**Catches:** a frontend setup that cannot work: the adapter, the adapter output against `svelte.outputDir`, the bundled manifest, `#api`, `tsconfig.json`, the SvelteKit version, Node, the package manager and port, packages that lost their files, and whether `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS` points to a file.

```bash
./gradlew svelteDoctor
```

```text
OK    Package manager bun is on PATH
OK    Uses adapter-static
OK    adapter-static writes to build, matching svelte.outputDir
OK    SvelteKit 3
ERROR src/routes/+page.svelte imports $lib. SvelteKit 3 uses #lib.
WARN  Node 20.10.0 is too old for Vite. Use Node 20.19, 22.12 or newer.
ktor-svelte: svelteDoctor --fix can fix 1 of these.
```

**Fix it for you:** `--fix` repairs what needs no decision from you: a missing `#api` import, a `tsconfig.json` that does not extend `$app/tsconfig`, `$lib` imports left over from SvelteKit 2, and a `node_modules` folder whose packages lost their files, which it deletes so the next build installs it again. Each change is printed as `FIXED`.

```bash
./gradlew svelteDoctor --fix
```

**Strict:** it fails when a finding is an `ERROR`. Warnings only inform. `./gradlew doctor` is its [short name](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/reference/gradle#short-task-names).

## Helpers

### svelteConfig

Prints every setting of `svelte { }` and of `install(Svelte) { }`, marks the ones you changed from the default, scores the setup and suggests what to turn on. It starts your app once to read the settings that really run.

```bash
./gradlew svelteConfig
```

```text
Scores
  Security              [#########-]  90%  10 of 11
  Performance           [##########] 100%  4 of 4
  Operations            [#######---]  66%  2 of 3
  Developer experience  [##########] 100%  5 of 5

Suggestions
  - [Security] Set maxJsonStringLength = 100_000, or the longest text your API accepts.
  - [Operations] Set healthEndpoint = true and point your orchestrator at /_ktor-svelte/health.
```

A suggestion is advice, not an error, and the task never fails on one. Details: [Review your configuration](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/reference/gradle#review-your-configuration).

### format and formatCheck

One command formats Kotlin and the frontend, and one checks them:

```bash
./gradlew format
./gradlew formatCheck
```

| Side | `format` runs | `formatCheck` runs |
|---|---|---|
| Frontend | the `format` script of `package.json` | the `lint` script |
| Kotlin with ktlint | `ktlintFormat` | `ktlintCheck` |
| Kotlin with Spotless | `spotlessApply` | `spotlessCheck` |

- Projects made by the setup script have both scripts, as `prettier --write .` and `prettier --check . && eslint .`.
- Without ktlint or Spotless, Kotlin is left alone and the task says so. A frontend without the script is skipped with a hint.
- If your build already has a task called `format` or `formatCheck`, ktor-svelte does not register its own. The frontend half is always there as `svelteFormat` and `svelteFormatCheck`.
