Details: [Format both sides](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/reference/gradle#format-both-sides).

### The git pre-commit hook

`svelteGitHooks` installs a pre-commit hook in your clone that runs `formatCheck` and `svelteVerifySync`, so an unformatted file or a stale generated file never reaches a commit:

```bash
./gradlew svelteGitHooks
```

```text
ktor-svelte: installed .git/hooks/pre-commit. Every commit now runs formatCheck and svelteVerifySync first.
ktor-svelte: generated files no longer conflict in this clone. When both sides of a merge or rebase changed one, one side is kept and svelteSync and svelteGenerateTs run afterwards.
```

- A commit that fails the check is stopped with the command that fixes it. `git commit --no-verify` skips the hook once.
- `./gradlew svelteGitHooks --remove` takes it out again.
- The hook lives in `.git`, which git does not share, so everyone on the team runs the task once.
- A pre-commit hook that something else installed is never replaced: the task stops and tells you to call the two tasks from your own hook.
- The same run keeps [generated files out of merge conflicts](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/reference/gradle#generated-files-without-merge-conflicts).

### svelteAdd

Creates a page with a typed `load`, and optionally a Kotlin route to start from:

```bash
./gradlew svelteAdd --page=notes/[id] --route
```

`--crud=Note` writes list, detail and form pages for a class of your API instead. It runs `svelteSync` afterwards. Details: [A new page](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/routes#a-new-page) and [Pages for a class](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/routes#pages-for-a-class).

### svelteRename

Moves a page and rewrites its typed route calls in the frontend and in Kotlin:

```bash
./gradlew svelteRename --page=notes/[id] --to=memos/[id]
```

It stops before it changes anything when a file it would rewrite has uncommitted changes, so the rename stays one clean diff. `--force` renames anyway. Details: [Renaming a page](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/routes#renaming-a-page).

### svelteLiveTemplates

Installs IntelliJ live templates such as `ksget`, `kspost` and `ksload`:

```bash
./gradlew svelteLiveTemplates --install
```

```text
Restart the IDE, then type ksget, kspost, kspage, ksdto, ksinput, ksapi, ksload or kserror and press Tab.
```

The list of templates is in [Live templates](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/dev-workflow#live-templates).

### Lint rules

`svelteSync` writes a small ESLint plugin to `src/lib/ktor-svelte/eslint.js`, so some of the checks above show up in the editor while you type:

| Rule | Same as |
|---|---|
| `ktor-svelte/no-string-page-links` | `svelteVerifyRoutes`, for the frontend |
| `ktor-svelte/fetch-in-load` | `svelteVerifyLoads` |
| `ktor-svelte/no-error-body-message` | No task: reading `error.body.message` without `isApiError` |

All three are warnings. Make one an error like any other ESLint rule. Setup: [Lint rules](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/frontend-libraries#lint-rules).

## Make a check part of check

Tasks that only list can fail the build when you set `strict`, and any of them can join `check`:

```kotlin
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.gradle.tasks.SvelteVerifyLinksTask

tasks.named<SvelteVerifyLinksTask>("svelteVerifyLinks") {
    strict.set(true)
}

tasks.check {
    dependsOn("svelteVerifyRoutes", "svelteVerifyLoads", "svelteVerifyLinks")
}
```

`svelteVerifyMessages`, `svelteVerifyApiRoutes` and `svelteApiChanges` have the same `strict` setting. Keep `svelteVerifyA11y` and `svelteSmokeTest` out of `check`: they need a browser or the production environment, which belongs in the pipeline.

## Full example

A GitHub Actions workflow that runs the fast checks on every pull request, and the checks that start the packaged app after them:

```yaml
name: Checks
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  checks:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0 # svelteApiChanges compares with origin/main
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with:
          distribution: temurin
          java-version: 21
      - uses: gradle/actions/setup-gradle@v4
      - uses: oven-sh/setup-bun@v2 # or set svelte { bunVersion } and skip this step

      - name: Build, unit tests and generated files
        run: ./gradlew check formatCheck

      - name: Frontend checks
        run: >
          ./gradlew svelteVerifyRoutes svelteVerifyLoads
          svelteVerifyLinks --strict
          svelteVerifyMessages --strict
          svelteApiChanges --strict

      - name: Production build
        env:
          DATABASE_URL: jdbc:h2:mem:ci
        run: ./gradlew svelteSmokeTest

      - name: Accessibility
        env:
          DATABASE_URL: jdbc:h2:mem:ci
        run: ./gradlew installBrowsers svelteVerifyA11y
```

- A Gradle option belongs to the task right before it, so each `--strict` goes after its own task.
- `installBrowsers` is the small task from [Browsers](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/browser-tests#browsers).
- The smoke test and the accessibility check start the app, so give them the environment it needs.

## Good to know

- `svelteVerifySync`, `svelteVerifyTs` and `svelteVerifyLeaks` already guard every build. The others are yours to add.
- The tasks that read your sources (`svelteVerifyRoutes`, `svelteVerifyLinks`, `svelteVerifyMessages`, `svelteVerifyApiRoutes`) skip the generated folders `src/lib/ktor-svelte` and `src/lib/api`.
- `svelteDoctor` is the first thing to run when a build fails for a reason you do not understand. See [Troubleshooting](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/reference/troubleshooting).

Source: https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/browser-tests

# Browser tests

Tests that drive a real browser against the packaged app, written in Kotlin.

<Badge type="info" text="Gradle" /> <Badge type="tip" text="ktor-svelte-test" />

A unit test cannot tell you that the login page still logs someone in. A browser test can, and with ktor-svelte both halves of the app are in one build, so the test can be Kotlin too: it starts the JAR you ship, opens a browser, and uses your typed routes and your own classes.

## Quick start

1. Add a test suite called `browserTest` (see [Set up](#set-up)).
2. Write a class that extends `BrowserTest` in `src/browserTest/kotlin`.
3. Run it:

```bash
./gradlew browserTest
```

Or let the browser write the first test for you with [`svelteRecordTest`](#record-a-test).

## Set up

Add a test suite called `browserTest`:

```kotlin
plugins {
    `jvm-test-suite`
}

testing {
    suites {
        register<JvmTestSuite>("browserTest") {
            useJUnitJupiter()
            dependencies {
                implementation(project())
            }
        }
    }
}
```

The name is what the ktor-svelte plugin looks for. For that suite it:

- adds `io.github.nijasc:ktor-svelte-test`, which brings [Playwright](https://playwright.dev/java/) (unless you turned `addRuntimeDependency` off, then add it yourself),
- packages the app before the tests, with `buildFatJar` or `shadowJar` when the project has them and `installDist` otherwise,
- tells the tests where the packaged app is,
- passes the browser on: `./gradlew browserTest -Pbrowser=firefox`. Chromium unless you say so, and `webkit` is the third.

`implementation(project())` gives the tests your typed routes and your classes. Tests go in `src/browserTest/kotlin`.

## A test

```kotlin
import com.microsoft.playwright.assertions.PlaywrightAssertions.assertThat
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.test.BrowserTest
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.test.problems
import kotlin.test.Test
import kotlin.test.assertEquals

class NotesBrowserTest : BrowserTest() {
    @Test
    fun `a new note shows up in the list`() {
        val problems = page.problems()
        val note: Note = api.post("/api/notes", NoteInput(title = "Written by a test"))

        page.navigate(FrontendRoutes.notes)
        assertThat(page.getByRole(AriaRole.LINK, Page.GetByRoleOptions().setName(note.title))).isVisible()
        assertEquals(emptyList(), problems)
    }
}
```

`BrowserTest` gives every test:

| Member | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `page` | A fresh Playwright page in its own browser context, so tests do not share cookies. Paths are relative to the app |
| `context` | That context, and `newContext()` for a second visitor in the same test |
| `api` | The app's API, called from that context: with its cookies, so as whoever the page is signed in as |
| `app` | The running app, with its `url` and its `log` file |

And you can override:

| Override | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `environment` | empty | Environment variables for the app. See [What the app needs](#what-the-app-needs) |
| `locale` | `"en-US"` | The browser's language for every context |
| `serviceWorkers` | `false` | Lets service workers run. See [Service workers](#service-workers) |

The app is started once and shared by all tests of the run. It is started the way production starts it, without the development flag, on a free port.

## Record a test

The slow part of a browser test is finding the right way to name each element. Let the browser tell you: click through the app once, and the steps are written down.

```bash
./gradlew svelteRecordTest --name=SignIn
```

The task packages and starts the app and opens it in a browser, with Playwright's recorder next to it. Do what the test should do. The recorder's toolbar can also add assertions: that an element is visible, or has a text. Close the browser, and the steps are in `src/browserTest/kotlin/SignInBrowserTest.kt`:

```kotlin
class SignInBrowserTest : BrowserTest() {
    @Test
    fun `sign in`() {
        page.navigate(FrontendRoutes.login)
        page.getByLabel("Email").fill("ada@example.com")
        page.getByLabel("Password").fill("secret")
        page.getByRole(AriaRole.BUTTON, Page.GetByRoleOptions().setName("Sign in")).click()
        assertThat(page.locator("#signed-in-as")).containsText("Ada Lovelace")
    }
}
```

- An address of your app is written as its typed route, `FrontendRoutes.tasksId("12")` for `/tasks/12`, so the test breaks at compile time when the page moves. An address with a query string stays a path.
- It is a starting point to edit, and the file is yours.
- What it typed in is in the file as you typed it, passwords too, so replace those before you commit.
- The task never replaces a test that is already there.
- Add `-Pbrowser=firefox` to record in another browser.

## The API with your own classes

`api` sends and reads JSON with kotlinx.serialization, so a request body and an answer are your classes:

```kotlin
val user: User = api.post("/api/session", Login("ada@example.com", "secret"))
val notes: List<Note> = api.get("/api/notes")
val changed: Note = api.put("/api/notes/${note.id}", NoteInput(title = "Renamed"))
api.delete("/api/notes/${note.id}")
```

An answer of 400 or above fails the test with the status and the body. To check a refusal, catch it or ask for the status alone:

```kotlin
val refused = assertFailsWith<ApiFailure> { api.get<List<Note>>("/api/notes") }
assertEquals(401, refused.status)
assertEquals(403, api.status("DELETE", "/api/admin/users/1"))
```

**Sign in through the API**
Because `api` shares the page's cookies, signing in through `api` signs the page in, which is much faster than filling in the login form in every test.

## What the app needs

The app runs with the environment of the build. Override `environment` for what the tests should set, such as a fresh database:

```kotlin
class NotesBrowserTest : BrowserTest() {
    override val environment = mapOf("DATABASE_URL" to "jdbc:h2:mem:tests", "ADMIN_PASSWORD" to "secret")
}
```

Test classes with the same environment share one app. A class with another environment gets its own.

The port goes to the app as the `PORT` variable and as `-port`, as with the [smoke test](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/deployment#smoke-test), so the app has to read one of them.

## Problems on the page

`page.problems()` collects what went wrong while the test ran: errors in the console, uncaught exceptions and answers of 500 and above. Assert that it is empty at the end of a test, and a broken page fails even when the thing you looked at happened to work.

```kotlin
val problems = page.problems()
page.navigate(FrontendRoutes.board)
// ... the test ...
assertEquals(emptyList(), problems)
```

## Service workers

Browser contexts block service workers by default. In WebKit, a page controlled by a service worker sends its requests past `page.route` and `context.route`, so a request you stubbed would not be stubbed. Blocking the worker keeps stubs working in every browser.

To test the [installable app](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/installable-app)'s worker or its offline page, let them run in that test class. The worker controls a page only from the next load after it is ready, so reload once before you go offline:

```kotlin
class OfflineBrowserTest : BrowserTest() {
    override val serviceWorkers = true

    @Test
    fun `the offline page shows without a network`() {
        page.navigate("/")
        page.evaluate("navigator.serviceWorker.ready")
        page.reload()
        context.setOffline(true)
        page.navigate("/about")
        assertThat(page.getByText("You are offline")).isVisible()
    }
}
```

## Accessibility

Many accessibility problems can be found by a machine: an image without a text, text that is too pale to read, a form field without a label. [axe](https://github.com/dequelabs/axe-core) finds them, and a task runs it on your app with no test to write:

```bash
./gradlew svelteVerifyA11y
```

```text
axe found 2 accessibility problems on 4 pages:
  /about in the light theme shadcn-light: image-alt: Images must have alternative text ([img])
  /about in the dark theme dracula: color-contrast: Elements must meet minimum color contrast ratio thresholds ([#content > p])
```

The task packages the app, starts it, and opens every prerendered page in a browser, twice: once light and once dark. With `daisyUi` it uses your `defaultTheme` and your `prefersDark` theme, because contrast is where themes differ. Without it the browser asks for light and for dark colors. It checks the rules of WCAG 2.1 at levels A and AA. The report is also written to `build/ktor-svelte/a11y.txt`.

| Option | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--path=/pricing` | Adds a page that is not prerendered. Can be given more than once |
| `-Pbrowser=firefox` | Picks another browser |

- Pages behind a login cannot be checked this way, because the task is not signed in: check those in a browser test.
- It is not part of `check`. It needs a browser, which is downloaded the first time, and the environment the app needs.

In a browser test the same check is one call, for any page in any state:

```kotlin
page.navigate(FrontendRoutes.settings)
assertEquals(emptyList(), page.accessibilityProblems())
```

While you build a page, the [dev panel](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/dev-workflow#accessibility-check) runs the same check on the page you are looking at.

**What a clean run means**
A machine finds about a third of what makes a page hard to use. A clean run means the easy mistakes are gone, not that the page is accessible.

## Browsers

| Browser | How to pick it |
| --- | --- |
| Chromium | The default |
| Firefox | `-Pbrowser=firefox` |
| WebKit | `-Pbrowser=webkit` |

The same property works for `browserTest`, `svelteRecordTest` and `svelteVerifyA11y`.

Playwright downloads the browser the first time it is used. A fresh Linux machine, such as a CI runner, also lacks system packages that a browser needs. Playwright's own command line installs both, and it is on the suite's classpath, so a small task runs it:

```kotlin
tasks.register<JavaExec>("installBrowsers") {
    classpath = sourceSets["browserTest"].runtimeClasspath
    mainClass = "com.microsoft.playwright.CLI"
    args("install", "--with-deps", providers.gradleProperty("browser").orElse("chromium").get())
}
```

## Full example

A test class that signs in through the API, checks a page as a signed-in user, checks it for accessibility, and runs in CI.

::: code-group

```kotlin no-check [BoardBrowserTest.kt]
import com.microsoft.playwright.assertions.PlaywrightAssertions.assertThat
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.test.BrowserTest
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.test.accessibilityProblems
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.test.problems
import kotlin.test.Test
import kotlin.test.assertEquals

class BoardBrowserTest : BrowserTest() {
    override val environment = mapOf("DATABASE_URL" to "jdbc:h2:mem:board", "ADMIN_PASSWORD" to "secret")

    @Test
    fun `a signed-in user sees their tasks`() {
        val problems = page.problems()
        api.post<Login, User>("/api/session", Login("admin@example.com", "secret"))
        api.post<TaskInput, Task>("/api/tasks", TaskInput(title = "Water the plants"))

        page.navigate(FrontendRoutes.board)

        assertThat(page.getByText("Water the plants")).isVisible()
        assertEquals(emptyList(), page.accessibilityProblems())
        assertEquals(emptyList(), problems)
    }

    @Test
    fun `a visitor is sent to the login page`() {
        page.navigate(FrontendRoutes.board)
        assertThat(page).hasURL(Regex(".*/login\\?next=.*"))
    }
}
```

```yaml [.github/workflows/browser-tests.yml]
name: Browser tests
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  browser-tests:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with:
          distribution: temurin
          java-version: 21
      - uses: gradle/actions/setup-gradle@v4
      - run: ./gradlew installBrowsers
      - run: ./gradlew browserTest svelteVerifyA11y
```

## Use cases

- Check the flows that must never break: sign in, sign up, checkout.
- Catch console errors and 500s that unit tests miss, with `page.problems()`.
- Check pages for accessibility in CI with [`svelteVerifyA11y`](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/checks-and-tooling#svelteverifya11y), and pages behind a login with `accessibilityProblems()`.
- Check the production build itself with the [smoke test](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/deployment#smoke-test), which needs no browser.

Source: https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/deployment

# Deployment

A ktor-svelte app is one JVM process. The frontend is inside the JAR, so there is no Node, no second server and no CORS setup in production.

<Badge type="info" text="Gradle" /> <Badge type="tip" text="Ktor plugin" />

## Quick start

```bash
./gradlew buildFatJar
java -jar build/libs/my-app-all.jar
```

Before the first deploy, run the [smoke test](#smoke-test) and go through the [checklist](#checklist). To watch the app once it runs, see [Monitoring](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/monitoring).

## Build the JAR

Any of Gradle's usual ways to package a Ktor app works, and each one builds the frontend first:

| Task | Comes with | Writes |
|---|---|---|
| `./gradlew buildFatJar` | The Ktor Gradle plugin | One runnable JAR in `build/libs/` |
| `./gradlew shadowJar` | Shadow | One runnable JAR in `build/libs/` |
| `./gradlew installDist` | The `application` plugin | A folder with start scripts and every dependency as its own JAR |

Run it:

```bash
java -jar build/libs/my-app-all.jar
```

The app starts in production mode unless you pass `-Dio.ktor.development=true`. In production:

- a missing frontend build stops the app at startup,
- the dev proxy is off,
- error details are hidden,
- every page gets its Content-Security-Policy.

At startup the app logs which ktor-svelte version and which frontend build it serves:

```text
ktor-svelte 0.9.0 serves frontend build b3f58012c3ff with 19 files
```

The fingerprint is a hash of every file in the build, so two servers with the same fingerprint serve exactly the same frontend. The status endpoint reports the full fingerprint.

**Secrets**
Keep secrets in environment variables, never in `publicConfig` or the frontend. Projects from the setup script read them in `Env.kt` and list them in `.env.example`. [`svelteVerifyLeaks`](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/runtime-config#secrets-in-the-frontend-build) fails the build when a secret value ends up in the frontend.

## Docker

The setup script writes this `Dockerfile` when you choose Docker. It builds the JAR in one stage and runs it as a non-root user in a small JRE image:

```dockerfile
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk AS build
COPY --from=node:24-slim /usr/local/bin/node /usr/local/bin/node
COPY --from=node:24-slim /usr/local/lib/node_modules /usr/local/lib/node_modules
RUN ln -s /usr/local/lib/node_modules/npm/bin/npm-cli.js /usr/local/bin/npm
RUN npm install -g bun
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN chmod +x gradlew && ./gradlew buildFatJar --no-daemon --console=plain
RUN cp build/libs/*-all.jar /app.jar

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
RUN useradd --system --no-create-home app
COPY --from=build /app.jar /app.jar
USER app
ENV PORT=8080
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "/app.jar"]
```

The `RUN npm install -g bun` line installs the package manager the project uses. Keep `node_modules`, `.svelte-kit`, `build` and `.env` out of the image with a `.dockerignore`:

```text
**/node_modules
**/.svelte-kit
**/build
.gradle
.env
```

Build and run it:

```bash
docker build -t my-app .
docker run -p 8080:8080 --env-file .env my-app
```

## Railway

`svelteDeploy` writes the deploy configuration for a host from what the project already knows. For [Railway](https://railway.com) it writes `.railway/railway.ts`, Railway's infrastructure-as-code file:

```bash
./gradlew svelteDeploy
```

```ts
import { defineRailway, github, preserve, project, service } from "railway/iac";

export default defineRailway(() => {
    const app = service("shop", {
        source: github("acme/shop"),
        build: "./gradlew buildFatJar --no-daemon",
        start: "java -jar build/libs/shop-all.jar",
        healthcheck: "/_ktor-svelte/health",
        healthcheckTimeout: 120,
        env: {
            DATABASE_URL: preserve(),
            SESSION_SIGN_KEY: preserve(),
        },
    });

    return project("shop", {
        resources: [app],
    });
});
```

| Part | Where it comes from |
|---|---|
| Names | The Gradle project name. |
| `source` | The `origin` remote, when it is on GitHub. Left out otherwise. |
| `build` and `start` | `buildFatJar` when the Ktor plugin is applied, `shadowJar` with Shadow, `installDist` otherwise. Left out when the project has a `Dockerfile`, because Railway builds with the Dockerfile it finds. |
| `healthcheck` | The built-in health endpoint. Turn it on with `healthEndpoint = true`. |
| `env` | The required variables in [`.env.example`](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/runtime-config#environment-variables). `preserve()` keeps the value you set in Railway, so no secret is written to the file. |

The file is written once and is yours from then on: add a database, replicas or domains to it as Railway's reference describes. Running the task again refuses to replace it unless you pass `--force`.

To use it:

1. Install Railway's package where the file is: `npm install railway`.
2. `railway login`, then `railway link`.
3. Set the listed variables in Railway before the first deploy.
4. `railway config plan` shows what would change, and `railway config apply` does it.

Railway is the only host so far. `--host` exists for the ones to come, and another value says so.

## A plain server

Copy the JAR to the server and run it as a service. A minimal systemd unit:

```ini
[Unit]
Description=my-app
After=network.target

[Service]
User=my-app
EnvironmentFile=/etc/my-app.env
ExecStart=/usr/bin/java -jar /opt/my-app/my-app-all.jar
Restart=on-failure

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

```bash
sudo systemctl enable --now my-app
journalctl -u my-app -f
```

## Behind a reverse proxy

Most deployments put nginx, Caddy, a cloud load balancer or a platform router in front of the app to terminate TLS. Then:

- **Install `XForwardedHeaders` or `ForwardedHeaders`** from `ktor-server-forwarded-header`. The rate limit tells clients apart by their address, and without these plugins every user shares the proxy's address and one limit. The origin check also compares hosts through them.
- **Send HSTS from the proxy**, since only the proxy knows about TLS.
- **Do not compress twice.** The app already compresses API responses and serves precompressed files. Let the proxy pass `Content-Encoding` through.
- **Point health checks at the health endpoint.** Turn it on with `healthEndpoint = true`, and check `GET /_ktor-svelte/health`. See [Built-in endpoints](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/endpoints#health-endpoint).

```kotlin
import io.ktor.server.plugins.forwardedheaders.XForwardedHeaders

install(XForwardedHeaders)
install(Svelte) {
    healthEndpoint = true
}
```

Only install `XForwardedHeaders` when a proxy really sits in front and sets those headers. Otherwise any client can claim another address.

### Caddy

Caddy gets a certificate by itself and sends the `X-Forwarded-*` headers by default:

```text
shop.example.com {
    header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains"
    reverse_proxy localhost:8080
}
```

There is no `encode` line on purpose: the app compresses its own responses.

### nginx

```nginx
server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    http2 on;
    server_name shop.example.com;

    ssl_certificate     /etc/letsencrypt/live/shop.example.com/fullchain.pem;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/shop.example.com/privkey.pem;

    add_header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains" always;

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8080;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Host $host;

        # Server-sent events and WebSockets
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
        proxy_set_header Connection $connection_upgrade;
        proxy_buffering off;
    }
}

map $http_upgrade $connection_upgrade {
    default upgrade;
    ''      close;
}
```

Leave nginx's `gzip` off for this server, which is its default, so responses are not compressed twice. `proxy_buffering off` matters only when your app [streams live updates](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/recipes/live-updates).

## Faster responses

- Add `io.ktor:ktor-server-compression-zstd` to serve API responses with zstd to browsers that accept it. It adds a native library of about 7 MB. See [Transport and compression](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/transport).
- Set `adapter({ precompress: true })` in `frontend/vite.config.ts`, or keep `svelte { precompress = true }`, so files are compressed once at build time instead of on every request.
- Hashed files under `_app/immutable/` are cached for a year, so returning visitors only download what changed after a deploy.

## Request log

The production access log moved to [Monitoring](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/monitoring#request-log).

## Errors from the browser

Reporting frontend errors to the server log moved to [Monitoring](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/monitoring#errors-from-the-browser).

## Page timings

Web vitals from real browsers moved to [Monitoring](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/monitoring#page-timings).

## Build info

The version and commit of a build, on the server and in the browser, moved to [Monitoring](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/monitoring#build-info).

## Smoke test

Tests run the app in development mode, from class folders. What you deploy is a JAR in production mode, and some mistakes only exist there: a frontend that did not make it into the JAR, a page that is no longer prerendered, a variable the app needs to start. `svelteSmokeTest` checks the thing you ship:

```bash
./gradlew svelteSmokeTest
```

```text
ktor-svelte: build/libs/my-app-all.jar runs in production mode on port 55269.
  200  /
  200  /about
  200  /login
  200  /_app/immutable/assets/0.CtcRfiw7.css
  200  GET /api/greeting
  401  GET /api/me
  401  GET /api/tasks
ktor-svelte: the production build answered 3 pages, 1 asset, 3 API routes correctly.
```

The task packages the app the way you do, with `buildFatJar` or `shadowJar` when the project has them and `installDist` otherwise, starts it on a free port without the development flag, and requests:

- Every prerendered page. Each must answer 200 with HTML.
- One file of the frontend build, which must answer 200.
- Every `GET` route of the API that needs no path parameter and no required query parameter. It sends no session, so 401 and 403 are correct answers. A 404 or a server error is not.

Then it stops the app. If anything was answered wrongly, or the app did not start, the build fails and says what happened. The app's output is in `build/ktor-svelte/smoke-test.log`.

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| `--path=/_ktor-svelte/health` | Adds a path that must answer with a status below 400. Can be given more than once |
| `--skip=/api/export` | Leaves an API route out, for a `GET` route that is slow or does something. Can be given more than once |
| `--start-seconds=120` | Gives a slow app more than the 60 seconds it has to start |

```bash
./gradlew svelteSmokeTest --path=/_ktor-svelte/health --skip=/api/export
```

The app gets the environment of the build, so it needs what it needs in production, such as a database. That is why the task is not part of `check`: run it in the pipeline, where that environment exists. The port is passed as the `PORT` variable and as `-port`, which `EngineMain` reads, so an app that takes its port from somewhere else cannot be tested this way.

In GitHub Actions, as a step before the deploy:

```yaml
- name: Smoke test the production JAR
  env:
    DATABASE_URL: ${{ secrets.STAGING_DATABASE_URL }}
    SESSION_SIGN_KEY: ${{ secrets.SESSION_SIGN_KEY }}
  run: ./gradlew svelteSmokeTest --path=/_ktor-svelte/health
```

More checks for the pipeline are in [Checks and tooling](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/checks-and-tooling#full-example).

## Checklist

- `./gradlew svelteSmokeTest` passes.
- The JAR was built without `-Psvelte.skip=true` or `-Psvelte.dev=true`.
- The app runs without `-Dio.ktor.development=true`.
- Secrets come from the environment.
- `XForwardedHeaders` is installed when a proxy sits in front.
- `GET /_ktor-svelte/health` answers 200 if your platform checks health.
- Logs reach you: see [Monitoring](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/monitoring).

## Good to know

- A page that shows a blank screen after a deploy usually means something in front of the app caches HTML. See [Troubleshooting](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/reference/troubleshooting#a-page-shows-a-blank-screen-after-a-deploy).
- `./gradlew svelteConfig` scores your setup for security and operations and suggests what to turn on. See [Review your configuration](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/reference/gradle#review-your-configuration).

Source: https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/monitoring

# Monitoring

What a running ktor-svelte app tells you in production: one log line per request, errors that happen in your visitors' browsers, how fast pages feel, which build is running, and whether the app is healthy.

<Badge type="tip" text="Ktor plugin" /> <Badge type="warning" text="Generated client" />

## Quick start

Everything on this page is off by default. Turn on what you need:

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    accessLog = true
    frontendErrors()
    webVitals()
    healthEndpoint = true
}
```

| Setting | You get | Where it shows up |
|---|---|---|
| `accessLog = true` | [One line per request](#request-log) | Logger `ktor-svelte.access` |
| `frontendErrors()` | [Uncaught errors from browsers](#errors-from-the-browser) | Logger `ktor-svelte.frontend` |
| `webVitals()` | [Page timings from real visits](#page-timings) | `svelteMetrics.webVitals`, status endpoint |
| `healthEndpoint = true` | [Up or down for load balancers](#health-and-status-endpoints) | `GET /_ktor-svelte/health` |
| `statusEndpoint = true` | [Build, proxy and refusal details](#health-and-status-endpoints) | `GET /_ktor-svelte/status` |
| `publicBuildInfo = true` | [Version and commit in the browser](#build-info) | `loadBuildInfo()` |

## Request log

To see every request in your production logs, turn the access log on:

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    accessLog = true
}
```

```text
method=GET path=/api/notes status=200 ms=12 id=8b0c6a52-5f0e-4a51-9a7e-0e5d6f0c1a2b
method=POST path=/api/notes status=422 ms=3 id=1f3e9d10-7c44-4d3b-b0a1-9a2f4e6c8d70
```

- Each line has the method, the path, the status, how long the app took in milliseconds, and the [request ID](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/calling-the-api#request-ids) that the browser also shows for a failed call.
- The query string is left out, because it can hold secrets.
- Requests for build assets under `/_app/` are not logged.
- The lines go to the logger `ktor-svelte.access` at INFO, so your logging config decides where they end up and can turn them off again.
- Development mode never logs these, since the dev log and the [dev panel](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/dev-workflow#request-log) already show requests.

## Errors from the browser

An error in the browser happens on someone else's computer, and in production nobody tells you about it. Turn reporting on and it reaches the log of your app:

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    frontendErrors()
}
```

```text
WARN  ktor-svelte.frontend Frontend error on /board: TypeError: x is not a function (at save (app.js:1:2))
WARN  ktor-svelte.frontend Frontend error on /notes: ApiError: Request to /api/notes failed with status 503, after the API call with request ID 9f2c41
```

The generated client then reports every error that nothing caught:

- uncaught exceptions,
- promises that were rejected and never handled,
- errors SvelteKit caught while loading or rendering a page.

Each line names the page, the first place in the stack, and for a failed API call its [request ID](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/calling-the-api#request-ids), so you can find the same request in the server's own log. Failed calls that the server answered with a 4xx are left out: those are answers, not faults.

### Limits

It is off by default, because it adds an endpoint that anyone can post to, `POST /_ktor-svelte/errors`. That endpoint is kept small:

- One browser reports an error once, and at most ten different errors per page load.
- One client address may send ten reports a minute. The rest get a 429.
- A report may be 8 KB.
- What is logged is cut to one line of limited length, so a report cannot write lines of its own into your log.
- The page is logged without its query string.

| Setting | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `perClientPerMinute` | `10` | Reports one client address may send per minute. At least 1 |
| `maxBodyBytes` | `8192` | Largest report in bytes, between 256 and 65536 |

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    frontendErrors {
        perClientPerMinute = 30
    }
}
```

The lines go to the logger `ktor-svelte.frontend` at `WARN`, so your logging setup decides where they end up. In development the browser's console already [reaches the dev log](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/dev-workflow#browser-console-in-the-server-log), and this works there too.

## Page timings

Your API's slow calls show in the server's log. A slow page does not: its time is spent in the browser. `webVitals` has browsers report it:

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    webVitals()
}
```

One page load in ten then measures the usual five timings and sends them once, when the page is left:

| Name | What it measures | Good up to | Poor above |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `TTFB` | Time until the first byte of the page arrived | 800 ms | 1800 ms |
| `FCP` | Time until something was painted | 1800 ms | 3000 ms |
| `LCP` | Time until the largest element was painted | 2500 ms | 4000 ms |
| `INP` | The slowest reaction to a click or a key | 200 ms | 500 ms |
| `CLS` | How much the layout moved while loading | 0.1 | 0.25 |

### Web vitals in metrics

The app adds them to its metrics, per page:

```kotlin
application.svelteMetrics.webVitals.forEach { vital ->
    println("${vital.page} ${vital.name}: ${vital.count} loads, average ${vital.average}, ${vital.poor} poor")
}
```

Each entry has the `page`, the `name`, a `count`, the `average`, and how many loads were `good`, `needsImprovement` and `poor`. Hand them to your metrics system from there. The [status endpoint](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/endpoints#status-endpoint) lists them too, under `webVitals`.

Pages are grouped by route and not by address: `/notes/my-first-note` counts for `/notes/[slug]` when that is one of your `paramRoutes`, and a segment that is a number or an id becomes `[id]`. At most 100 pages are kept, and the rest are counted together.

### Limits

Like error reporting, this is off by default, because it adds an endpoint anyone can post to, `POST /_ktor-svelte/vitals`:

| Setting | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `sampleRate` | `0.1` | Share of page loads that report. Above 0 and at most 1 |
| `perClientPerMinute` | `10` | Reports one client address may send per minute. At least 1 |

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    webVitals {
        sampleRate = 0.25
    }
}
```

A report may be 2 KB, only the five names are accepted, and only values that a real page could have.

The timings are measured with the browser's own `PerformanceObserver`, with no extra package. They are close to what the `web-vitals` library reports, not identical: `INP` here is the slowest interaction of the page load. The numbers are kept in memory and start again when the app restarts.

## Refused requests

ktor-svelte counts every request its guards refused, so attacks and misconfigurations show up as numbers. Read them from `application.svelteMetrics`:

| Counter | Counts |
|---|---|
| `crossOriginRefusals` | Writes refused by the origin check |
| `bodyTooLargeRefusals` | Bodies over `maxApiBodySize` |
| `rateLimitRefusals` | Requests over a rate limit |

The status endpoint reports them under `refusals`. How to bind them to Micrometer is in [API request guards](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/security#api-request-guards).

## Startup log

In production, the app logs which ktor-svelte version and which frontend build it serves, and nothing more:

```text
ktor-svelte 0.9.0 serves frontend build b3f58012c3ff with 19 files
```

The fingerprint is a hash of every file in the build, so two servers with the same fingerprint serve exactly the same frontend. The status endpoint reports the full fingerprint.

In development the app logs more: [the settings in effect](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/dev-workflow#settings-at-startup) and [what the startup time was spent on](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/dev-workflow#startup-timing), with the parts you named with `startupStep`. `startupStep` costs nothing in production, so you can leave it in your module.

## Build info

Every build knows what it is. The Gradle plugin writes the project's `version`, the git commit and the time of that commit into the JAR (the `svelteBuildInfo` task), and the app reads them without any setup:

```kotlin
get("/api/about") {
    val build = call.application.buildInfo
    call.respondText("Version ${build.version} (${build.shortCommit})")
}
```

| Property | What it is |
|---|---|
| `version` | The project's `version` from `build.gradle.kts` |
| `commit` | The full git commit |
| `shortCommit` | Its first seven characters |
| `time` | The time of that commit, as an `Instant` |

`version`, `commit` and `time` are `null` when the build could not know them: no `version` in `build.gradle.kts`, or no git repository. The time is the commit's, not the clock's, so building the same commit twice gives the same JAR.

### In the browser

The browser can read the same values once you allow it:

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    publicBuildInfo = true
}
```

```ts
import { loadBuildInfo } from '#api';

const build = await loadBuildInfo();
const label = `${build.version ?? 'dev'} (${build.commit?.slice(0, 7) ?? 'no commit'})`;
```

The values are served at `/_ktor-svelte/build.json`. It is off by default, because it tells every visitor which version and commit is running. For values only signed-in users or admins should see, leave it off and return `buildInfo` from a route of your own.

## Health and status endpoints

Two built-in endpoints answer the questions a platform and an operator ask:

| Endpoint | Turn on | Answers | Who may ask |
|---|---|---|---|
| `GET /_ktor-svelte/health` | `healthEndpoint = true` | `200 {"status":"up"}` or `503 {"status":"down"}` | Everyone |
| `GET /_ktor-svelte/status` | `statusEndpoint = true` | Build, dev proxy, refusals and web vitals as JSON | This machine, or whom you [allow](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/endpoints#who-may-see-internal-endpoints) |

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    healthEndpoint = true
    healthCheck { database.isReachable() }
}
```

Every `healthCheck` must return `true` for the app to be up. Details are on [Built-in endpoints](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/endpoints#health-endpoint).

## Full example

A production setup that writes the access log to its own file, reports browser errors, exports refusals to Micrometer and lets an admin page show page timings:

::: code-group

```kotlin no-check [Monitoring.kt]
@Serializable
data class VitalRow(val page: String, val name: String, val average: Double, val poor: Long)

fun Application.monitoring() {
    install(Svelte) {
        accessLog = true
        frontendErrors()
        webVitals { sampleRate = 0.2 }
        healthEndpoint = true
        healthCheck { database.isReachable() }
    }

    val metrics = svelteMetrics
    registry.gauge("svelte.refusals", listOf(Tag.of("reason", "cross_origin")), metrics) { it.crossOriginRefusals.toDouble() }
    registry.gauge("svelte.refusals", listOf(Tag.of("reason", "rate_limit")), metrics) { it.rateLimitRefusals.toDouble() }

    routing {
        get("/api/admin/vitals") {
            call.respond(metrics.webVitals.map { VitalRow(it.page, it.name, it.average, it.poor) })
        }
    }
}
```

```xml [logback.xml]
<configuration>
    <appender name="STDOUT" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
        <encoder><pattern>%d{HH:mm:ss.SSS} %-5level %logger{36} %msg%n</pattern></encoder>
    </appender>
    <appender name="ACCESS" class="ch.qos.logback.core.FileAppender">
        <file>logs/access.log</file>
        <encoder><pattern>%d{ISO8601} %msg%n</pattern></encoder>
    </appender>

    <logger name="ktor-svelte.access" level="INFO" additivity="false">
        <appender-ref ref="ACCESS" />
    </logger>
    <logger name="ktor-svelte.frontend" level="WARN" />

    <root level="INFO">
        <appender-ref ref="STDOUT" />
    </root>
</configuration>
```

Guard `/api/admin` with a [permission](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/auth#permissions) so only admins see it.

## Use cases

- Find the request behind a bug report: the browser shows the request ID, the access log has it.
- Notice a broken deploy before users write to you: frontend errors in the server log.
- See which pages feel slow on real devices: page timings per route.
- Tell which build is running on which server: build info and the frontend fingerprint.
- Let a load balancer or orchestrator take a sick instance out: the health endpoint.

## Good to know

- `frontendErrors()` and `webVitals()` each add an endpoint anyone can post to. Both are rate limited and size limited, which is why they are off until you ask.
- Page timings are kept in memory per instance. With several instances, collect them from each one.
- The access log and the frontend error log are ordinary loggers: route, filter or silence them in your logging configuration.

Source: https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/recipes/

# Recipes

Complete, step-by-step answers to tasks most apps need. Each recipe starts from what you want to build, shows the Kotlin and the Svelte side together, and uses only Ktor, SvelteKit and what ktor-svelte already does, so you can copy it and adapt the names.

## Pick a recipe

| You want to... | Recipe | Level | Time |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Go from a Kotlin class to a table, a detail page and forms | [CRUD in minutes](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/recipes/crud-in-minutes) | Beginner | 10 min |
| Let people sign in and stay signed in | [Sign in with a session cookie](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/recipes/sessions) | Beginner | 20 min |
| Give users roles that decide what they may do | [A role-based app](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/recipes/role-based-app) | Intermediate | 30 min |
| Add pages and routes that only admins can use | [Add an admin area](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/recipes/admin-area) | Intermediate | 20 min |
| Accept files with progress and shared size and type rules | [Upload files](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/recipes/uploads) | Beginner | 15 min |
| Show long lists one page at a time | [Page through long lists](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/recipes/pagination) | Beginner | 15 min |
| Update results while someone types | [Search as you type](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/recipes/search-as-you-type) | Beginner | 10 min |
| Push changes from the server to open pages | [Stream live updates](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/recipes/live-updates) | Intermediate | 15 min |
| Offer the site in several languages, with local dates and prices | [A multilingual site](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/recipes/multilingual-site) | Intermediate | 30 min |

## Build an app from them

The recipes fit together. A typical team app uses them in this order:

1. [CRUD in minutes](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/recipes/crud-in-minutes) for the first resource.
2. [Sign in with a session cookie](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/recipes/sessions) to put it behind a login.
3. [A role-based app](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/recipes/role-based-app) and [Add an admin area](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/recipes/admin-area) when not everyone may do everything.
4. [Page through long lists](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/recipes/pagination) and [Search as you type](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/recipes/search-as-you-type) once the lists grow.
5. [Upload files](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/recipes/uploads), [Stream live updates](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/recipes/live-updates) and [A multilingual site](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/recipes/multilingual-site) as the app needs them.

`examples/showcase` is such an app: a team board with sign-in, roles, an admin area, uploads, paged tables and two languages. Read its source next to the recipes, or see [Examples](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/examples).

## Smaller answers

Some tasks are a few lines and live on the feature pages:

| You want to... | Where |
| --- | --- |
| Keep a typed value in a cookie | [Typed cookies](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/recipes/sessions#typed-cookies) |
| Ask for consent before setting a cookie | [Cookie consent](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/recipes/sessions#cookie-consent) |
| Warn before a session ends | [When the session ends](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/auth#when-the-session-ends) |
| Check one field on the server while someone types | [Checks only the server can make](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/validation#checks-only-the-server-can-make) |
| Show a message from a route as a toast | [Toasts from the server](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/calling-the-api#toasts-from-the-server) |
| Check health from a load balancer | [Health endpoint](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/endpoints#health-endpoint) |

Source: https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/recipes/crud-in-minutes

# CRUD in minutes

You want to manage a list of things, such as books, customers or products: a table of them, a page per item, a form to add one and a form to change one, with a delete button. This recipe goes from a Kotlin class to working pages with two Gradle commands, and leaves you with ordinary files to redesign.

**Time:** about 10 minutes. **Level:** beginner. **You need:** an app with `generateTs = true`. `routes()` and `i18n` are used when they are on, and are not required.

What you use:

- [`resource`](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/typescript#resource-routes) on the server: five conventional routes, typed end to end.
- [`svelteAdd --crud`](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/routes#pages-for-a-class): list, detail and form pages written from the generated client.

## Step 1: the classes

One class for what the API returns, one for what a form sends. Bounds on the input class reach the browser, so the form checks the same rules as the server:

```kotlin no-check [Books.kt]
@Serializable
data class Book(
    val id: Int,
    val title: String,
    val author: String,
    val pages: Int,
    val inStock: Boolean,
)

@Serializable
data class BookInput(
    @JsonSchema.MinLength(1) @JsonSchema.MaxLength(120) val title: String,
    @JsonSchema.MinLength(1) val author: String,
    @JsonSchema.Minimum(1.0) val pages: Int = 1,
    val inStock: Boolean = true,
)
```

The pages need an `id` field to tell one item from another.

## Step 2: a store

Any storage works: a database table, Exposed, a file. For the recipe, a map:

```kotlin no-check [Books.kt]
class BookStore {
    private val ids = AtomicInteger()
    private val books = ConcurrentHashMap<Int, Book>()

    fun list(): List<Book> = books.values.sortedBy { it.id }

    fun find(id: Int): Book? = books[id]

    fun create(input: BookInput): Book =
        Book(ids.incrementAndGet(), input.title, input.author, input.pages, input.inStock).also { books[it.id] = it }

    fun update(id: Int, input: BookInput): Book? =
        books.computeIfPresent(id) { _, book ->
            book.copy(title = input.title, author = input.author, pages = input.pages, inStock = input.inStock)
        }

    fun delete(id: Int): Boolean = books.remove(id) != null
}
```

## Step 3: the routes

`resource` registers the five routes with the paths, statuses and names that the generated client expects:

```kotlin no-check [Routes.kt]
fun Route.bookRoutes(store: BookStore) {
    resource<Book, Int>("/api/books") {
        missing<Problem> { Problem("That book does not exist.") }
        list { store.list() }
        get { id -> store.find(id) }
        create<BookInput> { input -> store.create(input) }
        update<BookInput> { id, input -> store.update(id, input) }
        delete { id -> store.delete(id) }
    }
}
```

| Block | Route | Client |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `list { }` | `GET /api/books` | `api.books.list()` |
| `get { id -> }` | `GET /api/books/{id}`, 404 for `null` | `api.books.get(id)` |
| `create<BookInput> { }` | `POST /api/books`, 201 | `api.books.create(input)` |
| `update<BookInput> { id, input -> }` | `PUT /api/books/{id}`, 404 for `null` | `api.books.update(id, input)` |
| `delete { id -> }` | `DELETE /api/books/{id}`, 204, or 404 for `false` | `api.books.delete(id)` |

Call `bookRoutes(BookStore())` inside `routing { }`, then generate the client:

```bash
./gradlew svelteGenerateTs
```

## Step 4: the pages

```bash
./gradlew svelteAdd --crud=Book
```

The task finds the route that lists `Book` and the other four next to it, and writes:

| File | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `frontend/src/routes/books/+page.ts` | Loads the list |
| `frontend/src/routes/books/+page.svelte` | A table of the plain fields, a link to each book, a delete button per row and a link to the new page |
| `frontend/src/routes/books/new/+page.svelte` | The form, which creates a book |
| `frontend/src/routes/books/[id]/+page.ts` | Loads one book |
| `frontend/src/routes/books/[id]/+page.svelte` | The book, the same form filled with it, and a delete button |

It tells you what is left to do. For a detail page that is one line in `install(Svelte)`, so the app serves the page for every id:

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    paramRoutes("/books/[id]")
}
```

Start the app, open `/books`, and add the first book.

## What the pages use

- The form is a [`formState`](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/validation#form-state) of `BookInput`, with its `validate` and, per field, its `bounds`. An empty title is refused in the browser with the server's rule, before any request.
- With [`routes()`](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/routes) on, every link and `goto` is a typed route.
- With [`i18n`](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/frontend-libraries#i18n) on, every text is a message. The keys are added to each locale file in English, and keys that are already there are left alone. Translate them.
- Text, numbers and booleans get an input. Other fields, such as lists and enums, are left out of the form and named in the task's output, and the draft keeps their default.

Which pages appear depends on which routes exist: no `create` means no new page, no `delete` means no delete buttons, and so on.

## Step 5: make them yours

The files have no generated header and are never touched again. Change the table, add a search box, put the form in a dialog. For example, a search that filters as you type needs a query class on the `list` block and a few lines in the page: see [Search as you type](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/recipes/search-as-you-type).

To protect the pages and the API, add one guard. The API under `/api/books` is then closed by the server, and the pages send visitors to the login page:

```kotlin
install(Svelte) {
    guards {
        signedIn("/books")
    }
}
```

See [Page guards](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/auth#page-guards).

## Variants

| You want | Do this |
| --- | --- |
| The pages in another folder | `./gradlew svelteAdd --crud=Book --page=(app)/library` |
| A string id | `resource<Book>("/api/books")` without the second type |
| Only some of the routes | Leave blocks out. A block that is left out is no route, and the task writes no page for it |
| A Kotlin route stub for a single page | `./gradlew svelteAdd --page=books/[id] --route`. See [A new page](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/routes#a-new-page) |

## Good to know

- `svelteAdd --crud` reads the generated client, so run `svelteGenerateTs` first. It stops and says so when there is no client yet, or no route that lists the class.
- It works for routes one level below the API prefix, such as `/api/books`, not `/api/shop/books`.
- It only creates. It refuses when one of its files is already there, and never edits a file of yours.
- `resource` registers ordinary Ktor routes. Other routes of the same thing, such as `POST /api/books/{id}/lend`, go next to it in a normal `route("/api/books") { }`.

Source: https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/recipes/sessions

# Sign in with a session cookie

You want people to sign in with an email and a password, stay signed in across page loads, and land back on the page they wanted after signing in.

**Time:** about 20 minutes. **Level:** beginner. **You need:** an app from the [tutorial](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/tutorial) or `examples/basic`.

The frontend and the API share one origin, so a plain cookie is all you need: no tokens in `localStorage`, no CORS. The origin check that ktor-svelte turns on refuses cross-site writes, which protects the cookie from [cross-site request forgery](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/security#api-request-guards).

What you build:

- `POST /api/session` signs in, `DELETE /api/session` signs out.
- The browser knows the user through `currentUser`.
- Pages under `(app)` need a session, and a visitor is sent to `/login` and back.
- Five sign-in attempts per minute and client.

## Step 1: add the Ktor modules

Add `io.ktor:ktor-server-auth` and `io.ktor:ktor-server-sessions` to your dependencies, in the same version as your other Ktor modules.

## Step 2: the session and the cookie

The session holds only the user's id. Sign the cookie, so nobody can change the id in it:

```kotlin no-check [Auth.kt]
@Serializable
data class UserSession(val userId: String)

fun Application.sessionAuth() {
    install(Sessions) {
        cookie<UserSession>("session") {
            cookie.path = "/"
            cookie.httpOnly = true
            cookie.secure = !this@sessionAuth.developmentMode
            cookie.extensions["SameSite"] = "Lax"
            transform(SessionTransportTransformerMessageAuthentication(hex(System.getenv("SESSION_SIGN_KEY"))))
        }
    }
}
```

- `SESSION_SIGN_KEY` is a long random hex string. Generate it once per environment and keep it out of the repository. `openssl rand -hex 32` makes one.
- `httpOnly` keeps scripts away from the cookie, `secure` sends it over HTTPS only, and `SameSite=Lax` keeps it off most cross-site requests.

## Step 3: Ktor authentication

`authenticate("session")` blocks need a provider. Its challenge answers the API with a 401 and sends pages to the login page:

```kotlin no-check [Auth.kt]
install(Authentication) {
    session<UserSession>("session") {
        validate { session -> session }
        challenge {
            if (call.request.path().startsWith("/api/")) {
                call.respond(HttpStatusCode.Unauthorized, Problem("Sign in first."))
            } else {
                call.respondLoginRedirect()
            }
        }
    }
}
```

`respondLoginRedirect()` sends a visitor who asked for `/board` to `/login?next=%2Fboard`. See [The login page](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/auth#the-login-page).

## Step 4: tell ktor-svelte who is signed in

```kotlin no-check [Application.kt]
install(Svelte) {
    loginPage = "/login"
    currentUser<User> { sessions.get<UserSession>()?.let { users.find(it.userId) } }
    guards {
        signedIn("/board", "/settings")
    }
    rateLimit { limit("login", requests = 5, per = 1.minutes) }
    errorResponse<Problem>(HttpStatusCode.Unauthorized)
}
```

| Line | What it gives you |
| --- | --- |
| `loginPage` | A 401 from the API opens `/login?next=...` in the browser |
| `currentUser` | `currentUser` in the browser, `call.user` and `call.requireUser` in routes |
| `guards` | `/api/board` and `/api/settings` and everything below answer a visitor with 401, and the pages can be guarded with one line |
| `rateLimit` | A named limit for the sign-in route, five attempts per minute and client, on top of the default limit for all API writes |
| `errorResponse` | Adds the 401 to the typed errors of every endpoint, because `authenticate` answers it outside your route |

## Step 5: the routes

```kotlin no-check [Routes.kt]
fun Route.sessionRoutes() {
    rateLimit(RateLimitName("login")) {
        post("/api/session") {
            val login = call.receive<Login>()
            val user = users.check(login.email, login.password)
                ?: return@post call.respond(HttpStatusCode.Unauthorized, Problem("Wrong email or password."))
            call.sessions.set(UserSession(user.id))
            call.currentUserChanged()
            call.respond(user)
        }
    }
    delete("/api/session") {
        call.sessions.clear<UserSession>()
        call.currentUserChanged()
        call.respond(HttpStatusCode.NoContent)
    }
    get("/api/board") {
        val user = call.requireUser<User>()
        call.respond(boards.of(user))
    }
}
```

- `currentUserChanged()` tells the browser to load the user again, before your code continues after the call.
- Store passwords as a slow hash, such as bcrypt or Argon2, never as text. `users.check` compares against the hash.
- Give the same answer for an unknown email and a wrong password, so the form does not tell anyone who has an account.

Call `sessionAuth()` and `sessionRoutes()` from your module, and run `./gradlew svelteGenerateTs` so the client has `api.session.create` and `api.session.delete`.

## Step 6: the login page

`afterLogin` reads the page to go back to from `?next=`, and only ever accepts a path inside your app:

```svelte no-check [login/+page.svelte]
<script lang="ts">
    import { goto } from '$app/navigation';
    import { afterLogin, api, isApiError } from '#api';

    let email = $state('');
    let password = $state('');
    let message = $state('');

    async function signIn(event: SubmitEvent) {
        event.preventDefault();
        try {
            await api.session.create({ email, password });
            await goto(afterLogin('/'));
        } catch (error) {
            if (isApiError(error, 'session.create')) message = error.body.message;
            else throw error;
        }
    }
</script>

<form onsubmit={signIn}>
    <input type="email" autocomplete="username" required bind:value={email} />
    <input type="password" autocomplete="current-password" required bind:value={password} />
    <p role="alert">{message}</p>
    <button type="submit">Sign in</button>
</form>
```

On the login page a 401 means a wrong password, so the client does not redirect there.

## Step 7: guard the pages

Put the pages that need a session in a route group, and guard it in its layout:

```ts no-check [(app)/+layout.ts]
import { signedInUser } from '#api';

export const ssr = false;

export const load = async ({ url }) => ({ user: await signedInUser(url) });
```

A visitor who opens `/board` is sent to `/login?next=%2Fboard`, and after signing in, back to the board. Pages below get the user as `data.user`, never `null`.

## Step 8: show who is signed in, and sign out

```svelte no-check [+layout.svelte]
<script lang="ts">
    import { goto } from '$app/navigation';
    import { api, currentUser } from '#api';

    let { children } = $props();

    async function signOut() {
        await api.session.delete();
        await goto('/login');
    }
</script>

<header>
    {#if currentUser.user}
        <span>{currentUser.user.name}</span>
        <button type="button" onclick={signOut}>Sign out</button>
    {:else if currentUser.ready}
        <a href="/login">Sign in</a>
    {/if}
</header>

{@render children()}
```

## Going further

- **Warn before the session ends:** keep the end in the session and pass `sessionEnds` and `extendSession` to `currentUser`. See [When the session ends](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/auth#when-the-session-ends).
- **Members and admins:** add [permissions](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/auth#permissions), as in [A role-based app](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/recipes/role-based-app).
- **Keep the HTML private too:** [put the frontend behind a login](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/features/auth#put-the-frontend-behind-a-login).
- **Try it in the browser:** `examples/showcase` has all of this, with registration and a session warning.

## Typed cookies

A cookie that both sides use is three things written twice: its name, what its text means, and its options. Declare it once in Kotlin, name it in `install(Svelte)`, and read and write it with its type:

```kotlin
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.clearCookie
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.readCookie
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.typedCookie
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.writeCookie
import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.days

enum class Density { Comfortable, Compact }

val DensityCookie = typedCookie<Density>("density", default = Density.Comfortable, maxAge = 90.days)

install(Svelte) {
    generateTs = true
    cookies(DensityCookie)
}

routing {
    get("/api/density") {
        val density = call.readCookie(DensityCookie)
        call.writeCookie(DensityCookie, Density.Compact)
        call.clearCookie(DensityCookie)
        call.respond(density.toString())
    }
}
```

In the browser, the generated client has the same cookie under `cookies`, with the same name, type and options:

```ts
import { cookies } from '#api';

const density = cookies.density.get(); // 'Comfortable' | 'Compact'
cookies.density.set('Compact');
cookies.density.clear();
```

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `default` | `null` | What a missing or unreadable cookie reads as |
| `maxAge` | a year | How long the browser keeps it. `null` ends it with the browser session |
| `path` | `/` | The cookie's path |
| `sameSite` | `CookieSameSite.Lax` | `Lax`, `Strict` or `None` |
| `secure` | `false` | Only sent over HTTPS |
| `httpOnly` | `false` | Hidden from scripts, and left out of the generated client |
| `category` | `null` | A [consent category](#cookie-consent) |

- A cookie holds a `String`, `Int`, `Long`, `Double`, `Boolean` or an enum.
- A missing cookie, or one whose text does not fit the type, reads as the default, and as null (`undefined` in TypeScript) when there is none. Somebody editing a cookie by hand cannot break a page.
- Both sides write the cookie with the same options.
- A cookie with `httpOnly = true` is left out of the generated client, because a script cannot read it.
- The name in TypeScript is the cookie's name in camel case: `board-mine` is `cookies.boardMine`.
- `get` takes an optional `Cookie` header text, for code that runs where there is no `document`.

**Not for secrets**
Names and values are plain text in the visitor's browser. Do not keep anything in a typed cookie that the visitor must not read or change. For that, use a session.

## Cookie consent

A cookie the site does not need to work, such as one for statistics, may only be set after the visitor agreed. Give such a cookie a category where it is declared:

```kotlin
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.consentsTo
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.typedCookie
import io.github.nijasc.ktor.svelte.writeCookie

val VisitsCookie = typedCookie<Int>("visits", default = 0, category = "analytics")

install(Svelte) {
    generateTs = true
    cookies(VisitsCookie)
}

routing {
    get("/api/visit") {
        call.writeCookie(VisitsCookie, 1)
        if (call.consentsTo("analytics")) call.application.log.info("counted")
        call.respondText("ok")
    }
}
```

From then on, both sides follow the visitor's choice without further code:

- `call.writeCookie` and `cookies.visits.set` do nothing until the visitor has accepted the category.
- `call.readCookie` and `cookies.visits.get` give the default until then, also when an old cookie is still there.
- A cookie without a category is needed for the site to work, and is always read and written.

The generated client has the choice as `cookieConsent`, with the categories of all declared cookies:

```ts
import { cookieConsent } from '#api';

cookieConsent.decided(); // false until the visitor chose
cookieConsent.allows('analytics');
cookieConsent.accept(); // everything
cookieConsent.accept(['analytics']); // only these
cookieConsent.refuse();
cookieConsent.reset(); // ask again
```

Refusing a category, or leaving it out, also removes its cookies from the browser. `cookieConsent` is a Svelte store, so `$cookieConsent.accepted` in a component follows the choice, for a script that should only load after consent.

To ask the visitor, show the banner once, in the root layout:

```svelte
<script lang="ts">
    import { onMount } from 'svelte';
    import { cookieConsent } from '#api';

    onMount(() =>
        cookieConsent.banner({
            text: 'We use cookies to count visits.',
            accept: 'Accept all',
            refuse: 'Only what is needed',
            labels: { analytics: 'Statistics' },
            save: 'Save my choice',
            link: { href: '/privacy', text: 'Privacy' }
        })
    );
</script>
```

- The banner appears only while the visitor has not chosen.
- `labels` and `save` are optional: with them, each labelled category gets a checkbox and there is a third button.
- All text is yours, so it can come from your translations.
- It is a plain bar at the bottom of the page with the class `ktor-svelte-consent`, and its buttons carry daisyUI's `btn` classes. For your own design, build a component on `cookieConsent` and leave `banner` out.
- A settings page can call `cookieConsent.reset()` and show the banner again.

On the server, `call.cookieConsent` is the set of accepted categories, or null while the visitor has not chosen, and `call.consentsTo("analytics")` asks for one.

The choice is kept for 180 days in a cookie named `cookie-consent`, which itself needs no consent. This helper keeps the choice and follows it for typed cookies. It cannot know about cookies that other scripts set, and which cookies need consent where you operate is a legal question it does not answer.

Source: https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/recipes/role-based-app

# A role-based app

You want users with roles, such as viewers, editors and admins, where each role may do different things. The API must refuse what a role may not do, the pages must not offer it, and both must follow one rule that you write once.

**Time:** about 30 minutes. **Level:** intermediate. **You need:** a sign-in, as in [Sign in with a session cookie](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/recipes/sessions).

What you build:

- A `Role` on each user, and a `Permission` enum that says what each role may do.
- Permissions checked on the server, and the same names in the browser through `can`.
- Pages that need a session, and an admin page that needs a permission, declared once with guards.
- An admin page that changes roles, which never removes the last admin.

`examples/showcase` is a complete app built this way. Its `Auth.kt`, `Application.kt` and `(app)/admin` pages are the reference for this recipe.

## Step 1: roles and permissions

Roles describe people. Permissions describe actions. Keep them apart: a role is stored on the user, and the permissions of a role are a function in code, so a new role or a changed rule is one line.

```kotlin no-check [Model.kt]
@Serializable
enum class Role { ADMIN, EDITOR, VIEWER }

enum class Permission { EditTasks, DeleteAnyTask, ManageUsers }

@Serializable
data class User(
    val id: Int,
    val name: String,
    val email: String,
    val role: Role,
    val active: Boolean,
)

fun permissionsOf(user: User): Set<Permission> =
    when (user.role) {
        Role.ADMIN -> Permission.entries.toSet()
        Role.EDITOR -> setOf(Permission.EditTasks)
        Role.VIEWER -> emptySet()
    }
```

`User` is what the browser sees, so it has the role but no password hash.

## Step 2: tell ktor-svelte

```kotlin no-check [Application.kt]
install(Svelte) {
    loginPage = FrontendRoutes.login
    currentUser<User> {
        sessions.get<UserSession>()?.let { users.findActive(it.userId) }
    }
    permissions<Permission, User>(refusedMessage = { "Your role does not allow that." }) { user -> permissionsOf(user) }
    guards {
        signedIn(FrontendRoutes.board, "/tasks")
        permission(Permission.ManageUsers, FrontendRoutes.admin)
    }
    errorResponse<Problem>(HttpStatusCode.Unauthorized, HttpStatusCode.Forbidden)
}
```

| Line | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `currentUser` | Finds the user. `findActive` returns `null` for a deactivated account, so it is signed out at once |
| `permissions` | One function from a user to what they may do, for the server and the browser |
| `refusedMessage` | The text of every 403 that a permission check sends |
| `guards` | `/api/board`, `/api/tasks` and below need a session, `/api/admin` and below need `ManageUsers`. The pages follow the same rule |
| `errorResponse` | Puts the 401 and 403 into the generated error types |

## Step 3: check the actions on the server

The guards close whole paths. Actions inside a path that all signed-in users share need their own check:

```kotlin no-check [TaskRoutes.kt]
fun Route.taskRoutes(tasks: TaskStore) {
    route("/api/tasks") {
        get { call.respond(tasks.all()) } // every signed-in user, through the guard

        post {
            call.requirePermission(Permission.EditTasks)
            call.respond(HttpStatusCode.Created, tasks.create(call.receive<TaskInput>(), call.requireUser<User>()))
        }

        delete("/{id}") {
            val user = call.requireUser<User>()
            val task = tasks.find(call.parameters["id"]) ?: return@delete call.respond(HttpStatusCode.NotFound)
            if (task.creatorId != user.id && !call.can(Permission.DeleteAnyTask)) {
                return@delete call.respond(HttpStatusCode.Forbidden, Problem("Only the creator or an admin can delete this task."))
            }
            tasks.delete(task.id)
            call.respond(HttpStatusCode.NoContent)
        }
    }
}
```

| Check | Use it for |
| --- | --- |
| A guard | A whole area, such as `/api/admin` |
| `requires(Permission.X) { }` | A group of routes outside a guarded path |
| `call.requirePermission(Permission.X)` | One route |
| `call.can(Permission.X)` | A rule with more to it, such as "the creator, or anyone who may delete any task" |

## Step 4: the same rule in the pages

The browser gets the enum and `can`. Show what the user may do, and nothing else:

```svelte no-check [tasks/[id]/+page.svelte]
<script lang="ts">
    import { goto } from '$app/navigation';
    import { api, can, currentUser, Permission } from '#api';
    import type { PageProps } from './$types';

    let { data }: PageProps = $props();

    const mayDelete = $derived(data.task.creator.id === currentUser.user?.id || can(Permission.DeleteAnyTask));

    async function remove() {
        await api.tasks.delete(data.task.id);
        await goto('/tasks');
    }
</script>

<h1>{data.task.title}</h1>

{#if can(Permission.EditTasks)}
    <a href="/tasks/{data.task.id}/edit">Edit</a>
{/if}
{#if mayDelete}
    <button type="button" onclick={remove}>Delete</button>
{/if}
```

- `can` is reactive and comes with the current user, so the buttons change when someone signs in, signs out or gets another role, with no request of its own.
- Rename a permission in Kotlin, and every `can` with the old name fails `svelteCheck`.
- Every button that `can` hides still has its check on the route. The browser decides what is shown, the server what is allowed.

## Step 5: guard the pages

All signed-in pages live in one route group, and its layout guards them:

```ts no-check [(app)/+layout.ts]
import { signedInUser } from '#api';

export const prerender = false;
export const ssr = false;

export const load = async ({ url }) => ({ user: await signedInUser(url) });
```

A visitor goes to the login page and back. A viewer who opens `/admin` gets your error page with a 403, because the guard on `/admin` asks for `ManageUsers`.

The menu only lists what the user may open, from the same guards:

```svelte no-check [+layout.svelte]
<script lang="ts">
    import { can, currentUser, matchGuard, pageGuards } from '#api';
    import { nav } from '#routes';

    const links = $derived(
        nav.filter((item) => {
            const guard = matchGuard(pageGuards, item.to());
            if (!guard) return !currentUser.user;
            return currentUser.user !== null && (!guard.permission || can(guard.permission));
        })
    );
</script>

<nav>
    {#each links as link (link.to.id)}
        <a href={link.to()}>{link.title()}</a>
    {/each}
</nav>
```

## Step 6: change roles in the admin area

The admin page lists users and changes their role. Its routes are under `/api/admin`, so the guard already protects them. One rule is left: never remove the last admin, or nobody can manage users any more. Give that error a name, so the page can tell it apart:

::: code-group

```kotlin no-check [AdminRoutes.kt]
enum class AccountError { LastAdmin }

@Serializable
data class RoleChange(val role: Role)

fun Route.adminRoutes(users: UserStore) {
    route("/api/admin") {
        get("/users") { call.respond(users.all()) }

        put("/users/{id}/role") {
            val change = call.receive<RoleChange>()
            val target = users.find(call.parameters["id"]?.toIntOrNull() ?: -1)
                ?: return@put call.respond(HttpStatusCode.NotFound, Problem("No such user."))
            if (target.role == Role.ADMIN && change.role != Role.ADMIN && users.admins() <= 1) {
                return@put call.respondError(AccountError.LastAdmin, HttpStatusCode.Conflict)
            }
            val user = users.setRole(target.id, change.role)
            if (target.id == call.requireUser<User>().id) call.currentUserChanged()
            call.respond(user)
        }
    }
}

// in install(Svelte):
// errorCodes<AccountError> { _, code -> when (code) { AccountError.LastAdmin -> "Keep at least one admin." } }
```

```svelte no-check [(app)/admin/+page.svelte]
<script lang="ts">
    import { api, ErrorCode, hasErrorCode, Role, type User } from '#api';
    import type { PageProps } from './$types';

    let { data }: PageProps = $props();
    let users = $derived<User[]>(data.users);
    let message = $state('');

    async function setRole(user: User, select: HTMLSelectElement) {
        message = '';
        try {
            const changed = await api.admin.putUsersRole(user.id, { role: select.value as Role }, { silent: true });
            users = users.map((item) => (item.id === changed.id ? changed : item));
        } catch (error) {
            select.value = user.role;
            if (hasErrorCode(error, ErrorCode.LastAdmin)) message = error.body.message;
            else throw error;
        }
    }
</script>

<p role="alert">{message}</p>
<table>
    {#each users as user (user.id)}
        <tr>
            <th scope="row">{user.name}</th>
            <td>
                <select value={user.role} onchange={(event) => setRole(user, event.currentTarget)}>
                    <option value={Role.ADMIN}>Admin</option>
                    <option value={Role.EDITOR}>Editor</option>
                    <option value={Role.VIEWER}>Viewer</option>
                </select>
            </td>
        </tr>
    {/each}
</table>
```

The page load and the error page for a 403 are the same as in [Add an admin area](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/recipes/admin-area#step-4-the-admin-pages).

## Check it

1. Sign in as a viewer. The board shows no Edit or Delete buttons, and the menu has no Admin link.
2. Open `/admin` by hand. You see the 403 page.
3. Call the API directly: `curl -X POST /api/tasks` with the viewer's cookie answers 403 with "Your role does not allow that."
4. Sign in as the only admin and try to make yourself a viewer. The page says "Keep at least one admin."

The [Kotlin browser test kit](https://nijasc.github.io/ktor-svelte/main/guide/browser-tests) can run these steps on every build.

## Good to know

- Store the role, not the permissions. Then changing what an editor may do is a code change that applies to every editor at once.
